Join the rites in the plaza before the mound
Watch the shaman dance in a jaguar skin
Plant maize, beans and squash on the riverbank land
Chase the parrots from the maize
Raise the dogs and gather turtle eggs
Play with the puppies
Paddle a canoe after fish and turtles
Catch shrimp at the riverbank
Heap earth for a house platform above the floods
Trade with the merchants who come by canoe
Listen to the elders tell of people who became jaguars
Listen to grandmother’s stories of the forest animals
Lie under the stars and count the days to the rains
At the edge of the marsh an animal as big as three pigs put together walks out of the forest. Its nose stretches into a short trunk that twitches this way and that.
The tapir is Central America’s largest land animal, weighing over 300 kilograms. It is a distant cousin of horses and rhinos. Only a few thousand remain today, and it is endangered.
Before dawn a roar fills the forest like a hundred jaguars. You cling to your mother, who laughs and points up into the trees: a troop of small black monkeys.
Howler monkeys are among the loudest land animals on Earth; their calls carry for kilometres. Mexico’s howlers are endangered today as their forests are cut.
A little animal in jointed armour scuttles across your path and digs itself into the ground in a blink.
The nine-banded armadillo always gives birth to four young at once, and all four are identical twins from a single egg.
Your father paddles slowly, then points into the water. A huge grey back rises to breathe, with whiskers round its mouth like a grandfather’s.

The Antillean manatee grazes on plants in rivers and coastal lagoons; its closest living relatives are elephants. In 1493 Columbus wrote of seeing “mermaids” less beautiful than the stories said, probably manatees. Today they are endangered.
A gold-and-black furred animal climbs a tree and flicks a tongue as long as your arm into an ants’ nest, sending the ants scurrying.
The tamandua anteater has no teeth at all. Its sticky tongue, about 40 centimetres long, laps up thousands of ants and termites a day.
A band of a dozen long-nosed animals, tails held straight up, raids the village for fallen fruit until every dog is barking.
White-nosed coatis travel in bands of mothers and young, while males mostly live alone. Their upright tails help the band keep sight of one another in tall grass.
The first strange animal
Creep closer
It stops and looks at you for a moment, then vanishes into the forest. You tell everyone about it for days.
Run to fetch your friends
By the time everyone arrives it has gone. No one believes you until your father nods.
The ball that bounces
The children knock a small black rubber ball back and forth with their hips, no hands allowed. It bounces higher than your head.

The oldest rubber balls in the world come from the spring of El Manatí, in Olmec country, about 3,600 years old. They were made from tree latex dried into thin strips and wound round a core. Europeans had never seen bouncing rubber until they reached the Americas some three thousand years later.
Play until dark
Your hips are bruised all over, but you hit the ball three times in a row.
Ask the rubber maker to teach you
Your first ball is lopsided and bounces the wrong way, but it bounces.
The giant toad
A toad as big as your father’s hand sits by the house. The grown-ups shout at you not to touch it: it has poison behind its eyes.
The giant toad has poison glands behind its eyes. Toad bones turn up at several Olmec sites, and some scholars suggest its venom was used in rites, but this is only a guess.
Poke it with a stick
It puffs itself up, then hops slowly away as if you did not matter at all.
Pick it up to show your friends
Your hands go numb, your eyes sting, and you are sick all night. Your mother says nothing but “I told you.”
The jaguar baby
Grandmother gives you a clay figure of a plump baby with a snarling jaguar mouth. Long ago, she says, a woman had a child by a jaguar.

Olmec art is full of “were-jaguar” babies with snarling, down-turned mouths. Scholars read them differently: a rain god, a shaman transforming. The story of a woman and a jaguar ✦ is only one explanation.
Keep it by your bed
Every night you turn its face to the door so it can keep watch.
Ask whether jaguars still have children with people
Grandmother laughs until she coughs, and tells you to go and ask the shaman yourself.
The carver’s helper
The stone sculptors need strong young hands to pound basalt with hammerstones, day and night for months, until your ears ring.
Become a helper
In your first year you never touch the face, but you learn where the stone breaks easily.
Keep helping in the fields
Taming a peccary
You caught a baby peccary and raised it until it was grown. Now you want it to carry the maize baskets instead of your own back.

The Americas had only a few truly domesticated animals: dogs, and later turkeys; in the Andes, llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs. Peccaries live in fierce herds and will not breed in pens; a tapir carries its young for more than a year and has one at a time. There was no large animal that could pull a plough or a cart.
Tie a basket on its back
It shakes the basket off, bites your leg, and bolts into the forest for good.
Keep it as a companion instead
It follows you everywhere like a dog, until one day it hears a herd in the forest and never comes back.
Your family and a family from an upriver village talk of a marriage. They would like a jade bead.

We know very little about Olmec families, since there are no records we can read. What we know comes from houses, graves and buried offerings, such as jades often found in the mouth or on the body of the dead.
The wedding has dog meat, roast fish and a frothy cacao drink.
Dragging the great stone
The ruler orders every village to send people to move a basalt boulder heavier than ten houses, from the foot of the mountains down to the river, then onto rafts to the town.

No one knows for sure how the Olmec moved stones of tens of tons. Most likely hundreds of people hauled them on log rollers and floated them on great rafts down the rivers, with no wheels, no draft animals and no metal tools.
Go and haul
A roller slips and the stone slides onto your foot. You limp for months.
Helped haul the stone for a colossal head
For a month you sing in time with three hundred others, until the stone is on the raft.
Send food instead
The haulers eat every grain of your maize and ask for more.
The sacred spring
At the spring below the hill of El Manatí, people throw rubber balls, jade axes and carved wooden figures into the water as offerings. Your family must decide what to give.
At El Manatí, mud under the water preserved offerings for more than 3,000 years: the world’s oldest rubber balls, jade axes and carved wooden busts, things that almost never survive in the tropics.
Offer your best rubber ball
Made an offering at the spring of El Manatí
The ball sinks slowly into the brown water. You ask for the rains to come in season.
Offer grandfather’s jade axe
The green jade disappears into the mud. Three thousand years later someone will dig it up.
The riverbank land
The ruler’s men come to say that the riverbank land your family has farmed for three generations must now give half its maize to the ruler.
Give the share
Half the maize goes to the ruler’s stores, and your family must plant the higher ground, which yields less.
Move to clear land on another river
No one has claimed the new land yet, but it takes three years to farm it well.
The bitter drink
At the ruler’s feast a servant pours cacao from high up into a pot to make it froth, then hands it to you. It is bitter, with no sugar at all.

Scientists have found traces of cacao in pots from the Olmec region more than 3,000 years old. Cacao was drunk bitter at rites and feasts long before anyone added sugar, which arrived from the Old World after 1500.
Drain the cup
You pull a face; the host laughs and pours you another.
Ask for cacao beans to plant
The servant looks at you as if you had asked for gold.
The journey to the highlands
The merchants will walk thirty days over the mountains to trade for black obsidian and iron ore for mirrors. Everything goes on their backs.
Obsidian found in Olmec towns came from several highland volcanoes hundreds of kilometres away. With no pack animals, each person carried perhaps 20–30 kilograms per trip.
Go with the caravan
You fall on a fog-bound mountain path, break a leg, and spend a season in a strange village.
In the highlands you see a cliff carved with a figure seated in a cave mouth, rain clouds drifting out, just like the patterns on the jades at home.
The caravan comes back with obsidian and stories of cold so sharp it makes your teeth chatter.
Burying the ruler’s face
The shaman says the ruler is dead, and his stone face must be “killed” and buried too. People begin to batter the nose and lips of the colossal head.
Many monuments at San Lorenzo were battered and buried in rows. Scholars still argue whether this was ritual, enemy destruction or revolt.
Help bury it with care
You sprinkle red earth on the stone face before covering it, as you would on a body.
Watch from a distance
You remember that face all your life, though no one will see it again for three thousand years.
The treasure no one may see

Hundreds of people carry green serpentine blocks into a deep pit and lay them in layers, with a jaguar-mask mosaic on top. Then everyone heaps earth over it until it is gone. No one will see it again.
At La Venta archaeologists found “massive offerings”: tons of serpentine carried from far away and buried deep underground, some laid as jaguar-mask mosaics meant to stay hidden for ever.
Help carry the stones
Your shoulders are raw, but you know one of the most beautiful things in the world lies under your feet.
Ask why it must be buried
The shaman answers: “What is given to the gods is not for people to look at.”
Where to go
The island empties a little more each day. Your family must choose: west to Tres Zapotes, where people still live, or up to high ground beyond the floods.
After La Venta fell, Tres Zapotes lived on for centuries. A stone there bears a Long Count date of the Mesoamerican calendar equal to 32 BCE, one of the oldest such dates known.
Go to Tres Zapotes
At Tres Zapotes people still carve stone, but the art is beginning to look different.
Go up to the high ground
No colossal heads, no rulers: only maize fields and the howler monkeys at dawn.
Signs on a stone block
The chief shaman has you help scratch small signs into a pillow-sized serpentine block: maize, fish, insects, boxes, in rows. He says they are words the stone will remember.

In the late 1990s road builders in Veracruz found the “Cascajal block” in a pile of rubble. It carries 62 signs, some repeated. In 2006 scholars proposed it as the oldest writing in the Americas, from about 900 BCE, but because it was found out of its original layer, some still question its age and meaning, and no one can read it.
Carve every sign with care
Carved the signs on the Cascajal block
Your hand shakes, but not one sign goes crooked. The shaman nods once.
Ask what the stone will say
He says only those who can read will know. Three thousand years later, still no one can.
Whose face?
A grandchild stands craning up at the colossal head in the plaza and asks whose face it is.

Most archaeologists think each colossal head is a portrait of one ruler: every face is different and each wears a helmet with its own emblem. The claim, popular online, that they show Africans who crossed the ocean has no evidence behind it; the faces look like the native people of the Gulf Coast today.
Tell the ruler’s name, as you remember it
The child murmurs the name over and over, but no one writes it anywhere, and it vanishes with that generation.
Say it is everyone’s great-grandfather
The child laughs and runs to tell friends that great-grandfather was as big as a house.
The ruler’s face

The ruler sits still all day so you can study his face: full cheeks, thick lips, eyes slightly narrowed. The basalt before you stands almost three metres tall. You must choose whether to carve him as you see him, or as he wants to be seen.
San Lorenzo Colossal Head 1, called “El Rey” (the King) by local people, is almost 3 metres tall and weighs about 25 tons. Its face is so individual that scholars believe it portrays a real person.
Carve him as you see him
Carved the face of “El Rey”
The ruler looks at the stone face for a long time, then says, “Yes. That is me.”
Make him younger and fiercer
The ruler beams. His wife giggles behind him.
The old throne
No new basalt has come for years. The master carver points at the stone throne of the previous ruler and tells you to recarve it into a head of the present one.

Marks on the stone show that some heads, such as San Lorenzo Head 7, were recarved from old thrones, and at La Venta one throne was abandoned halfway through becoming a head. The Olmec recycled scarce stone.
Recarve it
The edge of the old throne still shows on the back of the head, for anyone who looks closely.
Ask to wait for new stone
The master grumbles that you are too soft-hearted and gives the job to someone else.
The mirror that lights fire
You polish black iron ore into a concave disc until it gleams. Turned to the sun, it gathers the light into one point until a dry leaf begins to smoke.

The Olmec made concave mirrors of iron ores such as magnetite, polished until they reflected images and focused light. Rulers probably wore them on the chest; they turn up in graves and offerings at La Venta.
Give it to the ruler
The ruler hangs it on his chest. When he passes, a flash of light catches every eye.
Keep it to look at your own face
For the first time you see your own face clearly, and you are shocked by how big your nose is.
A ball for the great rites
The ruler orders a ball as big as a human head for the great rites. It must bounce well and never split. You must tap latex for a month.

A 2024 study of the El Manatí balls found they were made of latex from the Castilla tree, dried into thin strips and wound layer by layer round a core, then coated with more latex to bind and bounce. The method is much like the one still used in the region today.
Wind it layer by layer, patiently
The ball is so heavy you lift it with both hands. Dropped, it bounces back to your chest, and everyone cheers.
Put a stone inside to make it heavy fast
The ball bounces crooked at the rites, and the ruler looks round for whoever made it.
No one finds out, but you lie awake for many nights.
Becoming the jaguar
At the night rites you wear the jaguar skin and dance round the fire until you drip with sweat. The people believe that tonight you will travel in jaguar form to speak with the ancestors.

Several Olmec figures show a person turning into a jaguar step by step. Scholars read them as shamans believed able to change into animals. Beliefs in an animal double like this are still found in some Indigenous communities in Mexico.
Dance until you fall
You wake at dawn remembering nothing, but everyone says you roared like a real jaguar.
Dance slowly and sing for rain
Three days later it rains. Everyone gives you the credit, though you know the rainy season was due anyway.
This morning paw prints as big as a grown-up’s hand circle the dog pen. One of the dogs is gone.
The jaguar is the most important animal in Olmec art. It swims well and hunts on land and in water. About 4,800 remain in Mexico today.
The biggest eagle you have ever seen drops from the treetops, seizes a monkey and is gone.
The harpy eagle has talons as long as a grizzly bear’s claws and hunts monkeys and sloths. Today it has all but vanished from Mexico.
In the night dozens of sea turtles crawl up the beach to lay their eggs. You help your father fill a basket, but your mother says to leave half.
Every species of sea turtle in the Gulf of Mexico is now endangered or threatened.
A crocodile drags a neighbour’s dog into the river as it bends to drink.
Small bats creep in at night to bite the dogs’ legs. In the morning there are spots of blood on the floor.
Vampire bats are real and live only in the Americas. They feed on animal blood, just a few teaspoons at a time.
The maize ears in the field are only as long as your palm, with small hard kernels. Your mother soaks them in lime water all night before they can be ground.

Maize came from a wild grass called teosinte, with just a few hard-cased kernels. People in Mexico began selecting it about 9,000 years ago, and it took thousands of years for the ears to grow big enough to be a staple. Soaking in lime water releases more of its nutrients.
There is a feast today. Your father kills the fattest dog in the pen.
Animal bones from San Lorenzo show that dogs were an important source of meat. The Americas had no pigs, cattle, goats or sheep, so most meat came from fish, turtles, deer and dogs.
A cold north wind blows for three days and nights. The sea goes wild and no canoe can go out.
People on the Gulf Coast call the winter north-wind storms nortes. They carry cold air from North America down into the tropics.
You stand before a colossal head twice as tall as your father, its face painted red, wearing a helmet carved with jaguar claws.

Seventeen Olmec colossal heads are known: ten from San Lorenzo, four from La Venta, two from Tres Zapotes and one from La Cobata. They stand from about 1.5 to over 3 metres tall, weigh from about 6 to as much as 40–50 tons, and were probably once brightly painted.
After heavy rain, water rushes through stone troughs buried under the plaza and spouts out at the edge of the plateau.
People slash the rubber trees in a herringbone pattern, and white latex trickles into the gourds below.
A trader from the highlands brings black obsidian blades to swap, sharp enough to split a hair.
Obsidian blades are sharper than steel scalpels, and were Mesoamerica’s main cutting tool for thousands of years, since no one on the continent worked iron.
On the cliff above the village a figure is carved seated in a cave mouth, with rain clouds drifting out and drops falling on maize plants.
Round black basalt boulders as big as houses lie scattered round the foot of the mountain. Carvers from the town walk among them, tapping each one and listening.
Your eyes are so dim a grandchild must help you strip the maize.
Before dawn the howler monkeys still wake you, as they did when you were small. You are not afraid of them now.

The rains never come. The highland soil cracks and the maize dies before it ears.
A few generations after you, the rulers of San Lorenzo will begin to have their faces carved in enormous basalt boulders, a custom that will last for centuries.
Not long after you, San Lorenzo will be emptied, its rulers’ stone faces buried, and La Venta will rise in the marshes to the east.

La Venta will be abandoned around 400 BCE, but what the Olmec began — the rubber ballgame, jade, the jaguar in religion, towns planned round ceremonial plazas — will live on among the Maya, the Zapotecs and later the Aztecs.

The Olmec name will be forgotten, but within a few centuries of you the Maya will build great cities in the eastern forests, using the same Long Count calendar carved at Tres Zapotes, and develop a script we can read today.

Then the colossal heads lay underground for more than two thousand years, until in 1862 a farmhand at Tres Zapotes dug one up, thinking at first it was the bottom of a huge upturned iron cauldron. It was reported in 1869; Matthew Stirling excavated Olmec towns from 1938 to 1946; the last head was found in 1994. When oil drilling came close to La Venta in the 1950s, the poet Carlos Pellicer had its monuments moved to a park museum in Villahermosa.
The tapir you saw as a child now survives in only a few thousand, in scattered patches of forest.
The howler monkeys that once frightened you are endangered in Mexico today.
The manatees you saw in the river are endangered today.
The jaguar that prowled round your dog pen now numbers about 4,800 in all of Mexico.
The harpy eagle has all but vanished from Mexico.

Why did the Olmec, or the Aztecs two thousand years later, not sail off to conquer Europe instead? Not because anyone was cleverer. Your continent had lost its large animals, its native horses among them, more than ten thousand years before, so there were no oxen, horses or camels to pull ploughs and carts, carry riders, or pass herd diseases to people until they built up resistance. Maize took thousands of years to turn from a wild grass into a staple, and the Americas run north to south, across deserts and jungles, so crops and knowledge spread slowly. Long after you, people on this coast made toy animals on wheels, but with nothing to pull a cart, the wheel stayed a toy. In 1519 Spanish ships landed on this same coast, near today’s Veracruz, bringing horses, steel and smallpox, which killed vast numbers of the native people. The difference came from geography, plants and animals, not from the people themselves.

The stone you helped haul became a ruler’s face. No one remembers the haulers’ names, but no head ever reached a town without them.
“El Rey”, San Lorenzo Head 1, stands today in the Museum of Anthropology in Xalapa. In this game, the hands that carved that face were yours.
The Cascajal block is real, and no one can read it yet. In this game, you scratched those signs.
The offerings at the spring of El Manatí were dug up from 1988 onwards. The rubber ball you threw in may be one of the oldest balls in the world.

The Olmec often buried their dead beneath or beside the house. The elite received jade, mirrors and red cinnabar sprinkled over the body. In the humid tropics bones rarely survive: some La Venta graves hold only jades laid out in the shape of a body that has vanished.

The green jade lies cool in the mouth, like a breath that has not yet left.
Sprinkle red powder over the body
Red as blood and as the sunrise; everyone sings as it falls.
Bury them beneath the house floor
They will lie beneath the family’s feet for ever, hearing the laughter and the grinding of maize every day.
You are buried with an iron-ore mirror on your chest, jade axes, and red cinnabar sprinkled over your body.
Your family buries you beneath the house floor with a clay pot and a jade bead in your mouth.
A five-year-old by an Olmec river has seen animals found nowhere else on Earth. If this child told a Thai child today about one of them, what would they say?
The Olmec hauled stones of tens of tons by human strength alone to carve their rulers’ faces. If you could carve one face for people to see three thousand years from now, whose would it be?

Athens was one of the largest Greek city-states, a town and its countryside of about 2,500 square kilometres. Democracy began here around 508 BCE, but only male citizens could vote, perhaps 10–20% of the people of the city-state.

Sparta had no city walls until late, for its warriors were its walls. Male citizens trained as soldiers from the age of 7, while the farming was done by helots, conquered people bound to work for Sparta for life, who far outnumbered the citizens. Spartan women could own land, unlike women in Athens.
Corinth controlled the narrow isthmus between two seas, with a paved track, the diolkos, for hauling ships over land. It grew rich on trade and pottery, until the Romans burned it in 146 BCE.

Miletus, on the coast of today’s Turkey, was home to Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes, the first thinkers to try to explain the world without appealing to the gods. It founded dozens of colonies round the Black Sea.
Lesbos was home to Sappho, the poet later Greeks called “the tenth Muse”. Only fragments of her poems survive, some found on papyrus used to wrap mummies in Egypt.
Syracuse was founded by Corinthians around 733 BCE and became one of the largest Greek cities, at times larger than Athens. Archimedes was born and died here.
Massalia was founded by Greeks from Phocaea around 600 BCE: it is Marseille in France today. Greeks planted colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, leaving Greek towns scattered round the sea.
Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BCE. It had a great Library that tried to collect every book in the world, and the Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders.

Most Greeks did not live in famous cities but were hill farmers growing barley, olives and grapes and keeping goats, going to town only on market or festival days. Mountains split Greece into a thousand small valleys.

Greeks had one name, followed by their father’s name and home district, such as “Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, of Alopeke”. Names often had meanings: Philip means “lover of horses”. The names in the game are invented.

Much of the work in Greek cities was done by non-citizens: slaves, resident foreigners and women. Upper-class Greeks looked down on manual work, yet some vase painters signed their pieces, so we still know artists such as Exekias by name.

In most Greek cities only male citizens had political rights. Citizen women could not vote, resident foreigners paid taxes and fought but had no rights, and slaves were bought and sold like property. Athens at its height may have had tens of thousands of slaves.
painted vases
The winter rains are thin, and the barley on the hillsides comes up thin-eared.

Greek soil is thin and stony and the rain falls only in winter, so there is little good grain land. Big city-states like Athens had to buy wheat from the Black Sea and Egypt, and founded colonies when there were more people than the land could feed.
You pay off your debt.
You cannot pay, and under Athenian law of this time the creditor takes you as a slave.
Before Solon’s reforms of 594 BCE, Athenians who could not pay their debts could be sold into slavery.
The creditor takes your animals for the debt.
A trader scratches strange marks on an oil jar and says they are sounds, not pictures: learn twenty-odd marks and you can write any word.

Greeks took their alphabet from the Phoenicians around the 8th century BCE and added letters for vowels. The Greek alphabet became the model for the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, and so for the letters used to write English today.
You are given a small round piece of metal stamped with an animal. The trader says every piece is worth the same, no weighing needed.

The world’s first coins were made in the kingdom of Lydia, near Ionia, around 600 BCE, and Greek cities quickly took them up. The silver “turtles” of Aegina and “owls” of Athens became money known all round the sea.
The Persian army breaks into Miletus, burns the temples and drives the people off as far as the Persian Gulf.
Miletus led the Ionian revolt against Persia and was destroyed in 494 BCE. When a play about its fall was staged in Athens, the audience wept so much that its author was fined.
The whole city takes to the boats and flees to Salamis. From across the water you watch smoke rise from the Acropolis: the Persians are burning the temples.
In 480 BCE the Athenians abandoned their city to the Persian army, then won the sea battle of Salamis a few weeks later.
On the Acropolis hundreds of masons are building a new temple of white marble. Every column swells a little in the middle, so that it looks straight from below.
The Parthenon was built in 447–432 BCE, partly with tribute paid by Athens’ allies. Its builders made almost no line truly straight, to correct optical illusions.
The Spartan army marches in, burning fields and cutting down olive trees outside the city. Every farmer is crammed inside the walls.
The Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BCE) drove country people inside the walls year after year. The crowding helped bring the plague of 430 BCE.
Freed from helotry
The Theban army has beaten Sparta and freed Messenia. After centuries as helots, you walk back to land your ancestors once owned.
After Sparta lost at Leuctra in 371 BCE, the Thebans helped the Messenians found a new city in 369. Many Messenian helots were freed, and Sparta never recovered its power.
Survived the day Rome burned Corinth
The Roman army enters the city. The men are killed, the women and children sold as slaves, statues and paintings loaded onto ships for Rome, and then the city is burned.
In 146 BCE Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth, the same year Rome destroyed Carthage. Greece fell under Roman power, yet the Romans took up Greek art, philosophy and gods wholesale.
You help carry wine jars onto the ships and are paid in bronze coins.
A labourer in Classical Athens earned about a drachma a day; a trireme rower about the same. Citizens serving as jurors were paid half a drachma a day, so even poor men could take part in the courts.
