In 133 BCE Tiberius Gracchus and hundreds of his supporters were clubbed to death, the first time in centuries that Roman politics ended in bloodshed in the city. Their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. Ten years later his brother was killed for much the same cause. Historians often date the start of Rome’s civil wars from here.
Stand with Gracchus
A club cracks your head. You wake by the river, not knowing how you survived.
You get away, though behind you people keep falling.
Stay hidden at home
In the evening you see bodies floating in the river and know Rome has changed.
Slaves on the volcano

A gladiator named Spartacus has broken out of the school at Capua with about seventy others. They have camped on the top of Mount Vesuvius, and slaves from the farms around slip away to join them every night. The slave beside you whispers: will you come tonight?
Rumour says runaway gladiators are camped on Mount Vesuvius. Slaves from the farms around run off to join them every night, and the army sent to catch them has been beaten.

Spartacus led a slave revolt in 73–71 BCE. His army may have numbered tens of thousands and beat Roman armies several times. In the end Crassus crushed them, and about 6,000 captured slaves were crucified along the Appian Way from Capua to Rome.
Run tonight
You climb the mountain in the dark. For the first time in your life nobody owns you, though you know it may not last.
The guards’ dogs catch your scent before you leave the estate. You are dragged back and flogged.
Stay: it is too dangerous
Two years later you walk the Appian Way and cannot count the crosses.
Hide food for the runaways
No one knows who takes it, but the bread vanishes every night.
Bolt the door
Crassus’ fire brigade

The block next to yours is on fire. Five hundred slaves of Crassus, the richest man in Rome, come running with buckets, then stand and watch while Crassus haggles with the weeping owner to buy the building cheap. Only when the price is agreed does he order them to put the fire out.
Plutarch says Crassus grew rich this way ✦. Rome had no public fire service until Augustus created the vigiles, about 7,000 strong, in 6 CE.
Run for water yourself
You and your neighbours keep it from spreading to your house. Crassus looks at you like a fly in the way of business.
Sell him your room too
You get a sum of money, but must move to the top floor of another block, even harder to escape from.
O the times! O the customs!
In the Senate Cicero points at Catiline, a senator plotting to seize power, and cries, “O the times! O the customs!” Catiline sits alone: everyone has moved away from the seats beside him.

Cicero gave his speeches against Catiline in 63 BCE; they are still taught in Latin classes today. His enslaved secretary Tiro devised a shorthand system used for centuries. Cicero was killed in 43 BCE. His name means “chickpea”.
Applaud loudly
Cicero turns and smiles at you. He is especially fond of applause.
Watch Tiro take it down in strange marks
Tiro writes as fast as Cicero speaks. His shorthand sign for “and” can still be seen on Irish-language road signs today.
Alesia

Roman soldiers have built two rings of walls around Alesia: one to keep those inside from escaping, one to hold off the army coming to help. Inside, the hunger is so great that women and children are sent out, but Caesar will not let them through.

In 52 BCE Vercingetorix, leader of the Gauls, surrendered to Caesar at Alesia. He was imprisoned for six years, then executed after Caesar’s triumph in Rome. Ancient writers claimed the Gallic wars killed or enslaved millions; the numbers may be exaggerated, but the devastation was enormous.
Share your last bread with a neighbour’s child
Two days later you see Vercingetorix ride out to lay down his arms before Caesar.
Slip through the walls at night
You are caught and sold into slavery with thousands of others.
You get out. It is the darkest night of your life.
A little stream
Your legion halts at a little stream called the Rubicon. The law forbids a general to lead his army across into Italy. Caesar stands still a long while, then says, “The die is cast,” and wades in.

In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon and started a civil war. Suetonius gives his words in Latin, but Plutarch says Caesar spoke them in Greek, quoting a play. “Crossing the Rubicon” still means a decision you cannot take back.
Wade in after Caesar
Crossed the Rubicon with Caesar
The water is knee-deep, but it feels like crossing an ocean.
Ask your mate whether this is against the law
Your mate says, “We are the law now,” and pulls you into the water.
Three words on a placard

In Caesar’s triumph, soldiers carry a great placard with just three words: VENI VIDI VICI, “I came, I saw, I conquered.” As custom allows, the soldiers sing rude songs mocking Caesar, about his bald head.

Caesar won at Zela in 47 BCE in a matter of hours, and Suetonius says these three words were carried in his triumph. Roman soldiers were allowed to sing mocking songs about their general on triumph day, to keep him from growing too proud.
Sing along with the mocking songs
Caesar hears and laughs. The laurel wreath on his head slips to one side.
Memorise the three words
Two thousand years later, people still have those words tattooed on their arms.
The Ides of March

This morning a soothsayer warned Caesar to beware this day, but he went to the Senate anyway. By afternoon the news is racing through the city: Caesar has been stabbed to death in the Senate. People run, and shops slam their shutters.

Julius Caesar was stabbed 23 times by a group of senators on 15 March 44 BCE. The famous “Et tu, Brute?” comes from Shakespeare’s play ✦. Suetonius says some reported Caesar saying in Greek, “You too, child?”, though he himself believed Caesar said nothing at all.
Run to the Senate to see
Three slaves carry Caesar’s body out on a litter, one arm hanging down. Not a single senator dares touch it.
Lock up and wait to see who wins
It will take thirteen years to find out, and the answer will be Caesar’s adopted great-nephew.
The queen of nine languages
Queen Cleopatra’s procession passes the harbour. She stops to talk with an Ethiopian merchant in his own tongue, then turns to answer a Jewish trader in Hebrew. Everyone gapes.

Plutarch wrote that Cleopatra spoke many languages and was the first of the Ptolemies to learn Egyptian, though they had ruled Egypt for nearly three hundred years. Her legendary beauty is a later embellishment; ancient writers praised her charm and intelligence more.
Bow to the queen
The queen glances at you and nods. You tell the story until the day you die.
Try greeting her in Egyptian
The queen laughs and corrects your accent.
A city of marble

Scaffolding everywhere: new temples, new theatres, marble markets. The emperor Augustus inspects the works himself. He is short, wears thick-soled shoes to look taller, and says he found Rome a city of brick and will leave it a city of marble.

Suetonius records both this saying and the thick-soled shoes of Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, who ruled from 27 BCE to 14 CE. August is named after him and July after Caesar, and the calendar used in Thailand today descends from the one Caesar reformed.
Hire on to carry marble
Your hands are calloused raw, but the temple you carried stone for will still have columns standing in two thousand years.
Look at the emperor’s shoes
The soles really are thick. You hold in your laughter until your eyes water.
The book that would not burn
The poet Virgil lies dying and has ordered his epic of Aeneas, ten years’ work, to be burned, because he thinks it unfinished. But the emperor Augustus forbids it.

Virgil died in 19 BCE. His Aeneid became Rome’s national epic, telling how the Romans descended from Aeneas, a prince who fled Troy. Roman schoolchildren memorised it, and lines from it are scrawled on walls all over Pompeii.
Rejoice that the book survives
For the rest of your life you can recite its first line: “I sing of arms and the man.”
Feel for the poet whose last wish was refused
You think that perhaps a book stops belonging to its writer once everyone loves it.
The poet in exile

The famous poet Ovid has been exiled by the emperor to a freezing town on the Black Sea, where people speak a language he cannot understand. He says his crime was “a poem and a mistake”, but never says what the mistake was.

Ovid was exiled to Tomis (today’s Constanța in Romania) in 8 CE and died there. His “mistake” has been a mystery for two thousand years. His Metamorphoses is where later ages learned most of the Greek and Roman myths.
Guess what the mistake was
Everyone in the market has a theory. Nobody knows, and two thousand years later nobody does.
Buy his books before they are pulled from the libraries
You hide the scrolls under your bed and read them every winter.
Give me back my legions
A starving man stumbles out of the eastern forest: a Roman soldier, the only survivor you will meet of three legions lost in the Teutoburg Forest.

News comes that three Roman legions have been ambushed in the German forests and almost wiped out. People say the emperor Augustus walks about banging his head on the doors, crying, “Varus, give me back my legions!”

In 9 CE Germans under Arminius, once an officer in the Roman army, destroyed Varus’ three legions; their numbers, 17, 18 and 19, were never used again. Suetonius records Augustus’ cry. Rome never conquered Germany east of the Rhine.
Give food and shelter
He eats in silence, then sleeps like a man who has not slept for months.
Ask what happened
He answers only, “Rain, mud, and trees full of men.”
The teacher from Nazareth

By the lake in Galilee a crowd sits listening to a Jewish teacher from the village of Nazareth named Jesus. He teaches them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. Fishermen, tax collectors and the sick sit side by side.

Nearly all historians agree that Jesus of Nazareth was a real person, a Jewish teacher from Galilee who was crucified in Jerusalem under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate around 30–33 CE. The Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish writer Josephus both mention him. The teaching quoted here comes from the Gospel of Matthew. Christians believe he rose from the dead, and Christianity later spread across the whole Empire.
Sit and listen until sunset
You remember the teaching on forgiveness all your life, and tell it to your children and grandchildren.
Listen a while, then go back to work
Years later, when people ask about that teacher, you can say you saw him with your own eyes.
The horse with a marble house
Rumour says the emperor Caligula has given his favourite horse, Incitatus, a marble stable and an ivory manger, with slaves to serve it, and plans to make it a consul.

The tale of Caligula’s horse comes from Suetonius and Cassius Dio, who wrote decades to more than a century after his death and loathed him ✦. Some historians think that if true, it was a jibe at the senators: a horse could do their job. Caligula was murdered by his own guards in 41 CE.
Sneak a look at the stable
You see no ivory manger, only a handsome horse that eats better than you.
Say the horse would probably do better than some senators
The whole tavern laughs, then falls silent as soldiers pass.
Elephants in Britain

The emperor Claudius has come to Britain in person, with war elephants. Britons who have never seen such beasts stand dumbstruck. The emperor stays just sixteen days, then goes home to celebrate his triumph in Rome.

Cassius Dio says Claudius brought elephants to Britain in the invasion of 43 CE ✦, and Suetonius says he stayed only sixteen days. The conquest gave Claudius, long mocked for his disability and stammer, a great triumph.
Get close to an elephant
It blows a gust of air in your face. You scream, then laugh.
Run to tell the village
No one believes in a beast with a nose as long as a man.
The queen who rose up
Queen Boudica of the Iceni leads tens of thousands of Britons to burn three Roman towns, Londinium among them, after Roman officials seized her people’s lands and abused her family.
Boudica’s revolt of 60–61 CE killed tens of thousands on both sides. A red burnt layer from that year is still found under London today. In the end the Roman army won, and Boudica died soon after.
Flee with the Roman soldiers
From a hill you watch smoke rise from the town you just left.
Understand why she is angry
You do not say it aloud in a Roman fort, but you think about it for a long time.
The emperor drives a chariot
At Olympia the emperor Nero races a chariot drawn by ten horses. He falls out on the way, climbs back up, fails to finish, and the judges still declare him the winner.

Suetonius says Nero fell from his chariot at Olympia in 67 CE and did not finish, but was crowned anyway. That year’s Games had been moved from 65 to fit his tour, and after Nero died his name was struck from the list of victors.
Clap like everyone else
Soldiers walk the rows checking who is not clapping. You clap until your hands are red.
Laugh on the inside
You hold it in until you reach your lodging, then laugh until your stomach hurts.
Money does not smell

The emperor Vespasian taxes the urine the fullers buy from the public latrines. When his son complains it is disgusting, the emperor holds a coin from the tax under his son’s nose and asks whether it smells.

Suetonius tells this story, which gave us the saying “money doesn’t smell”. Roman fullers used the ammonia in urine to whiten cloth. In France and Italy, public urinals were still named after Vespasian into the 20th century.
Laugh about it all day
Every time you get a coin, you sniff it before putting it away.
Sell urine to the fullers
Not much income, but the money really doesn’t smell.
A goddess from India
A rich neighbour shows off a new treasure: a woman carved in ivory, covered in jewellery, from a land beyond Egypt, brought over the sea on the monsoon winds.

In 1938 archaeologists found an Indian ivory goddess in a house in Pompeii, thought to be Lakshmi or a goddess of fertility, buried under the ash in 79 CE. It shows that Indian goods had reached ordinary houses in Italy.
Ask to hold it
It is lighter and warmer than you expected, its face smiling as if it knows something.
Ask how far India is
The neighbour says the round trip takes nearly a year. You decide that one day you will go.
The mountain that burst

At midday Vesuvius throws up a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine high into the sky. Small pumice stones rain down like hail, and roofs begin to sag under the weight. Everyone must choose: flee now, or shelter at home until it stops.

Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. The traditional date is 24 August, but a charcoal inscription found in 2018 suggests October. Most of Pompeii’s people got away early; those who stayed died in the surges of hot ash the next morning. Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and wrote it down.
Flee now, leave everything
Escaped from Pompeii
You run towards Naples under the falling stones and look back to see the town vanish under black cloud. Two days later you hear that Pliny the Elder sailed in to rescue people and never came back.
Shelter at home until it stops
That night is the longest of your life, and the last.
At dawn you crawl out and get away just before the hot ash arrives. Few were so lucky.
A hundred days in the new arena
The emperor Titus opens a new arena that seats around fifty thousand, with a hundred days of shows: gladiators, beast hunts and free bread. A vast awning shades the seats from the sun.

The Flavian Amphitheatre, later called the Colosseum, opened in 80 CE. Cassius Dio records some 9,000 animals killed at its opening games. Its exits were called vomitoria, not rooms for vomiting, as people often think, but passages that “spewed out” the crowd quickly.
Watch all day
You go home in the evening with three free loaves and a head pounding from fifty thousand voices.
Leave when the beast hunts begin
Outside the streets are empty as a ghost town: the whole city is in the arena.
A birthday invitation and some beer

At Vindolanda you help carry two wooden letter-tablets. One is a birthday invitation from the wife of a nearby fort’s commander to her friend. The other is from a cavalry officer begging his commander to send more beer: the men have run out.

The Vindolanda letters of around 100 CE are the oldest handwritten documents found in Britain. Claudia Severa’s birthday invitation to Sulpicia Lepidina ends in her own hand, one of the earliest known Latin writings by a woman. The beer request was from an officer named Masculus: Romans in Italy looked down on beer, but frontier soldiers drank it.
Go along to the party
At the party in the cold British fog, people speak three languages and not one complains about the weather… no, actually, everyone does.
Hurry the beer request along
Three days later a cart of beer arrives, and the whole fort hails you as a hero.
The bearded emperor

The emperor Hadrian has come to inspect the frontier himself, and orders a stone wall built across the island from sea to sea. He is the first emperor with a full beard, and within months half the fort has grown one too.

Hadrian’s Wall was begun around 122 CE and ran about 118 kilometres. Hadrian was the first emperor shown on coins with a full beard, perhaps copying Greek philosophers, and made beards fashionable for a century.
Grow a beard like his
Your family hates it, but the whole fort says you look like a philosopher.
Go and carry stone for the wall
You carve your unit’s name on one stone, as soldiers did all along the wall.
A statue in the temple of Isis

You travel with a caravan to the port of Berenike on the Red Sea. In the forecourt of the temple of Isis stands a marble statue of a calm figure with a halo around his head. Indian merchants tell you it is the Buddha, the Awakened One.

In 2023 Polish and American archaeologists announced a 71-centimetre marble Buddha found in the temple of Isis at Berenike, from around the 2nd century, carved from marble from the Greek island of Paros. It shows Buddhist merchants lived in Roman Egypt. In Thailand, at U Thong and Khlong Thom, pendants imitating coins of Roman emperors have been found from around the same period.
Buy a little Buddha image to wear round your neck
Wore a Buddha from India in the Roman Empire
Everyone at home asks which god he is. You say he is a man who taught how to quiet the mind.
Ask the merchants what the Buddha taught
Their Greek is poor, but you catch the words “suffering”, “craving” and “the middle way”.
The runner from Marathon
A satirist from Syria named Lucian tells the crowd a new story: a runner raced from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens, cried “Rejoice, we have won!” and dropped dead.

The story of a runner who ran from Marathon to Athens and died is not in Herodotus; it first appears in Roman-era writers, Plutarch and Lucian, about 600 years after the battle ✦. It inspired the marathon race at the first modern Olympics in 1896, and the distance of 42.195 km was fixed at the London Olympics of 1908.
Resolve to run that route yourself one day
You start running every morning, though you have no idea which way Athens is.
Ask whether the story is true
Lucian smiles: “As true as my story about sailing to the Moon.” ✦
The gladiators’ doctor
A Greek doctor named Galen cuts open a live pig before a crowd and severs one nerve in its neck. The pig stops squealing at once, though it still breathes. Everyone gasps.

Galen (about 129–216 CE) had been a doctor to gladiators at Pergamon and became physician to the emperor Marcus Aurelius. He showed that the laryngeal nerve controls the voice. His books were the basis of medicine in Europe and the Arab world for over a thousand years, though much was wrong, since he dissected apes and pigs, not humans.
Ask what gladiators eat
Beans and barley, he says, to put on fat that protects against deep wounds. People call them “the barley men”.
Ask him to treat your wound
He washes the wound with wine, binds it, and tells you to eat less.
The emperor who keeps a notebook
In a freezing camp on the Danube you see the emperor Marcus Aurelius sitting alone each night under a lamp, writing. Not battle orders: reminders to himself.

Marcus Aurelius ruled 161–180 CE and spent years at war on the Danube. The private notes he wrote in Greek, for himself alone, are known today as the Meditations, the most widely read book of Stoic philosophy.
Stand guard quietly outside the tent
One night he looks up and says, “You have done your duty well. Do not wait for anyone to praise it.”
Ask what the emperor writes
He says, “Things to stop myself forgetting I am only a man.”
The emperor in gladiator’s gear

The emperor Commodus enters the arena himself, dressed as Hercules, shoots ostriches with crescent-headed arrows and holds up a bird’s head towards the senators. The crowd must chant his praises on cue.
Cassius Dio, a senator who was really there, says he had to chew laurel leaves from his own wreath to keep from laughing. Commodus was strangled by a wrestler named Narcissus in 192 CE.
Chant along with the crowd
Your throat is raw, but you are safe.
Try not to laugh
A senator below is chewing leaves with a straight face. You understand him at once.
The Empire for sale
The Praetorian Guard has murdered the new emperor and shouts from its camp walls that the throne will go to whoever pays the soldiers most. Two rich men bid against each other over the wall.

In 193 CE Sulpicianus offered each soldier 20,000 sesterces; Didius Julianus offered 25,000 and became emperor. He reigned 66 days before a soldier killed him in the palace. Cassius Dio records his last words: “But what evil have I done? Whom have I killed?”
Shout a joke bid
“Three sesterces and a loaf!” The soldiers on the wall laugh, and you get away with it.
Go and tell everyone Rome has been sold
At the theatre the crowd boos the new emperor until he stops showing his face.
The queen of Palmyra
The army of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra has come out of the Syrian desert and taken Egypt. New coins in the market bear her face and her son’s, not the Roman emperor’s.

Zenobia ruled a Palmyrene realm that broke away from Rome and took Egypt in 270 CE. The emperor Aurelian won it back in 272. She was taken to Rome, and some writers say she lived out her days in a villa near Tivoli ✦.
Keep a coin with the queen’s face
Two years later such coins are forbidden. You hide yours under the floor.
Not caring who rules, so long as bread costs the same
It doesn’t. Bread grows dearer every year, whoever rules.
Rome needs walls again

For the first time in centuries Rome must build walls around itself. The emperor Aurelian drafts every craft guild to help. Houses in the way are pulled down; some buildings are simply built into the wall.

The Aurelian Walls, begun around 271 CE and about 19 km long, show that Rome was no longer safe in the crisis of the 3rd century, when emperors changed so fast some lasted only months. Most of the wall still stands, including the Pyramid of Cestius built into it.
Go and help build
You lay a course of bricks that will stand for nearly two thousand years.
Complain that your house is being pulled down
No one listens. Your family moves outside the wall, which is hardly safer.
Prices set by the emperor

Notices go up across the Empire fixing maximum prices for more than a thousand things, from eggs to a barber’s haircut. Anyone who charges more faces death, so the traders simply keep their goods at home.

Diocletian’s Edict on Maximum Prices of 301 CE tried to stop inflation but failed, as goods vanished from the markets; dozens of inscribed copies survive. A few years later Diocletian abdicated, and the story goes that when begged to return to power he said that if they could see the cabbages he grew himself, they would not ask ✦.
Go looking for the black market
Eggs at three times the posted price, but at least there are eggs.
Grow your own vegetables
You grow fine big cabbages, and understand the old emperor a little better.
A sign on the shields
Constantine’s soldiers march into the city after their victory at the Milvian Bridge. On their shields is a strange new sign, two Greek letters interlaced. People say it is the sign of Christ.

In 312 CE Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge. Christian writers of the time say that before the battle he saw a sign in the sky or in a dream ✦. The next year the Edict of Milan granted freedom of worship, and Christians who had been persecuted no longer had to hide.
Ask a soldier what the sign means
The soldier shrugs: the general ordered it painted, and they won. That is enough for him.
Tell your Christian neighbours they need not fear any more
The old woman next door weeps. She has hidden her Gospel book in the wall for thirty years.
A poem against beer
The young emperor Julian, who once served in Gaul, has written a poem mocking Gaulish beer: the god of wine smells of nectar, but this barley drink smells of goat.

The emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 CE) really did write a short poem about beer. Greeks and Romans often saw beer-drinking as a barbarian habit, though the Mesopotamians and Egyptians of earlier chapters had drunk beer for thousands of years.
Raise your beer and drink it in front of everyone
The whole Gaulish tavern raises its cups with you and shouts, “Smells of goat!”
Give up beer and switch to wine
Wine costs three times as much, but you feel more Roman at once.
An empire in two halves

The emperor Theodosius has died. His elder son takes the East at Constantinople; the younger, ten years old, takes the West. Nobody knows this is the last time one emperor will ever rule the whole Empire.

After 395 CE the Roman Empire was permanently governed in two halves. The West fell the next century; the East spoke Greek but called itself Roman for over a thousand years more, until Constantinople fell in 1453. “Byzantine” is a name later historians gave it.
Decide your half will survive
You are right: your half will last another thousand years.
You hope so.
Grumble that a ten-year-old rules half the world
In truth the one ruling is the general standing behind the boy.
The woman mathematician

Hypatia teaches mathematics, astronomy and philosophy to students from all over the Empire, pagans and Christians alike. She drives her own chariot through the city, and the governor comes to her for advice.

Hypatia of Alexandria is the first woman mathematician whose life we know in some detail. In 415 CE she was brutally murdered by a mob amid political and religious strife in the city. Her death became a symbol of the end of the old learning in Alexandria.
Ask to attend her lectures
She explains the curves you get by slicing a cone. You draw them in the sand for months.
Watch her chariot pass
The women in the market turn to watch. You see one girl standing very still, as if deciding something.
The City of God
After the news that Rome has been sacked, the bishop of Hippo near Carthage, named Augustine, preaches that every city of men can fall, even Rome, but the City of God never will.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) wrote The City of God after the sack of Rome in 410, and the Confessions, an autobiography in which he admits stealing pears as a boy though he wasn’t hungry. He died in 430 while the Vandals besieged his city.
You go home calmer, though the news from Rome is still frightening.
Ask about the pears
The bishop laughs: “I wanted them because they were forbidden. That is the whole trouble with us.”
The Pope and Attila
Attila, king of the Huns, has burned city after city in northern Italy, and everyone thinks Rome is next. Pope Leo goes north to meet him in person, and Attila turns his army back.

In 452 CE Pope Leo I joined an embassy to Attila, and Attila withdrew. Christian writers credited the Pope’s words, or a vision of Saints Peter and Paul threatening Attila ✦. Historians think disease and hunger in the Hunnish army also played a part. Attila died the next year.
Pray for the embassy
When news comes that Attila has turned back, every church bell rings at once.
Pack up to flee anyway
You don’t need to flee this year. But three years later the Vandals come from the sea, and this time no one stops them.
The last emperor

A German general named Odoacer deposes the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople, with word that the West needs no emperor any more. The farmers in your village go on ploughing as they did yesterday.

In 476 CE the Western Roman Empire ended without much noise. The last emperor was pensioned off to a villa by the sea. By coincidence his name combined that of Rome’s first king, Romulus, and its first emperor, Augustus; “Augustulus” means “little Augustus”.
Keep ploughing
No one in the village thinks today is special. Historians a thousand years later will do the thinking for them.
Sit and tell the grandchildren every emperor you remember
The list is so long the children fall asleep before you reach the last one.
The ship sunk on purpose

The emperor Claudius is building a giant new harbour beside Ostia. Workmen haul in the biggest ship you have ever seen: it once carried a single stone obelisk from Egypt for the emperor Caligula. Then they fill it with concrete and sink it.

Pliny the Elder records that Caligula’s obelisk ship was sunk as the foundation for the lighthouse of the new harbour at Portus, begun around 42 CE; archaeologists have found the remains. The obelisk itself still stands in St Peter’s Square in Rome today.
Hire on to pour the concrete
Roman concrete sets even under seawater. You don’t understand why, but the pay is good.
Watch the ship go down
It sinks slowly, like a great beast lying down. The whole harbour applauds.
The ball spun by steam
An engineer named Hero boils water in a pot, and steam jets from two pipes on a metal ball until it spins madly. For a temple he has built a machine that gives out holy water when you drop in a coin.

Hero of Alexandria, in the 1st century, described the aeolipile steam ball and a coin-operated holy-water dispenser, often called the world’s first vending machine. Yet no one put steam power to real work for more than sixteen hundred years.
Ask whether it could do any work
Hero laughs: “Slaves are cheaper.” You remember that answer for a long time.
Drop a coin for holy water
Exactly one palmful of water trickles out, then stops, as if the machine knows the price.
Stones the size of houses

King Herod is rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem grander than ever. Thousands of workers cut stones so huge it takes dozens of oxen to drag them. Some priests have trained as masons so that only priests work inside the holy precinct.

Herod began rebuilding the Temple around 20–19 BCE; Josephus tells of priests trained as builders. Some stones in the Western Wall weigh hundreds of tonnes. The Temple was finished only a few years before it was destroyed in 70 CE.
Hire on to haul stone
You help haul a stone that will stay in the wall for two thousand years.
Watch the work from the Mount of Olives
In the evening the white stone shines so bright in the sun it hurts your eyes.
Gauls in the Senate

News from Rome: the emperor Claudius, born at Lugdunum in Gaul, has argued in the Senate that Gallic nobles should become senators. Old senators grumble that men who wear trousers have no place in the Senate, but the emperor wins.

Claudius’ speech of 48 CE was inscribed on a bronze tablet found in Lyon in 1528, and Tacitus also reports it. Part of why the Roman Empire lasted so long was that it slowly let the conquered become Romans.
Feel proud
You wear your best trousers to market to celebrate.
Ask what ordinary people like you get out of it
The headman says, “Your grandchildren may become citizens,” which will take nearly two hundred years.
Riot at the arena
At a gladiator show in Pompeii’s amphitheatre, spectators from neighbouring Nuceria start jeering at the locals. Insults turn into stones, then into swords.

Tacitus records the riot between Pompeians and Nucerians in 59 CE, in which several people died. The Senate banned gladiator shows at Pompeii for ten years. A painting of it survives on a wall in Pompeii, like a football riot today.
Run for the exit
You get out. Behind you the screaming goes on and on.
Defend your neighbours
A stone cracks your head; you wake at home remembering nothing.
You get three children out. The whole street talks about it for years.
A young mother in prison

In Carthage a young Christian woman named Perpetua, twenty-two years old with a baby, has been arrested for refusing to sacrifice for the emperor. Her father comes to beg her to change her mind, but she will not. She is sent to the arena with an enslaved woman named Felicitas.
Perpetua and Felicitas were executed in the arena at Carthage in 203 CE. The diary Perpetua wrote in prison survives, one of the earliest writings by a Christian woman. Both are honoured as saints.
Stay away from the arena
The city is quiet that day. Even many who are not Christians say she was brave.
Help look after her baby
The baby sleeps in your arms, knowing nothing. You hope one day he can read his mother’s diary.
The New Rome

The emperor Constantine celebrates his new capital. Statues from all over the Empire have been brought to adorn it. In the hippodrome stands a bronze column of three twisted serpents, made by the Greeks after they beat the Persians eight hundred years before.

Constantinople was dedicated as capital in 330 CE. The Serpent Column was brought from Delphi, where the Greeks set it up after their victory at Plataea in 479 BCE; it still stands in the old hippodrome in Istanbul today. Players of the Greek chapter may have seen it new.
Go to see the celebrations
Free bread, music and the biggest crowd of your life.
Touch the serpent column
The bronze is ice-cold. The names of the Greek cities that fought are still engraved on it.
The thousand-year walls
The whole city helps build new triple walls on the landward side: a moat, a low wall, a high wall and nearly a hundred towers.
The Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, finished around 413 CE, protected the city for over a thousand years, until Ottoman cannon broke them in 1453. Much of them still stands in Istanbul today.
Help dig the moat
The clay stays under your nails for months.
Predict these walls will never fall
You are wrong, but only after another thousand years, which is nearly right.
The Vandals arrive

While the townsfolk are at the chariot races, the army of Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, walks in through the gates unopposed. Carthage, the second city of the West, falls to a Germanic people in a single day.

The Vandals took Carthage in 439 CE and used it as a naval base to sack Rome in 455. The word vandalism was coined in 1794 by a French cleric; in fact the Vandals plundered Rome in a fairly orderly way, destroying no more than other invaders.
Hide your money under the floor
Archaeologists may find it fifteen hundred years from now.
Go to work as usual
Life in the market barely changes, except that the taxes go into a new king’s purse.
To Olympia
You run faster than any girl in town. Women may not compete in the Olympic Games, but at Olympia there is a race for unmarried girls in honour of the goddess Hera, on the same track but shorter.

You have trained at running and wrestling every day for years, and your trainer says you are ready. Athletes must train at Elis for a month before the Games and swear before the statue of Zeus not to cheat.

Pausanias describes the Heraia, a footrace for young women at Olympia, run over a track about one sixth shorter than the men’s. Winners got an olive crown and a share of the sacrificed cow, and could set up their portrait in Hera’s temple.

By tradition the Games at Olympia began in 776 BCE and were held every four years until about 393 CE ✦. Romans could compete once Rome ruled Greece. Events included the one-stadion sprint, a long race of about four kilometres, wrestling, boxing and the pankration, where only biting and eye-gouging were banned. There was no marathon at the ancient Olympics. Cheats were fined to pay for statues of Zeus inscribed with their names.
Run the sprint: pure speed
f
Won the girls’ race at Olympia
Won at the Olympic Games
You cross the line first. The judges tie a red ribbon on your arm and set an olive crown on your head. Your home town will carve your name for ever.
Competed at Olympia
You come fourth. There is no prize for second at Olympia: there is the winner, and everyone else.
Enter the endurance event
Everyone leads early, but on the last lap you are the only one with anything left. The olive crown is yours.
You finish, legs shaking so hard you cannot stand. The crowd applauds, which is rare for anyone who did not win.
The run from Marathon
You reach the plain of Marathon, stand before the mound where the 192 were buried, and decide to run the forty-odd kilometres to Athens, as in the story you heard.
The burial mound of the Athenians at Marathon still stands. Roman-era travellers such as Pausanias visited it, and the Olympic marathons of 1896 and 2004 in Athens started from here.
Run all the way without stopping
Ran from Marathon to Athens
You run into Athens at dusk and cry, “Rejoice, we have won!” People stare as if you are mad, but you do not drop dead, which is an improvement on the story.
You walk after twenty kilometres and hitch a ride on a donkey cart into the city. No one need ever know.
Walk slowly and enjoy the view
You take two days, stopping for olives in every village, and conclude this is the wisest way.
The she-wolf
Your father takes you to see a bronze of a she-wolf suckling twin babies, and tells you one of them, Romulus, later killed his brother and founded Rome, naming it after himself.

Romans believed Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus ✦. Archaeologists have found a village on the Palatine Hill from around that time, but nothing of twins or a wolf. The famous wolf bronze in a Rome museum today may have been cast in the Middle Ages, and the twins were added in the Renaissance.
Ask why he killed his brother
Your father says the brother jumped over the wall he had built. You decide never to jump over your sibling’s wall.
Howl like a wolf
The street dogs howl back, and your father hurries you home.
The charm at your neck
Your mother ties a round locket at your neck with charms inside against bad luck. You must wear it until you grow up.

Freeborn Roman children wore a bulla locket against evil. Boys gave it to the household gods on coming of age, around 14–16. Romans carried many charms, including phallus amulets believed to ward off the evil eye, found everywhere from walls to loaves of bread.
Never take it off, not even in the bath
You believe it saved you from a fever once. Who knows?
Open it to look inside
Inside is only a tiny folded note and a pebble. You shut it quickly in case the magic leaks out.
Zeus or Jupiter (again)
Your Greek tutor, a slave, is teaching Greek poetry. You ask whether Zeus and Jupiter are the same god. He sighs a long sigh, like a man who has answered this a hundred times.

Rich Roman children learned Greek from Greek tutors, many of them slaves or freedmen, and upper-class Romans were bilingual. Players of the Greek chapter will know this question was argued in the markets long before you were born.
Insist they are not
The tutor shakes his head: “Every generation.”
Ask where the tutor comes from
He comes from Corinth, a city that is no more. He says nothing further.
The public latrine

Your first visit to the public latrine: a long row of stone seats with no partitions. The man beside you talks politics with someone across the room. Water runs beneath, and a stick with a sponge on the end soaks in a channel.

Roman public latrines seated dozens and were places to chat. The sponge on a stick, the tersorium, is thought by most scholars to have been for wiping, though some suggest it cleaned the toilets ✦. Romans even had a goddess of the sewers, Cloacina.
Chat with your neighbour
You pick up more political gossip than a month in the market.
Ask what the sponge is for
Everyone laughs and no one gives a straight answer. Two thousand years later scholars are still arguing.
Writing on the wall

The town walls are covered in writing: election slogans, the names of gladiators the girls adore, lost-and-found notices, and one line complaining: “I am amazed, O wall, that you have not collapsed under the weight of so many people’s boring scribbles.”

More than ten thousand pieces of writing have been found on the walls of Pompeii. The complaint to the wall appears in several places. Some election posters were pranks, such as one saying “all the late-night drinkers ask you to vote for Vatia.” These walls were the Romans’ social media.
Write your own name on the wall
You scratch your name with a nail. In this game, perhaps it is still there.
Read every single message
You learn to read faster than the children at school, because the walls are more interesting.
The toga of manhood
On the feast of the wine god you dedicate your childhood locket to the household gods and put on a plain white toga for the first time. Your family walks you to the forum to be enrolled as a citizen.

Roman boys swapped the purple-bordered toga of childhood for the plain white toga of manhood at around 14–16. A toga was several metres of wool that needed help to drape and was stifling in summer; most people wore just a tunic day to day.
Walk tall with pride
The toga comes loose halfway, and everyone helps rewrap it in the middle of the street.
Ask whether you must wear it every day
Your father laughs: “Only on days you want to be seen as a citizen,” and takes his own off the moment he gets home.
Twenty-five years in the army
A recruiter reaches the village promising pay, food, doctors and land on discharge. But service is 20–25 years, and soldiers may not marry while serving.

Imperial legionaries served 20 years or more, carried 30–40 kg of kit, marched about 30 km a day, and built a ditched camp every night. Those who survived to discharge received a lump sum or land. Soldiers from every corner of the Empire spread Latin everywhere.
Sign up
Joined a legion
In the first three months you march until your feet blister, dig until your hands split, and learn fifteen Latin curses.
The recruiter shrugs and points at your friend instead.
Your family arranges your marriage. The groom is about ten years older. You wear a flame-orange veil, and he must carry you over the threshold of your new home.
Your family and a neighbour’s discuss a marriage. The bride is sixteen; her family will give a dowry of money and woven cloth.

Roman women usually married in their late teens, men in their late twenties. Carrying the bride over the threshold is a Roman custom still kept in many countries. Roman women could divorce and kept more control of their own property than women in Athens.
The guests throw walnuts for many children, and the new house smells of pine torches for days.
A room on the sixth floor

You rent a room at the top of a tenement block. No kitchen, no water: you haul water up six flights, eat at the hot-food counters in the street, and lie awake all night listening to the carts, which are only allowed to move after dark.

Roman tenements rose many storeys; Augustus capped their height at about 20 metres. The ground floor held shops and richer flats. Caesar banned delivery carts from the city by day, and the poet Juvenal complained no one could sleep in Rome for the carts at night. Hot-food counters with jars set into stone survive at Pompeii and Ostia.
Put up with it and save
After a year you have saved enough for a pot of your own to boil water in, and are very proud.
Move down to a dearer floor
The second floor costs three times as much, but if there is a fire you can jump out of the window.
The baths

Entry to the baths costs less than a loaf. Inside are hot rooms, warm rooms, a cold pool, an exercise yard, masseurs, snack sellers, armpit-pluckers crying for customers, and men doing business in the water.

The baths were the heart of Roman social life; the Baths of Caracalla in Rome held about 1,600 bathers at once. The philosopher Seneca complained in a letter of lodging above a bathhouse and being kept awake by armpit-pluckers and people singing in the water. Romans had no soap as we know it: they oiled themselves and scraped it off with a metal strigil.
Go every day after work
You land two new jobs from people you chat to in the warm pool.
Try the armpit-plucker
You scream louder than anything Seneca complained of, and never go back.
Election day
A candidate arrives with ten followers, shaking every hand and remembering every name, thanks to a slave who whispers the names in his ear, and hands out coins to anyone who promises his vote.

Roman candidates had a slave called a nomenclator to whisper the names of people approaching. Vote-buying was illegal but so common that laws against it had to be passed again and again. Thousands of painted election notices survive on Pompeii’s walls.
Take the coin and vote for someone else
No one knows. You feel a little guilty. Only a little.
Refuse, and vote for the one you believe in
Your candidate loses, but you walk home tall.
Greeting the patron
Before dawn you put on your toga and queue outside a rich man’s house with dozens of others, to greet him and hope he will help with a lawsuit, find you work, or at least hand out a basket of food.

The patron–client system was the heart of Roman society. Clients backed their patron politically and called every morning; patrons helped clients in trouble. The poet Martial grumbled about getting up early and putting on a toga to greet a patron for a pittance.
Go every morning, patiently
After a year he knows your name, and helps you win a case against your neighbour.
Stay in bed
You get no food basket, but you sleep past sunrise for the first time in months.
The rod of freedom

Your owner decides to free you before a magistrate. The official touches your head with a rod, and you are free. You will take your former owner’s family name, and must still pay your respects to him on special days.

Slaves in Rome were freed more often than in many slave societies, and those freed by a citizen became citizens too. Many freedmen grew rich in business, to the envy of the elite; the writer Petronius mocked them in the figure of Trimalchio, a vulgar millionaire ex-slave.
Open a shop of your own
Was set free
Your shop sign bears three names like any citizen: the second your old owner’s, the third your own.
Keep working for your old owner, for wages
The same work, but tonight you go home to a place that is yours.
Greens or Blues

At the great racecourse two hundred thousand people split into factions by team colour: Greens, Blues, Reds and Whites. Some fans bury lead curse-tablets under the track to hex the rival team’s horses.

The Circus Maximus held perhaps 150,000–250,000 people. Star charioteers like Diocles, from Spain, won over a thousand races and grew richer than many generals. Archaeologists have found many lead tablets cursing horses and drivers.
Cheer for the Greens with all your heart
The Greens win. You hug a stranger in the same colour and curse the Blue standing next to you.
Bury a curse tablet
The rival’s horse stumbles on the seventh lap. Curse or luck, you’ll never know, and you tell no one.
Dice in the tavern
In a tavern people are gambling at dice, though the law forbids it outside the winter festival. A painting on the wall shows two men quarrelling over a throw until the landlord throws them out.

A painting in a Pompeii tavern really does show dice players quarrelling, with speech captions like a comic. Romans gambled widely though it was illegal, except at the Saturnalia in December, when slaves and masters swapped roles for a while, one of the ancestors of Europe’s year-end festivities.
Play a round
You throw three sixes and the whole tavern roars.
You lose a week’s food money and swear never to play again, until next week.
You witness a quarrel exactly like the one in the painting.
Beer or wine
A Roman trader arrives with jars of Italian wine. Civilised people drink wine mixed with water, he says, not barbarian barley beer. Your village headman has already switched.

Before the conquest the Gauls bought enormous amounts of Italian wine; one ancient writer claims a trader could get a slave for a single jar ✦. Millions of Roman wine jars have been found across France. Yet Roman soldiers on the frontier drank the local beer too. Drinking wine became a way of showing you were “Roman”, like bathing in the baths and wearing a toga.
Give up beer and drink wine
Gave up beer for wine
The wine is sourer than you expected, but you drink it with a sophisticated face.
Grandfather’s beer is best
The whole tavern raises its beer to you. The Roman trader shakes his head and orders one to try.
Pirates
Your merchant ship is chased by two fast boats full of armed men under an unknown flag. The captain asks: fight, flee, or pay the ransom?

Before 67 BCE pirates were so common that even the young Caesar was captured for ransom; Plutarch says he promised to come back and crucify them all, and did ✦. Pompey later swept the pirates from the sea within months.
Run before the wind
Your ship is heavier but has more sail. As the wind rises the pirate boats shrink to nothing.
They catch you, take the whole cargo, and leave you on an empty ship.
Pay the ransom
The pirates count the money politely and wish you a safe voyage, which is the most infuriating part.
Water from the mountains

A new aqueduct reaches the town, bringing water from mountains tens of kilometres away down a slope so gentle you can barely see it, until it pours out of street-corner fountains day and night. In rich houses the pipes are lead.

Rome had 11 aqueducts, delivering more water per person than many cities today. Most ran underground, with arches only in places. Our word plumbing comes from Latin plumbum, “lead”. Rome’s hard water coated the pipes with limescale, limiting lead poisoning from water, but Romans took in lead from elsewhere, like grape syrup boiled in lead pots.
Go and drink from the fountain
Cold mountain water runs down your throat. You think of whoever measured the slope of every metre of that channel.
Secretly tap the pipe for free water
The water officials catch you and fine you heavily.
No one finds out. Your back garden now has its own little fountain.
The ancestors’ masks
At your grandfather’s funeral, family members wear the wax masks of every ancestor who held high office and walk in procession to the forum, as if the whole line of the dead had come to escort him.

Polybius describes this custom. Elite families kept their ancestors’ masks in cupboards in the hall and wore them at funerals. Roman tombs lined the roads outside towns; epitaphs often began “To the spirits of the departed” and gave the dead person’s age in years, months and days.
Wear the mask of the most famous ancestor
The mask is cold and smells of wax. You walk all day like someone else.
Give the eulogy
You tell of your grandfather’s deeds, and those of every masked ancestor present. The forum falls silent to listen.
A new faith
Your neighbour goes out before dawn every Sunday to meet with a group who follow Christ. They share food with the poor and will not burn incense to the emperor, which makes others suspicious.

The early Christians were a small group in the big cities, persecuted from time to time, especially under Nero and in Diocletian’s Great Persecution of 303 CE. Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to deal with Christians; the letter survives. After 313 Christianity was free, and in 380 it became the religion of the Empire.
Go along with your neighbour once
In a small room slaves and masters share bread at the same table. You have never seen anything like it.
Mind your own business
You don’t ask and he doesn’t tell, but he greets you warmly every morning as always.
How often do you think about the Roman Empire?
Out of nowhere a grandchild asks, “How often do you think about the Roman Empire?”

In 2023 a social media trend had women asking their partners or fathers, “How often do you think about the Roman Empire?”, and many answered: every day. Two thousand years after you, Rome still lives in millions of heads.
“Every day. I live in it.”
The child nods as if this makes sense, though it doesn’t.
“Less often than I think about dinner.”
The most honest answer in history.
A runner’s tale
A Greek traveller tells a tale in the tavern: six hundred years ago, after the battle on the plain of Marathon, a runner raced to Athens, cried “Rejoice, we have won!” and fell dead.

This story is not in Herodotus; it first appears in Roman-era writers, Plutarch and Lucian ✦. Yet it inspired the marathon at the 1896 Olympics, and the 42.195 km distance comes from the London Olympics of 1908.
Resolve to run that road one day
You start running every morning. The neighbours assume you are fleeing a debt.
Order another drink
You conclude that running that far is a terrible idea.
The stamp on the bread
You carve a wooden stamp with your shop’s name to press into every loaf before it goes into the oven, so customers know it’s yours.

At Pompeii 81 carbonised loaves were found in one oven, some still bearing the baker’s stamp. Roman loaves were usually scored into eight wedges for easy sharing, and big bakeries used donkeys to turn their millstones.
Carve your full name
Two thousand years later, in this game, one of your loaves might be dug up still bearing your name.
Carve a little donkey instead of a name
Every child on the street wants the donkey bread.
The urine vats
All day you tread cloth in vats of urine and fuller’s earth. The smell clings so badly your mother makes you sleep outside, but the cloth comes out so white the rich customers come back every month.

Roman fullers left jars on street corners for passers-by to pee in, then collected them. A wall in a Pompeii fullery says, “I sing of fullers and the owl, not arms and the man,” mocking the first line of the Aeneid; the owl was the fullers’ emblem.
Expand the business
Bigger shop, bigger smell, but money doesn’t smell: the emperor said so.
Write a joke poem on the shop wall
Every customer who reads it laughs, and word spreads until your shop is famous up and down the street.
The crowd’s thumbs
Your opponent falls and raises a finger to beg for mercy. The whole arena looks to the sponsor, and the sponsor looks to the crowd.

The image of the crowd turning thumbs down for death comes from a 19th-century painting ✦; scholars are unsure what the real signal was. Most gladiators did not fight to the death every time, as they were expensive to train. A study of gladiators’ bones from Ephesus found they ate mostly beans and barley and drank a plant-ash tonic for their bones.
Wait calmly for the verdict
The crowd roars for mercy. Your opponent looks at you with eyes you will remember all your life.
Help him up yourself
The crowd falls silent a moment, then applauds louder than when you won.
A road for two thousand years

The master builder explains how to make a road: dig nearly a metre deep, lay big stones, then gravel, then sand and lime, then great paving slabs on top, cambered so water runs off to the sides. It takes three times longer than cutting corners.

The Appian Way was begun in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius Caecus, whose nickname means “the blind”. Roman roads ran over 80,000 km, and some Roman concrete is still sound after two thousand years; a 2023 study suggested small lumps of lime in it help cracks heal themselves.
Build it properly, every layer
In this game, the stretch you built still has cars driving over it today.
Skimp on a layer to finish faster
The first winter rains turn your stretch to potholes, and everyone knows who built it.
Discharge
After years of service the survivors receive two bronze tablets confirming citizenship and land. You must choose: take land on the frontier, or take the money and go home.

Roman veterans were often settled on land in new veteran colonies that became cities across Europe, such as Cologne in Germany. Non-citizen auxiliaries received bronze diplomas granting citizenship after 25 years’ service, and many survive in museums.
Take land on the frontier
You settle among the locals and learn their language until you speak it as well as Latin.
Take the money and go home
Home has changed past recognising, but your mother still knows you.
The haunted house in Athens
You rent a big house suspiciously cheap. On the first night the clank of chains draws closer, and a gaunt old man with a beard and fetters on his hands and feet stands at the door, beckoning.

Pliny the Younger tells this story in a letter to a friend ✦. A philosopher named Athenodorus rented a haunted house in Athens and followed the ghost to the courtyard, where it vanished. Digging there, they found a skeleton in chains; once it was given proper burial, the ghost never returned. It is one of the oldest recorded haunted-house stories.
Follow the ghost
The ghost vanishes in a corner of the courtyard. You mark the spot with leaves; tomorrow you will call the magistrates to dig.
Keep writing, like the philosopher
The chains rattle by your ear all night. You manage one page and never read it again.
The soldier under the moon
On a full-moon night you travel with a soldier past the roadside tombs. He strips off his clothes, pees a circle around them, then turns into a wolf and runs howling into the woods.

This comes from the Satyricon, a 1st-century novel by Petronius ✦: a character named Niceros tells it at Trimalchio’s dinner. It is one of the oldest werewolf stories in European literature. The soldier’s clothes turn to stone, and next day he has a wound on his neck just where the wolf was speared.
Draw your sword and stand among the tombs
You slash at shadows all night, until the cock crows.
Run home without looking back
Next day you see the soldier in bed with a bandaged neck and a doctor tending him. You ask no questions.
The lion who remembered
In the arena, a runaway slave is thrown to the biggest lion. It charges, then stops, sniffs him, and licks his hands like a dog. The whole arena falls silent.

The tale of Androcles and the lion is told by Aelian and Aulus Gellius, who says he had it from another writer claiming to be an eyewitness ✦. The runaway, hiding in Africa, pulled a thorn from a lion’s paw; later both were captured, the lion knew him in the arena, and the emperor set both man and lion free.
Shout for them to be freed
The whole arena joins in. The slave walks out leading the lion on a loose cord, and people press coins on him all the way.
Not believe your own eyes
You tell the story all your life, and no one believes you either.
The bird reborn from fire

Word runs through Egypt that a phoenix has been seen: a great bronze-gold bird with a flock of others trailing in wonder. It comes from the east once every five hundred years, carrying its father’s body in a nest of spices to burn at the Temple of the Sun.

Tacitus records that a phoenix was seen in Egypt in 34 CE ✦, though he himself doubted it was genuine, since five hundred years had not yet passed. Scholars of the time argued over whether the phoenix came every 500 or every 1,461 years.
Travel to the Temple of the Sun
Saw the phoenix (or something)
You glimpse a great golden bird circling the temple for a moment. You will never be sure what it was.
Ask whether the five hundred years are really up
The priests unroll old records and count on their fingers, arguing until sunset.
The Sibyl’s cave

At Cumae near Naples you walk down a long stone tunnel to the chamber of the Sibyl, a prophetess said to be a thousand years old. She writes prophecies on leaves, and the wind scatters them into a jumble.

Legend says the Sibyl of Cumae offered nine books of prophecy to Rome’s last king; when he refused the price, she burned three, then three more, until he bought the last three for the full price ✦. Romans kept the Sibylline Books in a temple and consulted them in crises. The tunnel at Cumae can still be walked, though archaeologists debate whether it was really the Sibyl’s cave.
Ask how long you will live
The leaf that blows to your feet reads, “Longer than you fear, shorter than you hope.”
Gather the scattered leaves and put them in order yourself
You assemble one sentence that makes no sense but sounds terrifying.
A cross above the sun

Before the great battle, the general Constantine gathers his troops. He says he saw a cross of light above the sun, with the words “In this sign, conquer,” and orders every man to paint the sign on his shield.

Eusebius, a bishop and Constantine’s biographer, wrote that the emperor told him this himself years later and swore it was true ✦; Lactantius says it was a dream the night before the battle. Some scientists suggest a solar halo caused by ice crystals in the air.
Look up at the sun
You see a ring of light around the sun and a bar of light across it. Or perhaps your eyes are simply dazzled.
Paint the sign carefully on your shield
The paint isn’t dry before the march and your sign smears half away, but you survive.
The freedman millionaire’s banquet

You are invited to a banquet thrown by a millionaire who was once a slave. He serves a whole boar from which live birds fly out, a hare fitted with wings like Pegasus, and a water clock with a trumpeter announcing every hour that a little more of life is gone.

This is Trimalchio’s feast from Petronius’ Satyricon ✦, a satire, not a record. Romans did not have rooms for throwing up between courses: a vomitorium was a theatre or arena exit. Real rich Romans dined reclining on couches, eating eggs, fish, sausages and honey.
Eat everything served
By the eleventh course you begin to see why people invented the vomiting room.
Listen to the host tell how he got rich
He once lost five ships in a single storm, then built bigger ones. You can’t quite manage to dislike him.
The hot-food shop in the street has clay pots sunk into its stone counter. People stand eating stewed beans, bread dipped in garum, and wine mixed with warm water.

Garum was a fish sauce fermented from fish guts and salt in the sun for months; Romans put it in almost everything, rather like Thai fish sauce. Dozens of these hot-food bars have been found at Pompeii, because most poor people’s rented rooms had no kitchen. Romans usually mixed their wine with water before drinking.
In the evening Mother fills the clay lamp with olive oil. The little flame lights the room just enough to see each other’s faces, and black soot streaks the ceiling.
Clay lamps are among the commonest Roman finds. Many are stamped with gods, gladiators or jokes on top, and with a factory mark that shows how far they were sold.
Mother combs your hair with a fine-toothed comb and grumbles that the lice in this town never go away, even in the rich houses.

Archaeologists have found lice combs and nits at many Roman sites. A study of parasites in Roman latrines found that despite baths and sewers, Romans had as many lice, fleas and worms as earlier peoples, perhaps because the bath water was not changed often.
Fire breaks out in a tenement on the next street. Everyone runs out with buckets, and the people on the top floor throw their things out of the windows.
Fire was a daily danger in crowded Roman towns, built of timber and brick and lit by lamps and braziers. The poet Juvenal wrote that the man on the top floor is the last to know the house is burning.
Lightning strikes the big tree in the middle of the village. Priests fence off the spot and forbid anyone to touch it: Jupiter has chosen it.
Romans took lightning as a sign from Jupiter. Places it struck were buried and fenced off as sacred. Etruscan priests had books for reading the meaning of lightning from the direction it struck.
Before a great assembly a priest watches the birds from a hilltop. They fly the wrong way, so the assembly is put off to another day.

Romans read omens from the flight of birds, the auspicium; English auspicious comes from it. Some politicians used bad omens to postpone meetings they disliked. Sacred chickens on warships were watched too: if they wouldn’t eat, it was no day to fight.
Every morning Father puts bread and a drop of wine at the little household shrine, painted with two household gods and a snake.
Almost every Roman house had a lararium shrine for the household gods, the Lares. The painted snake stood for the family’s guardian spirit. Hundreds of these shrines survive in houses at Pompeii.
The master is in a foul mood and you are beaten for breaking a dish. Another slave whispers that he is saving coin by coin to buy his freedom.

Roman slaves had no legal rights and could be harshly punished. Some were allowed to keep savings and use them to buy their freedom. Household slaves in rich town houses had a far better chance of freedom than those in mines and on estates.
The family visits the ancestors’ tomb by the road outside town, leaving roses, bread and wine, and eating a meal together beside it. Some tombs have a pipe for pouring wine down to the dead.

At the Parentalia in February and the rose festival in summer, Romans dined with their dead at the tomb, much like ancestor rites in many Asian cultures. Some tombs had pipes for pouring drinks down to the dead.
The whole town talks of a famous gladiator. A wall scrawl calls him “the girls’ heart-throb”, and shops sell lamps with his picture.

A Pompeii wall calls the gladiator Celadus “the girls’ heart-throb”. Most gladiators were slaves or prisoners of war, but a few stars were as famous as athletes today, and their pictures appeared on lamps and cups.
At the theatre the crowd boos a bad actor. Actors are looked down on and cannot be full citizens, yet some stars have fans who brawl over them.
Actors in Rome had low status; many were slaves or freedmen. Yet the pantomime, a single dancer playing every role, was so popular that some emperors had to banish performers when their fans rioted.
The great grain ship from Egypt arrives and the whole harbour turns out to watch. The sailing season has opened: from late spring to early autumn. After that, hardly anyone dares go to sea.

Rome imported hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain a year, mostly from Egypt and North Africa, and the city’s poor got a free monthly grain dole. Roman ships hardly sailed in winter, because of storms and skies too cloudy to steer by the stars.
A trader is back from India with sacks of black pepper, cotton cloth and pearls. More than a hundred ships sail there every year on the monsoon, he says.

The geographer Strabo wrote that under Augustus about 120 ships sailed from Egypt to India each year. The Muziris papyrus records a contract for Indian cargo, and many Roman coins have been found in south India and Sri Lanka. In Thailand too, beads and pieces imitating Roman coins have been found.
A flower seller goes by with garlands of roses and violets. Weddings, funerals and banquets all need flowers.
At Pompeii there are paintings of garland-makers and gardens growing flowers for sale. Romans wore flower garlands at banquets and scattered rose petals on graves.
A cobbler in the alley hammers iron hobnails into soldiers’ boots. Every soldier’s step rings on the paving stones.
Roman soldiers’ boots had dozens of iron hobnails in the soles for long marches. Thousands of leather shoes have been found at Vindolanda, belonging to soldiers, women and children.
The money-changer bites the denarius you hand him and gives it back: a fake, he says, just a thin skin of silver over copper.

Fake coins, silver-plated over a copper core, are common Roman finds; some are so good archaeologists need instruments to spot them. Emperors also used coins to spread news (victories, festivals, the face of an heir), like advertisements everyone carried around.
In the courtyard grown-ups play a board game scratched into the paving, throwing dice to move their pieces. The children watch and learn new curses.

Game boards scratched into steps and paving are found all over the Roman world, including on the steps of buildings in the Roman Forum. Ludus latrunculorum was a strategy board game rather like draughts.
A toothache keeps you awake all night. The doctor suggests rinsing with wine and herbs; the old folk say the best mouthwash is urine.

Roman teeth from Pompeii are better than expected, as people ate little sugar, but worn down by grit in stone-ground flour. The poet Catullus mocked a Spaniard for brushing his teeth with urine. Dentistry meant pulling teeth.
A Greek doctor opens his instrument case: bronze scalpels, forceps and a speculum. A wound must be kept clean, he says, and the body’s four humours kept in balance. Nobody knows about germs.

The “House of the Surgeon” at Pompeii held more than 40 instruments. Roman doctors followed the Greek theory of four bodily humours, used herbs, and knew wounds should be kept clean, but infection was a common killer, since no one yet knew about germs.
The soldiers in the fort speak many languages: Germans, Syrians, North Africans and locals. The one everyone understands is soldiers’ Latin, thick with curses.

Rome’s auxiliaries came from every corner of the Empire; units on Hadrian’s Wall came from Syria, Iraq and North Africa. The tombstone of a woman named Regina at South Shields is inscribed in Latin and in the Aramaic of her Syrian husband. Soldiers mixed with locals, and their everyday Latin is the root of French, Spanish and Portuguese.
A farmer ploughs up a strange object: a bronze twelve-sided shape with a hole of a different size in each face and little knobs on the corners. Nobody knows what it is for.

Over a hundred bronze dodecahedra like this have been found, mostly in Gaul and Britain. No ancient text says what they were for. Suggestions include a measuring device, a calendar, a toy, or a tool for knitting gloves ✦. They remain a mystery.
The army besieges a hilltop town. Engineers build a wheeled wooden tower, great stone-throwers and an earth ramp up to the walls. The crash of stone on stone goes on day and night.

The siege ramp the Romans built at Masada in 73–74 CE can still be seen today. Roman engineers used torsion-powered bolt- and stone-throwers, and messages travelled by mounted couriers, fire signals and relay stations along the roads.

After a full day’s march everyone must dig a ditch, raise an earth bank and plant a stake fence. Every unit’s tents go up in the same layout every night, so even somewhere new you can find your own tent in the dark.

Roman marching camps followed the same plan every time. Many European towns began as Roman forts, including English towns ending in -chester, from Latin castra, “camp”. In the army, disease and cold killed more soldiers than battle.
A slave empties a chamber pot into the street and you are nearly hit from an upper window. A great sewer runs under the main street, but the little alleys stink every summer.
Rome’s great sewer, the Cloaca Maxima, still partly works today, but most houses were not connected to it. Roman law had rules for compensating people hit by things thrown from windows.
At the grape harvest the whole village treads grapes together in a stone vat, singing as they go. The juice runs down into clay jars buried in the ground.
Roman wine and oil jars were so numerous that a hill in Rome, Monte Testaccio, is made of the broken pieces of some 50 million olive-oil jars.
On the Sabbath the whole village rests. No one lights a fire or travels far, and the Roman soldiers stationed there grumble that they can’t find any workers.
Jews in Roman times kept the Sabbath every week, which some Roman writers found strange. Yet a regular weekly day of rest became a custom most of the world follows today.
Your knees ache when winter comes. You sit at the door telling the grandchildren that bread used to cost half as much.
The neighbour’s young slave asks you to write his name on a wax tablet; he wants to see what his name looks like.
Romans jotted notes on wax-covered wooden tablets with a metal stylus, then smoothed the wax with its flat end to write again. English style comes from Latin stilus, the name of that pen.
Carts rumble all night, since they are banned from town by day.
The smell of baking bread drifts out before dawn.
Children roll walnuts in the alley.
Hawkers shout over each other in the market.
The corner fountain never stops running.
A donkey turns the millstone in the bakery.
Someone has written on a wall that the neighbour owes money.
Soldiers pass, hobnails ringing on the stones.
The geese in the yard honk at a stranger.
Smoke rises from the bathhouse every afternoon.
the Antonine Plague
wounds in the arena
a tenement fire
the hot ash of Vesuvius
No rain all season. The wheat withers, and the price of bread soars until the poor queue for the free grain dole for blocks.
A violent earthquake. Tall tenements collapse, temple columns crack, and the fountains stop running.
A great storm from the sea sinks several grain ships, and the harbour fills with broken jars.
The river bursts its banks, flooding the low streets waist-deep and ruining the granaries.
After you, Rome will rule the whole Mediterranean. But the wealth of conquest will make the rich richer and the poor poorer, and generals will start using their armies to fight each other for power.
After you, the civil wars will end when Caesar’s adopted great-nephew beats everyone and calls himself Augustus. The Republic will keep its name, but the emperor will decide everything.

After you, the Empire will have nearly two hundred years of peace, with roads and aqueducts reaching every corner. Then will come plagues, emperors made and murdered by soldiers one after another, and coins with less silver every year.
After you, the western Empire will break up into Germanic kingdoms, while the East goes on calling itself “Roman” for another thousand years, until Constantinople falls in 1453.

Rome left more than ruins. Latin became French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian. Roman law is a root of the law of many countries, including Thailand’s Civil and Commercial Code. The calendar Caesar reformed is the ancestor of the one used in Thailand today, and Christianity, which began with a Jewish teacher in a small province of the Empire, spread across the world along Rome’s roads. Yet this empire was built on conquest and the labour of millions of slaves. Citizenship spread to every free person, but never to the enslaved.
Two thousand years after you, many people still think about the Roman Empire every day.
You won the olive crown at Olympia; your name may have been carved in your home town.
You went from Marathon to Athens as in the tale, two thousand years before there was a marathon race.

You saw an image of the Buddha in the Roman Empire. In the same centuries, at U Thong and Khlong Thom in Thailand, people made ornaments imitating Roman emperors’ coins. The two worlds already knew each other through the sea trade.
You gave up your grandparents’ beer for Roman wine. Centuries later Gaul would become France, the land of wine.
You were born a slave and died free, which was more possible in Rome than in many slave societies, though still the lucky few.
You survived the day your city fell.

Romans mostly cremated their dead until around the 2nd century, when burial became more common. The law forbade burial inside towns, so tombs lined the roads outside the walls. Epitaphs often began D·M, “To the spirits of the departed”, giving the name, the trade, the age in years, months and days; some speak to passers-by. The poor pooled money in burial clubs to be sure of a grave.
Carve on the tomb: “I was what you are; you will be what I am”
Passers-by stop to read it, then walk on a little faster.
Put a lamp and a coin in the grave
A little lamp for the dark, a coin for the ferryman, just in case.
Pay up the burial club dues
The club members all turn out and walk to the tomb with pipes and song.
Your body is carried to the forum behind relatives wearing the wax masks of your ancestors, then burned on a pyre outside town. The ashes go into a marble urn in the family tomb by the road.
The household’s slave burial club pays for your cremation and sets your little urn in a niche of a shared tomb, with your one name written beneath.
Your family cremates you and buries the ashes in a clay pot in the roadside cemetery, under a small stone with your name.
Romans believed Rome was founded by a boy raised by a wolf. If you told a child the founding story of your own town or village, what would it be?
Rome gave citizenship to every free person, but never to slaves. Who today works for a society but still lacks the rights others have?

D·M stands for Dis Manibus, “to the spirits of the departed”. The game’s stone is only an imitation.
