A name on clay
At the temple granary a scribe presses signs into clay: 29,086 measures of barley, 37 months, and at the end two more signs that read “Kushim”.

A tablet from Uruk of around 3100–3000 BCE bears the word “Kushim”. Many scholars think it names the official in charge, perhaps the oldest known name of a person, though some think it is a title ✦. The first person whose name history recorded may have been an accountant, not a king.
Ask him to write your name too
He laughs: there is no sign for your name yet. Someone will have to invent one.
Help count the sacks
You miscount by two sacks. Kushim corrects it without a word.
The king of Kish
The procession of King Enmebaragesi of Kish brings a stone vase carved with his name to the temple. People say he fought as far as the mountains of Elam and brought back the enemy’s weapons.

Enmebaragesi, around 2600 BCE, is the first king on the Sumerian King List whose existence is confirmed by inscriptions of his own time: his name survives on fragments of stone vases. In a poem about Gilgamesh, his son Agga besieges Uruk ✦.
Bow down with the others
The king looks over your head, but you see the vase up close.
Ask a soldier about Elam
He tells of mountains with snow on them, which you do not believe exist.
Gilgamesh’s wall
The young king of Uruk, Gilgamesh, has drafted the whole city to build a brick wall around it. He inspects the work himself every day. The old folk grumble that he gives nobody’s children any rest.

Gilgamesh may have been a real king of Uruk around 2700 BCE, but the epic in which he seeks immortality, fights the Bull of Heaven and loses his friend Enkidu is legend ✦. In the epic, the people complain to the gods that Gilgamesh oppresses the young. The walls of Uruk ran about 9 km.
Go and lay bricks
Two thousand years later people still sing of the wall you helped build.
Slip off to work in the fields
Nobody comes looking. The king has more workers than he can count.
The queen’s funeral
Queen Puabi has died. Her body, crowned with golden leaves and covered in lapis and carnelian beads, is carried down into a deep tomb. Dozens of attendants follow her down, and none come back up.

The Royal Tombs of Ur, around 2500 BCE, were excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s. The largest pit held the bodies of 74 attendants. Scholars still debate whether they died willingly or were killed; scans of two skulls in 2009 found signs of blows to the head.
Lyre music rises from the deep pit, then falls silent. You dream of it for years.
Go home and hold your family
That night your small house feels warmer than any palace.
The Stele of the Vultures

After beating Umma in a war over a border canal, King Eannatum of Lagash sets up a stone carved with soldiers in a tight wall of shields, marching over enemy corpses, and vultures flying off with heads.

The Stele of the Vultures, around 2450 BCE, is one of the oldest war monuments and the oldest known image of soldiers fighting in a shield wall. Lagash and Umma fought over the same strip of land for generations. Its fragments are in the Louvre.
Look for yourself among the soldiers
Every soldier has the same face. Only the king is big.
Look at the vultures
You think of the relatives who did not come back from the war.
Return to mother

The new king of Lagash, Uruinimgina, proclaims the cancelling of debts, sends debt-slaves home to their families, forbids the rich to force poor men to sell their donkeys, and bars officials from preying on widows and orphans. The proclamation is called amargi.

Uruinimgina’s reforms of around 2350 BCE are among the oldest recorded attempts at social reform. Amargi literally means “return to mother”, going home free, and is often called the oldest known word for freedom. A few years later Lagash was overrun by Umma.
Go and bring a debt-slave relative home
Your uncle weeps the whole way home.
Wonder how long it will last
You are right to wonder: within a few years the city falls. But the word survives.
A king in a neck stock
Sargon of Akkad’s soldiers drag Lugalzagesi, the defeated king of Uruk, in a neck stock to the gate of Enlil’s temple at Nippur, for everyone to see.

Around 2334 BCE Sargon united the Sumerian cities and lands around them into one of the world’s first empires. His inscriptions tell of Lugalzagesi in the neck stock. The story that his mother set him adrift in a basket on the river, like Moses, is a much later legend ✦.
Jeer at the beaten king
Yesterday he was a king. You begin to think high places are not always safe.
Get a good look at Sargon
He is not as tall as you expected, but everyone steps out of his way.
A hymn with a signature
The high priestess of the moon god at Ur is Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon. She composes hymns to the goddess Inanna so moving the whole temple weeps, and at the end of a hymn she puts her own name.

Enheduanna, around 2285 BCE, is the first author in history whose name we know, man or woman. In one hymn she tells of being driven from her temple in a revolt and later restored. Her hymns were copied in scribal schools for centuries.
Learn the hymn by heart
You can sing one verse into old age, never knowing people will still read it four thousand years later.
Ask why she put her name in it
She says, “So the goddess knows who is singing.”
The king who became a god
King Naram-Sin of Akkad has his name written with the sign for a god in front of it, like a deity’s. The priests at Nippur whisper that Enlil will not be pleased.

Naram-Sin (about 2254–2218 BCE) was the first Mesopotamian king to call himself a god; his victory stele is in the Louvre. Centuries later a poem, the Curse of Agade, blamed his destruction of Enlil’s temple for the empire’s fall ✦, which historians do not believe happened.
Make an offering to the king
The soldiers nod approvingly. The priests watch you out of the corner of their eyes.
Make your offering to Enlil instead
You are not sure which god is watching, so you choose the older one.
Gudea’s dream
King Gudea of Lagash says the god Ningirsu came to him in a dream and ordered a new temple. The whole city must stop quarrelling, wash clean, and come to help mould the first brick.

Gudea ruled Lagash around 2144–2124 BCE. About two dozen of his black diorite statues survive, several inscribed with the story of his dream and the temple building. The diorite came from far away, perhaps from today’s Oman.
Help mould the first brick
Everyone sings as the brick dries. No one quarrels all day, which has never happened before.
Ask if the dream was real
Your neighbour says, “The temple will be real,” which is answer enough.
Fines in silver
At the city gate an official reads out King Ur-Nammu’s laws: whoever cuts off another man’s foot pays ten shekels of silver; whoever knocks out a tooth pays two.

The Code of Ur-Nammu, around 2100 BCE, is the oldest surviving law code, some three hundred years older than Hammurabi’s. Many injuries were punished with fines in silver rather than an eye for an eye. Ur-Nammu also began the great ziggurat of Ur, which still stands.
Count your own teeth
Your teeth are worth two shekels each. You smile more carefully.
Go and sue the neighbour who punched you
The judge makes him pay, and the neighbour never greets you again.
The king who ran
Word is that King Shulgi will run from Nippur to Ur and back in a single day, to attend the festival in both cities. People line the road to watch.

In a hymn Shulgi had written about himself (he reigned about 2094–2047 BCE), he claims to have run from Nippur to Ur and back, some 160 km each way, in a single day ✦. Shulgi also claimed to speak five languages and never forget a lesson.
Run after the king for a while
You give out before the first canal. The king vanishes in the dust.
Bet that he can’t do it
No one dares take your bet, in case the soldiers hear.
Ur falls
Elamites from the mountains storm Ur and carry King Ibbi-Sin away as a captive. The moon god’s temple is plundered, and bodies lie in the streets like broken pottery.
Ur was destroyed by the Elamites around 2004 BCE, ending the Third Dynasty of Ur. The poem Lament for Ur mourns it, one of the oldest laments for a fallen city.
Flee towards the marshes
Survived the fall of Ur
You hide in the reeds for three days and return to a city as quiet as a tomb.
Hide the family’s tablets
You bury them under the floor. In this game, they may still be waiting for an archaeologist.
The stone of laws

In the temple stands a black stone taller than a man. At the top Hammurabi receives the laws from the sun god; below are nearly three hundred laws. Anyone who cannot read may have a scribe read them aloud.

Hammurabi’s stele, around 1754 BCE, is in the Louvre. Some laws are “an eye for an eye”, but only between nobles; injuring a commoner or a slave was paid for in silver, so the law was not the same for everyone. Hammurabi said he wrote it “so that the strong should not oppress the weak”.
Pay a scribe to read the laws that concern you
You learn that if your field dyke breaks and floods your neighbour’s field, you must pay. You go home and mend the dyke at once.
Ask why the laws are not equal
The scribe glances left and right and tells you to ask more quietly.
Bad copper

The house next door belongs to a copper merchant named Ea-nasir. Today another clay letter arrives: a man named Nanni complains the copper he received was poor, and that his servant was sent away empty-handed.

Nanni’s letter to Ea-nasir, around 1750 BCE, is in the British Museum and is often called the world’s oldest customer complaint. Archaeologists found several complaints in Ea-nasir’s own house, which has made him an internet meme.
Buy copper from him anyway
Your copper cracks at the first blow. You start writing complaint number eleven.
Listen to the customers shouting outside his door
Better than any show, and free.
The king who dug
King Nabonidus has the ground dug beneath the sun god’s temple at Sippar. The workers find an inscription of King Naram-Sin. The king announces it is 3,200 years old and has it carefully reburied.

Nabonidus (ruled 556–539 BCE) is often called the first archaeologist, because he dug for and recorded old inscriptions. He reckoned Naram-Sin lived 3,200 years before him; the real gap was about 1,700. His daughter Ennigaldi-Nanna kept old objects in a room some call the first museum.
Help dig, carefully
You touch a brick made nearly two thousand years before you. Your hands shake.
Grumble that the king cares more for old things than the country
Many grumble the same. A few years later, the Persians arrive.
Cyrus enters the city
Cyrus’s Persian army enters Babylon almost without a fight. The priests open the gates in welcome, and gods seized from other cities are sent home to their own temples.

Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE. The Cyrus Cylinder tells the story from his side; some call it the first charter of human rights, but most historians see it as royal propaganda in the Mesopotamian tradition. Exiled Jews were allowed to go home.
Go to watch the procession
Life in the market goes on as before. Only the soldiers’ language has changed.
Help your Jewish neighbours pack for home
They were born in Babylon, but sing of Jerusalem all the way.
Two crowns
King Narmer appears before the crowd wearing the white crown of the south, and at another ceremony the red crown of the north. People say the land along the Nile now has one king.

The Narmer Palette, around 3100 BCE, shows the king wearing both crowns. Greek historians said a king called Menes united Egypt ✦, perhaps Narmer or Hor-Aha. It is unclear whether unification came from one war or happened gradually over generations.
Cheer the king
You do not know you are cheering the start of three thousand years.
Ask whether taxes will go up
The answer is yes, and for the next three thousand years.
A mountain of stone steps

At Saqqara the master builder Imhotep is stacking six tombs of stone one on top of the other towards the sky. No one has ever built anything so big in stone. Everyone calls it a staircase for the king to climb to heaven.

King Djoser’s Step Pyramid, around 2670 BCE, is one of the oldest large stone buildings in the world. Imhotep was a real man whose name appears on the base of Djoser’s statue; over a thousand years later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine.
You are paid in bread and beer, and watch a man-made mountain grow every month.
Ask Imhotep why not use brick
He says, “Brick lasts a hundred years. Stone lasts for ever.”
Merer’s logbook
You join the boat crew of an inspector named Merer, shipping white limestone from the Tura quarries across the river to Khufu’s pyramid. Merer records every trip on a papyrus roll.

Merer’s diary was found in 2013 at the ancient harbour of Wadi al-Jarf, the oldest inscribed papyri known, around 2560 BCE. It and the workers’ town at Giza show the pyramids were built by fed and paid workers, not slaves as in the films.
Row an extra trip
Merer notes down your crew. In this game, you may be in the oldest papyrus in the world.
Ask how many stones the king needs
Merer says, “More than the stars in the sky,” and goes back to writing.
A letter from the boy king

Harkhuf, governor of Elephantine, returns from a long journey south with a small dancer from a faraway land. Soon a letter arrives from King Pepi II, still a boy, ordering him brought with the greatest care, with men watching all night so he doesn’t fall in the river.

Harkhuf had Pepi II’s letter, of around 2270 BCE, carved on the front of his tomb at Aswan. It is one of the liveliest letters from ancient Egypt: a king of about eight so excited he orders the dancer checked on ten times a night.
Volunteer to keep watch on the boat
At midnight the dancer teaches you one step. You remember it into old age.
Laugh at the king’s letter
The king is a child like any other. You feel closer to him.
Driving out the foreigners
Ahmose’s army from Thebes sails north against the Hyksos, who have ruled northern Egypt for a hundred years. Some soldiers drive chariots taken from the enemy himself.

The Hyksos, “rulers of foreign lands”, ruled northern Egypt for about a century until Ahmose drove them out around 1550 BCE and began the New Kingdom. Egyptians took up the horse and chariot widely in this period.
Go and see the horses up close
The beast runs three times faster than a donkey. You want one.
Send bread to the soldiers
A young soldier smiles at you. You hope he comes back.
Ships from Punt
Pharaoh Hatshepsut’s ships come back from the land of Punt in the south, loaded with whole incense trees, roots still in baskets, baboons, ivory and leopard skins. All Thebes comes down to the quay.

Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh who ruled around 1479–1458 BCE. Reliefs in her temple at Deir el-Bahari show the expedition to Punt, including the queen of Punt. Punt probably lay around Eritrea or Somalia. After her death many of her images were destroyed.
Smell the incense from a living tree
The scent makes you dizzy. Next year these trees will grow before the temple.
Go to see the baboons
One snatches your bread, and the whole quay laughs.
The narrow pass

Thutmose III brings the army before the city of Megiddo. Every general begs him to go round by the wide road, but the pharaoh chooses a narrow pass where soldiers must walk in single file, and leads the way himself.

The Battle of Megiddo in 1457 BCE is the first battle recorded in detail, on the walls of Karnak. The enemy never expected an army through the narrow pass and broke, but the Egyptian soldiers stopped to loot the enemy camp, so the city had to be besieged for seven more months.
Follow the pharaoh into the pass
Fought at Megiddo
All night you walk in the dark, feeling the breath of the men ahead and behind.
Loot the enemy camp
You get one gold ring, and seven months of your general’s curses.
A single god
In a new city in the desert, Pharaoh Akhenaten worships only one god, the sun disc Aten. The carvings show sunbeams ending in little hands, holding out life to the pharaoh and Queen Nefertiti.

Akhenaten ruled around 1353–1336 BCE, moved the capital to Amarna and tried to push aside the other gods. Carvings of the time show the royal family playing affectionately with their children, unlike other Egyptian art. After his death the city was abandoned and his name struck from the king lists.
Sing the hymn to the Aten
“You rise beautiful on the horizon,” you sing every morning, though a figure of Taweret is still hidden at home.
Ask where the other gods have gone
No one answers, but the workers here still wear charms of the old gods under their clothes.
The sculptor’s workshop
In the workshop of a sculptor named Thutmose stands a painted bust of Queen Nefertiti. One eye has not yet been inlaid; the sculptor uses it as a model for his apprentices.

The bust of Nefertiti was found in 1912 in the ruins of a workshop at Amarna, where the name Thutmose appears on an ivory piece found in the same place. It is in a Berlin museum today, and Egypt still asks for it back. The empty left eye may be because it was a teaching model.
Ask to be an apprentice
You polish limestone for three months before you are allowed to touch paint.
Ask why the other eye is missing
He smiles: “So the pupils can see how an eye is made.” Three thousand years later, people still ask the same question.
The young pharaoh
Pharaoh Tutankhamun has died at about nineteen. His tomb was not ready in time, and the craftsmen must hurry to cram gold, furniture and chariots into small rooms until they are packed full.

Tutankhamun died around 1323 BCE after restoring the old gods. His tomb was found almost intact by Howard Carter in 1922. The “curse of the pharaoh” was a newspaper invention ✦; most of the expedition lived long lives.
Help finish the wall paintings in time
Your painting has one drip of paint in it. In this game, tourists will stand looking at it three thousand years later.
Weep with the funeral procession
He was younger than you. Death does not care who is pharaoh.
Peace with the enemy
Envoys return with a treaty engraved on silver. Ramesses II and the Hittite king, old enemies from Kadesh, agree to be brothers, never to fight again, and to send back each other’s runaways.

The Treaty of Kadesh, around 1259 BCE, is the oldest peace treaty to survive in full from both sides: the Egyptian version carved on temple walls, the Hittite on a clay tablet in Akkadian. A replica of that tablet hangs at the United Nations headquarters.
Celebrate with the neighbours
Mothers of soldier sons weep with relief.
Wonder whether the kings will keep their word
Surprisingly, they do, until both kingdoms have far bigger problems.
The Great Bath

On the high mound in the middle of the city, workers lay fired bricks tightly into a long pool with steps down at both ends, then seal it with bitumen so no water leaks. No one tells you what the pool is for.

The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, around 2500 BCE, is one of the oldest public water tanks in the world, about 12 m long and 2.4 m deep. Archaeologists think it may have been used for ritual cleansing, but since the Indus script cannot be read, no one knows for sure.
Help spread the bitumen
Your hands stay black for a week, but the pool will not leak for four and a half thousand years.
Sneak down to dip your feet
An old man chases you out. You still don’t know what you did wrong.
The tilting ground
In the middle of the night the ground at Kalibangan shakes violently. House walls tilt, the street cracks into steps, and some wells run dry overnight.

Archaeologists found tilted walls and displaced layers at Kalibangan from around 2600 BCE, interpreted as one of the oldest excavated traces of an earthquake. Afterwards the town was rebuilt on the planned grid of the mature Indus cities.
Get everyone out of the house
Survived the Kalibangan earthquake
Your house still stands, but nobody dares sleep inside for a month.
Help rebuild on the new street plan
The new streets are straight as if drawn with a rule. You like them better.
News from a king in the west

Sailors back from the city of Akkad in the west say the king there, Sargon, boasts that ships from the land of “Meluhha” moor at his quay, and that a man there earns his living interpreting your language.

Sargon’s inscriptions of around 2300 BCE mention ships from Meluhha at the quay of Akkad, and most scholars think Meluhha was the Indus civilisation. A seal of a man named Shu-ilishu calls him “interpreter of the Meluhhan language”. Many Indus-style seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia.
Ask the sailors to teach you words of their language
You only remember the words for “beer” and “too expensive”.
Send carnelian beads with the next ship
In this game, your beads may end up in a royal tomb at Ur.
Big letters over the gate
Craftsmen set pieces of white stone into a long wooden board to make ten signs, each as big as a man’s head, and mount it over the city gate for everyone coming in to see.

The Dholavira signboard bears ten Indus signs, each about 37 cm tall; it was found fallen in a room beside the north gate. It is the largest public Indus inscription known. No one can read it: it might be the city’s name, a ruler’s, or a blessing.
Ask what it says
The craftsman tells you, and you nod. Four thousand years later, no one knows the answer any more.
Copy the signs in the sand
The fish sign is the one you draw best.
The great basin
At Lothal workers dig a brick basin longer than any field, with a sluice to the river. Some say it is for ships, some for storing fresh water, and they argue about it all day.
The brick basin at Lothal, about 220 by 37 m, was interpreted by Indian archaeologists as the world’s oldest dockyard, though some scholars argue it was a water reservoir. The debate is not settled.
Side with the dockyard camp
Four thousand years later, scholars are having the same argument as you.
Side with the reservoir camp
The bearded man of stone

In a large house near the central mound stands a stone figure of a bearded man, eyes half closed, wrapped in a cloak patterned with trefoils, a band around his head. No one in the city can tell you whether he is a king, a priest or an ancestor.

The figure archaeologists call the “Priest-King” is only about 17.5 cm tall and was found in 1927. The name is the archaeologists’ own; there is no evidence the Indus civilisation had kings or priests of that kind. Indus cities had no great palaces or royal tombs like Egypt’s or Mesopotamia’s.
Bow to the figure
You do not know who you are bowing to, but it feels right.
Look closely at the cloak pattern
The trefoils still have traces of red. You go home and weave the same pattern.
The disc no one can read

A merchant from Phaistos shows a round clay disc stamped on both sides with little pictures spiralling to the centre: a plumed head, a fish, a shield, a flower. He says even the palace scribes cannot read it.

The Phaistos Disc was found in 1908 in the palace of Phaistos on Crete and may date to around 1700 BCE. Its 241 signs were pressed in with stamps, which some call the oldest “printing”. No one has deciphered it, and some scholars even suspect it is a fake ✦.
Buy the disc
You can’t read it either, but it makes the house look expensive.
Try to guess what it says
You guess it is a song. Thirty-seven centuries later, people are still guessing the same.
The warrior and the seal

A high-ranking warrior has died and is buried with bronze swords, combs, a mirror, gold rings and a tiny stone seal carved with a battle scene so fine you must squint to see it. Many of the things came from Crete.

The tomb of the “Griffin Warrior”, around 1450 BCE, was found at Pylos in 2015. Its Pylos Combat Agate is only 3.6 cm long but so detailed scholars study it under microscopes. It shows how much mainland Greeks had absorbed of Minoan culture.
Look at the seal up close
You count three men in the scene, and every muscle on them.
Help carry the coffin
His family gives you a copper ring as a keepsake.
The palace in flames

Palaces and great houses all over Crete burn, all but Knossos. Soon people who speak a different tongue, from the mainland, are running the palace, and the scribes start keeping accounts in a new script.

Around 1450 BCE most Minoan centres were destroyed and Mycenaeans from the mainland took control of Knossos. The palace tablets switched from Linear A, still unread, to Linear B, an early form of Greek deciphered in 1952.
Learn the new script
The new scribes laugh at your accent, but teach you anyway.
Keep a tablet in the old script
Soon no one will be able to read it, not even in your own house.
The Lion Gate
At Mycenae workers heave stones weighing many tons into the walls, and set above the gate a slab carved with two lions facing a column.

The Lion Gate of Mycenae, around 1250 BCE, is the oldest large sculpture in Europe still standing where it was made. Later Greeks thought only the giant Cyclopes could have lifted such stones ✦, and the walls are still called “Cyclopean”.
Help push stones up the ramp
No giants needed: just enough men, rope and beer.
Watch the lions being carved
The heads are made separately and fixed on. Three thousand years later both heads are gone.
The great ship that never came home

A great merchant ship leaves harbour carrying ten tons of copper in oxhide-shaped ingots, a ton of tin, blue glass, ebony, ivory and gold. A month later word comes that it struck a rocky cape and sank.

The Uluburun wreck, around 1300 BCE, was found off Turkey in 1982 by a sponge diver. Its cargo came from many cultures, including a gold scarab bearing Queen Nefertiti’s name, evidence of how widely Bronze Age trade linked the world. Ten parts copper to one of tin is the recipe for bronze.
Help load the copper ingots
Each ingot weighs as much as you. Three thousand years later, archaeologists will lift it from the seabed.
Mourn the sailors
There is no grave to visit, only the sea, looking as calm as ever.
A letter to a brother

Envoys return from the Hittite lands in Anatolia with a clay letter from the Hittite king. In it, one of the greatest kings in the world calls your king “my brother”, then complains about a raider hiding in your lands.

Several Hittite royal letters mention a land called Ahhiyawa, which most scholars identify with the Mycenaean Greeks. In the Tawagalawa letter of around 1250 BCE the Hittite king calls the king of Ahhiyawa his brother and asks him to hand over a raider named Piyamaradu.
Feel proud of your king
Your king puts on airs for a month. So do the taxes.
Ask who the raider is
No one knows. Or everyone knows and won’t say.
The city on the straits
The warriors of your town are gathering ships to raid Wilusa, the high-walled city on the straits to the east. The leaders promise gold and captives. The old men say they will bring back only bodies.

Hittite records mention a city called Wilusa, which most scholars identify with Troy (Ilios in Greek). Troy VII was destroyed around 1180 BCE. The Trojan War of Homer’s epic, with its wooden horse and Helen, is legend ✦; how much of it happened no one knows.
Join the raid
An arrow from the walls takes you in the thigh. You come home empty-handed and limp for the rest of your life.
You come back with one copper cup and a story that grows longer every year.
Half of those who went never return. Those who do tell stories until they become songs.
The enemy ships have come

In the palace a scribe writes the king’s letter to the king of Cyprus: “My father, behold, the enemy’s ships came; my cities were burned, and they did evil things in my country. All my troops are far away in the Hittite land.”

Ugarit was destroyed around 1185 BCE in the Bronze Age collapse. This letter was found in the palace archives; the popular story that the tablets were still in a kiln, waiting to be sent when the city fell, is a misunderstanding passed down ✦. Ugarit also gave us one of the oldest alphabets, written in cuneiform signs.
Help carry the letter to the harbour
The sea is full of strange sails. You are not sure the messenger ship can get out.
Escaped Ugarit before it fell
From the hills you watch smoke rise from a city no one will ever rebuild.
The fire that saved the words
The palace of Pylos goes up in flames. The archive room, full of clay tablets listing sheep, oil and rowers, grows so hot that the unbaked tablets are fired as hard as pottery.

About a thousand Linear B tablets survive because fire swept the palace of Pylos around 1180 BCE; clay records were normally temporary and unbaked. Some of the last tablets mention sending rowers to guard the coast, as if danger were known to be coming.
Help fight the fire
The fire is too strong. All you can do is get people out.
Flee to the mountains
Survived the burning of Pylos
The world of the palaces ends in a night. Life in the mountain villages goes on.
News from Egypt

A trader says Pharaoh Ramesses III has defeated the “Sea Peoples” at the mouths of the Nile and had the battles on land and water carved on the walls of a great temple. Some survivors have fled back to your coast.

The reliefs at Medinet Habu, around 1177 BCE, show the oldest surviving picture of a sea battle. “Sea Peoples” is a modern scholars’ name for several groups on the move by sea during the Bronze Age collapse, who were invaders and refugees at once.
Feed the survivors
They speak a tongue you don’t know, but hunger is understood in every language.
Drive them from the harbour
Their boats put to sea again. You don’t know where they will land.
The biggest bronze
Hundreds of casters pour molten bronze from dozens of crucibles at once into a clay mould the size of a room, making a four-legged cauldron for the late mother of the king.

The Houmuwu (or Simuwu) ding, weighing 832.84 kg, is the largest known Shang bronze, made around the 13th–12th century BCE. Villagers dug it up in 1939 and reburied it to hide it from Japanese soldiers during the war. It is now in the National Museum of China.
Help work the bellows
Half your eyebrows are singed, but the vessel comes out perfect.
Count the crucibles
You count seventy before everything turns to smoke and light.
Burying the masks

The people of the river city dig great pits, break and burn bronze masks with bulging eyes, bronze heads, hundreds of elephant tusks and a bronze tree taller than a man, then bury it all. No one tells you why.

The pits at Sanxingdui in Sichuan were found in 1986, and six more in 2019–2022. New dating suggests they were filled around 1100 BCE. The culture was very different from the Shang and left no writing; why they smashed and buried such treasures is still a mystery.
Help carry the tusks
The tusks are heavy and cold. You feel you are burying something bigger than things.
Secretly keep a little scrap of gold foil
You hide it all your life and never dare show anyone.
A lake of wine, a forest of meat
Rumour from the palace says King Di Xin has dug a pool filled with wine deep enough to row a boat in, and hung meat from the trees like a forest, where naked guests chase each other all night.

The tale of the “lake of wine and forest of meat” of Di Xin, last Shang king, was written by later historians drawing on the stories of the victorious Zhou ✦. There may be some truth in it, but winners tend to paint losers as monsters to justify taking power.
Believe the rumour
You pass it on, and the story grows each time.
Wonder who is spreading it
Most of the tellers have just come back from the west, where the Zhou are gathering strength.
The prisoner who drew lines

Ji Chang, Lord of the West and head of the Zhou, has been imprisoned by the Shang king at Youli. People say that in prison he lays out sticks in whole and broken lines, arranging them into sixty-four figures of six lines each.

Chinese tradition says King Wen of Zhou arranged the 64 hexagrams of the Yijing (I Ching) while imprisoned ✦. Modern scholars think the book grew out of early Zhou divination over a long time, not from one man.
Smuggle food in to him
He says nothing but sends back a figure of sticks. You don’t understand it, but keep it.
Try laying out the sticks yourself
You get to ten figures and lose track. Three thousand years later, people around the world still consult this book.
Two brothers on the mountain
Two brothers, Bo Yi and Shu Qi, refuse to accept that the Zhou had the right to overthrow the Shang. They will not eat Zhou grain, and go up Mount Shouyang to live on wild ferns.

The story of Bo Yi and Shu Qi is told by the historian Sima Qian, writing about a thousand years later ✦. The brothers starved on the mountain and became models of loyalty in Chinese culture; Confucius praised them.
Take them grain
They thank you but will not touch it: it was grown on Zhou land.
Think them too stubborn
Three thousand years later, people still argue whether they were heroes or simply stubborn.
A mountain of earth
On an island in the swamps thousands of people carry clay in baskets, heaping it into a mound higher than any tree in the forest. The leaders say it is a sacred mountain made by human hands.
The Great Pyramid of La Venta is built of clay, about 30 m tall, one of the oldest pyramids in Mesoamerica, around 900–400 BCE. It may imitate the volcanoes of the nearby Tuxtla mountains.
Carry basket after basket of clay
You carry three hundred baskets. The mountain rises by the width of a finger.
Climb up to see the swamps from the top
For the first time in your life you see the rivers, the sea and the far-off volcanoes.
Burying the most beautiful thing

Craftsmen lay hundreds of green serpentine blocks into a huge jaguar-face mosaic on the ground. It takes months. When it is finished, everyone helps cover it with earth until nothing shows, and no one sees it again.

At La Venta archaeologists found “massive offerings”: thousands of tons of serpentine blocks buried underground, and mosaic pavements of animal faces covered over as soon as they were finished. Burying such wealth may have been an offering to the underworld.
Help lay the stones
You set the jaguar’s eye: the most beautiful work you will ever do, and no one will ever see it.
The shaman says, “Because the most beautiful things belong to the gods below.”
Sixteen stone figures

The priests set sixteen little jade and stone figures in a circle, with six stone celts standing behind them like a wall. One figure stands with its back to the wall, and all the others face it. Then the whole scene is buried.

Offering 4 at La Venta is a buried scene of 16 figurines and 6 celts. Remarkably, years later someone dug a small hole precisely down to the figures’ heads and then filled it in again, showing someone remembered exactly where it was. What the scene meant, no one knows.
Memorise the spot
Years later, in this game, you are the one who digs the little hole to look at it again.
Ask who the figure with its back to the wall is
The priest smiles but won’t say. Three thousand years later, archaeologists are still guessing.
In one lifetime you met or witnessed
, and almost no one knew you were there.
Each ingot weighs as much as a child. Three thousand years later, archaeologists will lift it from the seabed.
Small children were usually not cremated. Your family buries your small body by the river.
One of your children falls ill and dies. Small children were usually not cremated, so the family buries the little body by the river.
the sixteen realms and the wandering teachers
Magadha rises: the Nandas and the Mauryas
the age of Ashoka and his edicts
after the Mauryas: the Shungas, the Greeks, and the scriptures written down

Pataliputra, where the Son meets the Ganges
Savatthi, capital of Kosala
Vesali, the Licchavis’ city, ruled by an assembly
Varanasi, the holy city on the Ganges
the Shakya country, near Kapilavatthu and Lumbini
Vidisha, a merchants’ town near the Sanchi hill
Taxila, the crossroads city of Gandhara
Kalinga, on the eastern sea coast
Anuradhapura, capital of the island of Lanka
a farming village on the Ganges plain
wheat, barley and grapes
rice, pulses, sugar cane and cotton
A sloth bear from the Lankan forest
A tiger from the riverside forest

Rajagaha sat in a ring of five hills, joined by a dry-stone wall some 40 km long whose remains can still be seen. King Bimbisara ruled here in the Buddha’s time; later Magadha’s capital moved to Pataliputra. Its hot springs have drawn bathers since then.

Pataliputra began as a small fort by the river and became the capital of the Nandas and the Mauryas. The Greek envoy Megasthenes recorded a city some 80 stades (about 15 km) long, with 570 towers and 64 gates; archaeologists have dug up stretches of its timber palisade. Today it is Patna, in Bihar.

Savatthi was the capital of Kosala. According to the texts, the Buddha spent more rainy seasons at its Jeta Grove than anywhere else, so many discourses open: “Once the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi.”

Vesali was the city of the Licchavis in the Vajji league, which had no single king but decided great matters in assembly. Some historians call it an early republic, though the voices in the assembly belonged to noble clans, not to everyone.

Varanasi, or Kashi, was a holy city before the Buddha. Its cloth was so famous that the Pali texts use it as the very example of fine fabric. About 10 km away lies the deer park at Isipatana, Sarnath, where the texts say the Buddha first taught.

The Shakyas were a warrior clan governed in assembly. Scholars think the Buddha’s father was probably a clan leader, not the great king of later stories. Where Kapilavatthu stood is still argued over: Tilaurakot in Nepal or Piprahwa in India.
Vidisha was a merchants’ town on the trade route from the Ganges plain to the west. Nearby is the hill of Sanchi, where Ashoka built a stupa and later generations carved its splendid stone gateways.

Taxila sat at the crossroads of India, Persia and Central Asia. It was ruled in turn by Persians, Alexander, the Mauryas, Greeks, Sakas and Kushans. People here wrote in Kharosthi, read right to left, and the oldest surviving Buddhist manuscripts come from this land of Gandhara.
Kalinga lay on the eastern coast. Its seafarers traded across the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia; the Malay word “Keling” for people from India comes from its name.

Anuradhapura was Lanka’s capital for over a thousand years, its people farming with the water of huge reservoirs. The island’s chronicles say Buddhism arrived in Ashoka’s time, and the Pali canon chanted in Thai temples today descends from the line written down on this island.

Most people in the Ganges valley grew rice. Iron axes and ploughshares let them clear the riverside forest for paddy. A village had its headman, its sacred tree, and a steady stream of wandering ascetics of many schools coming to beg for food.

Carver
Carve wood and ivory, and in later times stone railings and gateways for stupas
a child who polishes the carvings

Most work in this age ran in families. Craftsmen of one kind formed guilds called seni, with heads and rules of their own, and some were rich enough to pay for part of a stupa. Those who renounced the world left work and family behind and lived on the food lay people put in their bowls.
a Brahmin family
a khattiya family, of the warrior and ruling class
a householder family of farmers and traders
a family of labourers and craftsmen
a candala family, pushed outside the varnas

Brahmin texts divided society into four varnas: brahmins, khattiyas, vessas and suddas, with some groups such as the candalas pushed outside. Real life was divided far more finely, by birth group and occupation. The Pali texts usually list khattiyas before brahmins, and one discourse teaches that no one is low or high by birth, only by deeds.
black polished pots

a monk or nun in the Buddha’s Sangha

a Nigantha ascetic, a follower of Mahavira
a Nigantha monk
a Nigantha nun
an Ajivika ascetic
The grown-ups talk of the sixteen great realms fighting over the Ganges plain. Magadha and Kosala are growing; the small realms are swallowed one by one.

Buddhist and Jain texts speak of sixteen “great realms”, the mahajanapadas, in this age. Some had kings; some were governed by assemblies of warrior clans. Within about two hundred years Magadha swallowed nearly all of them.
Ajatasattu’s Magadhan army crosses the Ganges against the Vajjis. Vesali falls, and the Licchavi assembly meets no more.

Jain texts say Ajatasattu used two new weapons, a great stone-throwing engine and a chariot fitted with a swinging mace ✦. In the discourses, a minister is sent to ask the Buddha before the war, and he answers that the Vajjis will not decline as long as they meet often and in harmony.
Taxes are up again. People say the Nanda king at Pataliputra has hoarded more gold than anyone can count.

The Nanda dynasty ruled Magadha in the 4th century BCE. Greek and Roman writers heard that the Nanda army was so vast that Alexander’s soldiers refused to march on into the Ganges valley. Indian stories tell of the Nandas’ wealth and greed ✦.
Survived the Kalinga war
The Mauryan army invades Kalinga. Villages burn; people are killed and driven off as captives. Your family flees into the forest.

Ashoka’s Rock Edict 13 says that in the Kalinga war 150,000 people were carried away, 100,000 killed, and many times that number died afterwards. He wrote of his deep remorse. Strikingly, the edicts set up in Kalinga itself leave this passage out.
Word comes that the Yavanas, the Greeks from the north-west, have marched as far as the Ganges valley.
Indians called the Greeks Yavanas, from Ionia. In the 2nd century BCE Greek kings ruling Gandhara pushed deep into India; the grammarian Patanjali and later Puranic texts mention the raid.
The Kosalan army of King Vidudabha storms the Shakya land. The town is burned and many are killed. Your family escapes.

The commentaries say Vidudabha took revenge because the Shakyas had tricked his father into marrying a slave girl’s daughter ✦. It happened shortly before the Buddha’s passing; after that the Shakyas are barely heard of as a realm again.
A merchant shows off a strange gold coin with a man in a leaf crown on it. He says it comes from a far western city called Rome.

In the 1st century Roman ships sailed to South India every year on the monsoon, and hoards of gold and silver coins of Augustus and Tiberius have been found in India. The Roman writer Pliny complained that India drained the Empire of money every year. Players of the Rome chapter may have seen the Buddha at the Red Sea port of Berenike.
You help load sacks of rice onto a cart and are paid in copper coins.

India’s earliest coins were karshapana: bits of silver punched one stamp at a time with symbols such as a sun, an elephant or a hill, with no king’s name and no face. The Pali texts price things in karshapana more than in anything else.
