Kanishka’s “BODDO” coin
Ashvaghosha, the poet of the Buddha’s life
A young ascetic at Rajagaha

A young ascetic of the Shakya clan walks his alms round in Rajagaha so calmly that people stop to stare. The king’s men report it, and King Bimbisara rides out to the foot of the hill to offer him wealth and an army. He declines: he is seeking awakening.

This story is told in the Pabbajja Sutta of the Sutta Nipata, among the earlier layers of the texts. At the time he was just one of hundreds of wandering ascetics in the Ganges valley; no one knew that 2,500 years later hundreds of millions would call him the Buddha.
Put rice in his bowl
He glances at you, thanks you with a nod, and walks on in silence.
Follow to hear what the king says
The king asks him to come back and teach at Rajagaha if he finds what he seeks. You remember that.
The milk-rice

In the village of Uruvela a young woman named Sujata cooks rice in the richest milk to offer to the spirit of the banyan. But at the foot of the tree sits a gaunt ascetic, so she offers the rice to him instead.

The story of Sujata comes from much later commentaries ✦, but its core matches the early discourses, which say the Buddha gave up starving himself and began eating again before his awakening. It also shows villagers already worshipping tree spirits before Buddhism existed.
Help Sujata stir the pot
The rice smells so good that parrots gather round the pot.
Peek at the ascetic eating
He eats slowly, mouthful by mouthful, as though he has not tasted rice in years.
Five men in the deer park
You graze the cattle near the deer park at Isipatana and see five thin ascetics listening all day to another ascetic. He speaks of a middle way, between indulgence and self-torment.

According to the texts this was the first teaching, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which Thais remember on Asalha Bucha day. The ruins at Sarnath today include a pillar of Ashoka whose four-lion capital became India’s national emblem.
Sit and listen too
You don’t understand every word, but you remember “the middle way” all your life.
Drive the cattle home before dark
At home you mention six thin men in the forest. Mother says that forest is always full of odd ascetics.
Two teachers quarrel
In a potter’s workshop at Savatthi, the naked ascetic Makkhali Gosala shouts at Mahavira, a teacher he once wandered with for six years. The whole market crowds in to watch.

The Jain Bhagavati Sutra tells this ✦. Gosala led the Ajivikas, who taught that everything is fixed by fate and human effort changes nothing. The Ajivikas were once big enough for Ashoka to give them caves, but they vanished, and not one of their own texts survives. We know them only through their rivals.
Side with Gosala: fate decides everything
If everything is fixed, there is nothing to worry about. You sleep well that night.
Side with Mahavira: our deeds matter
You walk home taking care not to tread on the ants, for the first time in your life.
Paving the ground with coins

The merchant Anathapindika wants to buy Prince Jeta’s grove to give to the Buddha. The prince jokes that he will sell only if the ground is covered in coins, so the merchant has cartloads of coins brought and laid out for real.

The story is in the Vinaya ✦. A carving on the Bharhut stupa railing, about 2,100 years old, shows a cart of coins and men covering the ground, with a label naming the scene, so the story was already widely told by then. It is in the Indian Museum in Kolkata.
Get hired to lay the coins
You are paid one coin, and privately think the merchant has gone mad.
Ask why he would pay so much
He answers, “So the monks have shelter in the rains,” and goes back to counting coins.
The women who walked barefoot
Mahapajapati, the Buddha’s foster mother, and hundreds of Shakya women shave their heads, put on earth-dyed robes and walk barefoot to Vesali until their feet swell, to ask to be ordained.

According to the Vinaya the Buddha refused three times until Ananda pleaded for them, and the order of nuns began ✦. Many scholars think some of the special rules for nuns were added later. The Therigatha keeps poems said to be by the first nuns, perhaps the oldest literature by women in India.
Wash their feet
An old woman smiles at you and says, “We have walked far, but we are not there yet.”
Ask why women want to renounce
A young woman answers, “Because we grow old, fall sick and die just as men do.”
People in Rajagaha talk of a young physician named Jivaka, once a baby abandoned on a rubbish heap, who studied seven years at Taxila and now treats both the king and the monks.

The Vinaya tells that Jivaka’s teacher sent him to find a plant within a day’s walk that was not a medicine, and he came back saying he could find none ✦. In Thailand Jivaka Komarabhacca is honoured as the father of traditional medicine, and Thai massage practitioners pay respect to him before they begin.
Have Jivaka treat your wound
He smears on a green, very smelly paste. The wound heals in three days.
Ask to be his helper
You learn that every leaf around you can be medicine, if you know how to use it.
The night Pava lit its lamps
Word comes that Mahavira, teacher of the Nigantha ascetics, has passed away at Pava. That night people fill the town with lamps, because the light of knowledge has gone out.

The Jain Kalpa Sutra says eighteen kings lit lamps on the night of Mahavira’s nirvana ✦, and Jains still celebrate it at Diwali. Jain tradition puts it in 527 BCE, but many historians think it was later, close to the Buddha’s time. Buddhist discourses themselves say the Nigantha teacher died at Pava while the Buddha was alive.
Light a lamp at your door
The whole street glows with little flames. You have never seen so lovely a night.
Ask what the teacher taught
“Harm no living thing, not even the smallest insect,” a monk answers, sweeping the ground before he sits.
A king in prison
Prince Ajatasattu has locked up his father, King Bimbisara, and starves him. People whisper that the queen hides food in her hair to smuggle it in.

According to the commentaries and later texts, Ajatasattu seized power from his father ✦. The details differ between Buddhist and Jain texts, but both agree he made Magadha stronger than ever and began the fort that became Pataliputra.
Help the queen smuggle food
The guard stares at you until your heart pounds, but lets you pass.
Keep well away from palace affairs
The affairs of kings are for kings. You have rice to plant.
A fort by the river

At the village of Pataligama, Magadha’s workmen are building a fort by the Ganges. An old ascetic passes with his disciples and says this place will become a great city, threatened by fire, by water and by quarrels.
The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says the Buddha foretold this on his last journey ✦. A few generations later Pataliputra was the capital of the largest empire India had yet known; today it is Patna.
Help haul logs for the palisade
In this game, a log you carried may be one archaeologists dig up two thousand years from now.
Follow to watch the ascetic cross the river
The gate he leaves by is named the Gotama Gate, and the ford he crosses gets the same name.
Ambapali’s mango grove
Ambapali, Vesali’s richest courtesan, invites the Buddha to a meal before the Licchavi princes can. They offer her a hundred thousand coins for the honour, but she refuses.

The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells this; after the meal she gave her mango grove to the Sangha. The Therigatha has verses said to be hers, written when she became a nun in old age, comparing her once glossy black hair with its white age. Some scholars doubt she wrote them herself.
Help prepare the meal
The whole town gossips that a courtesan has beaten every prince in it. You hide a smile.
Go and watch the princes’ sulky procession
Princes in yellow, red and white ride home in their chariots with faces you will describe for years.
Between the twin sal trees

At Kusinara, a small town of the Mallas, the old teacher people call the Buddha falls ill after a meal at a smith’s house and lies down between two sal trees. His last words, people say, are that all things pass away: strive on with care.

The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says that after the cremation the relics were divided into eight shares for eight towns ✦. The year is still argued: Thai tradition counts the Buddhist Era from 543 BCE, while many historians estimate around 400 BCE, the figure this game uses. In 1898 a stone casket found at Piprahwa bore an inscription about relics of the Buddha of the Shakyas; a set of gems from that find nearly went to auction in 2025 before returning to India.
Help build the pyre
You hear people weeping, and others sitting perfectly still, not weeping at all. You are not sure which understood more.
Remember the last words
“Strive on with care.” You repeat it whenever you feel lazy, and sometimes it even works.
Five hundred voices reciting together

In a cave outside Rajagaha hundreds of monks gather. Ananda recites the teachings he remembers, one after another; Upali recites the rules of the order. All listen and repeat, so that everyone remembers them the same way.

Tradition says the First Council of 500 arahants met three months after the Buddha’s passing ✦. Most scholars think the canon took shape over centuries, not in one meeting. But group recitation is how the teachings survived for centuries without writing: about 370 years by historians’ estimates, or over 500 by the Thai Buddhist Era.
Bring water for the monks
The chanting echoes until you feel the rock itself is reciting.
Try to recite one passage along
You get the first three lines by heart. In this game, they are still chanted in Thai temples today.
Four thousand rules

Teachers at Taxila talk of a grammarian named Panini, who set down the rules of Sanskrit in about four thousand formulas so short they must be chanted like spells. Students recite them all day without writing a word.

Panini’s grammar, the Ashtadhyayi, has about 4,000 rules. Its date is uncertain ✦, usually put around the 5th–4th century BCE. Modern linguists rank it among the most detailed analyses of language from the ancient world. Many Pali and Sanskrit words in Thai still follow its rules.
Learn the first rule by heart
The first rule is two words long. It takes you three days to understand what it means.
Ask why nobody writes it down
The teacher looks at you oddly. “If it were written, why would you bother to remember it?”
Each man owns only the earth he stands on
A foreign king named Alexander enters Taxila; its ruler opens the gates to him. In a grove outside town, a group of naked ascetics stamp their feet on the ground when they see him.

The Greek historian Arrian tells that the ascetics explained: each man possesses only as much earth as he stands on, yet Alexander roamed the world seizing other people’s land, and would end with just enough earth to bury him ✦. In 326 BCE Alexander’s soldiers refused to march beyond the River Beas.
Stamp your feet with the ascetics
The Greek soldiers turn and laugh. You are not sure they understood.
Sell fruit to the Greek soldiers
They have never seen a mango, and pay three times the price.
A new dynasty

A young man named Chandragupta takes Pataliputra from the Nanda king. People say behind him stands a cunning Brahmin called Chanakya, once insulted by the Nanda king, who swore not to tie up his hair until he had his revenge.

Chandragupta founded the Maurya dynasty around 321 BCE; Greek writers called him Sandrokottos. The tales of Chanakya come from later plays and legends ✦, and many scholars think the Arthashastra, the treatise on statecraft under his name, was put together centuries later.
Go out to watch him enter the city
He is hardly older than you, but the elephant he rides is bigger than your house.
Hide the rice, just in case
Kings change; taxes stay. You know that much.
The Greek who wrote everything down
A Greek named Megasthenes has come as envoy to the court. He questions everyone in the market and writes that Indians are divided into seven classes, and that there is not a single slave in India.

Megasthenes’ book is lost; only quotations by Greek and Roman writers survive. His claim that India had no slaves was wrong: Indian texts of the same age plainly mention slaves. Scholars think he was comparing with the Greek slavery he knew, or misunderstood his informants. A good example of how outsiders see only part of another society.
Tell him there’s a slave next door
The interpreter translates. He nods, but does not change what he wrote.
Ask him about his homeland
He tells of cities where people argue philosophy in the market. You say it’s the same here.
Twelve years of famine
Rain fails year after year. An old Nigantha teacher named Bhadrabahu leads thousands of disciples south to where there is still rice. Others stay behind and, out of need, begin wearing white cloth.

Jain tradition places this famine in Chandragupta’s reign, and says Chandragupta himself gave up the throne to follow Bhadrabahu south ✦. Jains trace to it the split between the Digambara (“sky-clad”) and Svetambara (“white-clad”) traditions, both of which still exist today.
Share rice with the monks who stayed
You have less rice left, but sleep more easily than you expected.
Follow the group heading south
You walk for months until you see a great granite hill later called Shravanabelagola, then decide to walk home.
Monks who took money

In Vesali the Vajjian monks set out bowls of water for lay people to drop copper and silver coins into. A monk from the west sees it and is furious: it breaks the rules. A great meeting is called to decide.

According to the texts, the Second Council met at Vesali about a hundred years after the Buddha’s passing to settle ten disputed points, including accepting gold and silver ✦. Scholars think the Sangha began splitting into schools around this time or soon after, a path that led in the end to both Thai-style Theravada and the Mahayana.
Drop a coin in the bowl
The monk smiles. The western monk looks at you as if you were the one breaking the rules.
Give rice instead of money
Monks of both sides accept your rice. On that, at least, no one argues.
The king’s words on a rock

A royal officer reads aloud the words carved on a great rock: once the royal kitchen killed many hundreds of thousands of animals a day; now only two peacocks and a deer, and soon none at all. The king has had wells dug and trees planted along the roads, and medical care given to both people and animals.

Ashoka’s Rock Edicts 1 and 2 really do say these things, and Rock Edict 12 asks respect for all religions, because “contact between religions is good”. Most are in Brahmi script, the earliest securely dated writing in India after the Indus age, and a distant ancestor of the Thai alphabet.
Ask him to read it again, slowly
You learn the shapes of three letters, and start to want to read for yourself.
Wonder about the chicken you still plan to eat
The king forbids killing certain animals on certain days. You count the days carefully.
All men are my children
In newly conquered Kalinga an officer reads the king’s words on a rock near town: “All men are my children,” with orders that officials treat people fairly, without anger or cruelty.

At Dhauli and Jaugada in Kalinga the edicts leave out Rock Edict 13, the one expressing remorse for the war, and add two special edicts instead. Historians ask whether the king did not want to remind the bereaved, or whether the remorse was meant for readers elsewhere.
The words are gentle, but your village still has many empty houses.
Walk away in silence
Some things fine words do not mend.
Caves polished like mirrors

Royal craftsmen hollow caves out of the granite hills near Gaya and polish the walls until they reflect a lamp flame like glass. The king gives these caves to the Ajivika ascetics for the rains, not to Buddhist monks.

Inscriptions at Barabar say Ashoka gave the caves to the Ajivikas in the 12th and 19th years of his reign. The Mauryan polish on the walls still shines today. Ashoka supported many faiths, though he followed the Buddha, yet the Ajivikas vanished in the end: royal support alone was not enough to make a faith survive.
Help polish the walls
You polish until you see your own face in the stone, and are startled by what you look like.
Take food to the Ajivika ascetics
The naked ascetic says your coming today was fixed from the beginning. You are not sure how to feel about that.
The king comes to Lumbini
Ashoka’s elephants arrive at the village of Lumbini. He has a stone pillar set up to mark that the Buddha was born here, and announces that the village will pay only an eighth of its harvest in tax.

The Lumbini pillar says the king came in person in the 20th year of his reign and cut the village of Lummini’s tax to one-eighth. Rediscovered in 1896, it is one of the oldest datable records that mention the Buddha.
Celebrate the tax cut
The whole village celebrates for three days, not for the pillar but for the tax.
Go and bow at the foot of the pillar
The stone is cold in the morning. You think of a child born here more than two hundred years ago.
Sorting out the monks

At Pataliputra an elder named Moggaliputta Tissa questions the monks one by one on what the Buddha taught. Those who answer wrongly are made to disrobe; people say many had joined only because the king gave the Sangha so much.

The Third Council is told only in the Theravada texts of Lanka ✦. Ashoka’s edicts do not mention it directly, though one warns that monks who split the Sangha must disrobe. The texts say that after this council missions went out in nine directions, including to Lanka and Suvarnabhumi.
Give robes to the monks who passed
An old monk accepts the cloth with trembling hands and smiles at you.
Feel sorry for the ones made to disrobe
Some are glad, some weep. One of them ends up working in your fields.
To the Land of Gold
At the riverside two monks named Sona and Uttara prepare to set off east for the land people call Suvarnabhumi, the Land of Gold. No one on the quay knows exactly where it is.

The story of Sona and Uttara comes from Lanka’s Mahavamsa chronicle, composed around the 5th century ✦. Thailand and Myanmar each believe Suvarnabhumi was their land, at places such as Nakhon Pathom or Thaton. Historians note no Southeast Asian evidence as old as Ashoka has been found, but sea trade certainly linked India with what is now Thailand within a few centuries.
Give them dried rice for the journey
One monk says that if they get there, he will tell the people whose rice it was.
Ask if the Land of Gold really has gold
A merchant nearby laughs. “Gold, spices and storms. You may not come back.”
The riddle of the mango tree

Hunting deer on the hill of Mihintale, King Devanampiya Tissa meets a stranger monk named Mahinda. The monk asks: what tree is this? Are there other mango trees? Are there trees that are not mangoes? And besides the other mangoes and the other trees, is there any other tree?

The Lankan chronicles say the king answered rightly, “This tree itself,” and Mahinda judged him wise enough to hear the teaching ✦. According to the chronicles Mahinda was Ashoka’s son. Sri Lankans still celebrate Poson every year to remember the day.
Try to answer the riddle before the king
You get stuck on the last question. The king answers first and everyone applauds him.
Put down your bow and listen
The deer you were aiming at runs off, and you don’t mind at all.
A branch across the sea

A ship arrives from India. A nun named Sanghamitta has brought a branch of the Bodhi tree, planted in a golden vessel. The whole city comes out, and the king wades into the sea up to his neck to receive it.

The chronicles say Sanghamitta was Ashoka’s daughter ✦. The Sri Maha Bodhi in Anuradhapura, grown from that branch, is still alive today and is recognised as the oldest living human-planted tree with a known planting date, more than 2,200 years old.
Help water the sapling
In this game, the bucket you poured is still somewhere in the wood of the tree people bow to today.
Go and look at the ship from India
The sailors speak a language half like yours and tell of a city bigger than your whole island.
The grandson’s caves
King Dasaratha, Ashoka’s grandson, has caves cut into the Nagarjuni hill for the Ajivika ascetics to shelter in the rains, “for as long as the sun and moon endure”.

An inscription in the Nagarjuni caves says the Vahiyaka cave was “given by Dasaratha, dear to the gods, to the venerable Ajivikas”. The sun and moon endure, and so do the caves, but the Ajivikas do not.
Help carry rock out of the caves
The granite dust stays in your lungs for months.
Ask an ascetic how long his faith will last
He answers, “All is already fixed.” Which is true, though not in the way he means.
The last review of the troops
Brihadratha, the last Mauryan emperor, comes out to review the army. In front of every soldier, his general Pushyamitra draws his sword and kills him. Not one soldier moves.

The Harshacharita, written in the 7th century, says Pushyamitra used a review of the army as the pretext to kill his master, around 185 BCE ✦. The Maurya dynasty ended less than fifty years after Ashoka’s death.
Stand still like everyone else
That night no one in camp speaks of it, and next day everyone takes pay from the new master.
Leave the army
You go home to plant rice, which looks like the wisest move at the time.
The horse that may go anywhere

A white horse wanders through the village with hundreds of guards. For a year it may go wherever it likes; any realm that bars its way must fight. At the year’s end it will be led back and sacrificed, to proclaim Pushyamitra supreme.

The ashvamedha was the grandest Vedic rite a king could hold; an inscription at Ayodhya says Pushyamitra performed it twice. Later Buddhist texts accuse him of killing monks, but most historians doubt it, since the stupas at Bharhut and Sanchi were repaired and enlarged under his dynasty.
Offer the horse some grass
The horse eats your grass and wanders off. The guards nod as if you had earned great merit.
Ask what happens if it eats the rice in your field
“The horse may eat anything,” a guard replies. You watch your field all night.
The chariot that isn’t there
King Milinda, a Greek king who loves debate, asks the monk Nagasena his name. Nagasena says a name is only a label, then asks in return: what is your chariot? Is it the wheels? The axle? The body?

The Milindapanha records this dialogue ✦. Milinda was Menander I, a Greek king of Gandhara around 165–130 BCE; some of his coins bear a wheel that may be the Dhamma wheel. The text is still popular in Thailand.
Side with the king: a chariot is a chariot
The Greek soldiers applaud you, but by the time you get home you are no longer sure.
Side with Nagasena
That night you count the parts of your own cart and cannot find the “cart” anywhere.
Ashes divided
King Menander dies in camp. The cities quarrel over who will keep his ashes, and at last agree to share them equally, each building a monument of its own.

The Greek writer Plutarch tells this ✦. Many scholars notice how closely it resembles the division of the Buddha’s relics; some think Menander was honoured in a Buddhist way, others that Plutarch mixed the two stories up.
Help build your city’s monument
The little domed monument looks just like a stupa, and passers-by bow to it.
Wonder who started this custom
An old man in town says he has heard of the same thing happening to a teacher, centuries ago.
The Buddha you cannot see

Carvers cover the stone railing round the stupa with Jataka scenes, kings, and yakkhas standing guard. But in scenes from the Buddha’s life there is no figure of him at all: only a tree, footprints, an empty seat.

The Bharhut stupa, about 2,100 years old, is an example of early Buddhist art that shows the Buddha only by symbols. Many scenes carry labels naming the story, and yakkhas and yakkhinis guard the gates; Thais see their descendants at temple gates today. The railing was found in 1873 and most of it is in a museum in Kolkata.
Ask the carver why he leaves the Buddha out
The carver says, “He has gone out like a flame. How do you carve someone who is not there?” and goes on carving footprints.
Give coins for one railing post
The carver cuts your name at the foot of the post. Very small, but in this game, it is still there.
The Greek who worshipped Vasudeva
A Greek envoy from Taxila named Heliodorus sets up a stone pillar topped with a Garuda, dedicated to Vasudeva, god of gods, and has it carved that he is a Bhagavata, a devotee.

The Heliodorus pillar at Vidisha, set up around 113 BCE, is early evidence of the worship of Vasudeva-Krishna, which grew into one of the largest strands of Hinduism, and shows Greeks adopting local faiths. Villagers still worship it today as Khamb Baba, Father Pillar.
Join the pillar’s dedication
The Greek sings the hymn in an odd accent, but his devotion is easy to understand.
Read the other face of the pillar
“Three steps to immortality: self-control, giving up, and watchfulness.” It sounds familiar from somewhere.
The Jina comes home
King Kharavela of Kalinga marches home from Magadha bringing back the Jina of Kalinga, carried off by a Nanda king centuries before. The whole city turns out to welcome it.

Kharavela’s Hathigumpha inscription opens with salutations to the Arhats and Siddhas, like a Jain prayer, and tells of bringing back “the Jina of Kalinga”. Its date is debated ✦, usually put around the 1st century BCE. A century and more after Ashoka conquered Kalinga, it had a strong king of its own again.
Join the welcoming procession
The old weep, for their grandparents’ grandparents spoke of this image.
Count the elephants in the procession
You count seventy-two elephants, then count again and get seventy-four.
The gate the ivory carvers made

The ivory carvers of Vidisha pool their money and carve the southern stone gateway of the Sanchi stupa, as finely as if it were ivory. On one pillar they inscribe that this is the work of the ivory workers of Vidisha.

The inscription is still on Sanchi’s southern gateway. The northern gateway carves the Vessantara Jataka, which Thais hear every year at the Thet Mahachat sermon. Sanchi has hundreds of donor inscriptions, many by women, monks and nuns.
Ask to help with the carving
You get to carve one leaf on one branch, and look for it every time you pass.
Give money towards the railing
Your name is carved alongside hundreds of others.
Write it down before it is forgotten

After years of war and famine many monks have died, and some lines of recitation have nearly broken. So the monks at the Aluvihare caves decide to do what has never been done: write all the teachings down on palm leaves.

The Lankan chronicles say the canon and its commentaries were first written down in the reign of King Vattagamani Abhaya, around 29–17 BCE ✦, after the teachings had passed by mouth for about 370 years if the Buddha died around 400 BCE, as many historians estimate, or more than 500 years counting by the Thai Buddhist Era. The Pali canon used in Thai temples descends from this line.
Help prepare the palm leaves
You boil the leaves, dry them and rub them smooth. The monks say your work matters as much as their reciting.
Ask why they don’t just go on reciting
An old monk answers, “Last year only one of us still had a whole collection by heart.”
A scroll in a clay pot
The monks put a worn-out birch-bark scroll into a clay pot and bury it beside a stupa, because sacred words are too precious to throw away, even once a new copy has been made.

In 1994 the British Library acquired about 80 fragments of birch-bark scrolls from Gandhara that had been stored in clay pots. Dated to roughly the first half of the 1st century CE and written in Kharosthi script in the Gandhari language, they are among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts ever found.
Help dig the hole
Two thousand years later, in this game, someone digs where you dug.
Ask to see the writing before it is buried
The letters run right to left. You recognise one, and then the lid goes on.
A red statue from Mathura

A monk named Bala, a master of the scriptures, brings a larger-than-life red sandstone bodhisattva statue from Mathura and sets it up at Sarnath. People stand and stare; many have never seen a human figure meant to evoke the Buddha.

The monk Bala’s bodhisattva is inscribed with the 3rd year of King Kanishka’s reign, in the early 2nd century CE, and was found at Sarnath in 1904–05. In this period carvers at Mathura and in Gandhara began making the Buddha in human form, after centuries of Buddhist art that used only symbols.
Bow to the statue
You never saw him, but now you can picture his face. Or at least one carver could.
Grumble that the old way was better
A young monk calls you old-fashioned. You say you simply remember how it used to be.
A coin with the Buddha on it
At the market a gold coin of King Kanishka comes into your hands. On one side is the king; on the other a standing figure in a monk’s robe, with Greek letters spelling “BODDO”.

Gold coins of Kanishka from around 127–150 CE, some showing the Buddha with his name in Greek letters, are in the British Museum. Kanishka’s Kushan empire reached from Central Asia to the Ganges, and along its Silk Road links Buddhism travelled to China.
Keep it as a charm
You never spend it, not even in the hungry years.
Spend it on a cow
The cow does not know it was bought with the Buddha’s image, and you think he would not mind.
A poem of the Buddha’s life

A poet named Ashvaghosha recites a long Sanskrit poem telling the Buddha’s life from his birth in a palace, the pleasures of the palace, the sights of an old man, a sick man, a dead man and a monk, to his awakening. The listeners weep and laugh as the story goes.

Ashvaghosha’s Buddhacarita was composed around the 1st–2nd century CE ✦; tradition places him at Kanishka’s court. It is among the first works to tell the Buddha’s life as one complete story. In the early discourses the sights of age, sickness, death and a renunciant are told of an earlier Buddha named Vipassi; only later were they told of Gotama himself.
Listen to every canto
The story Grandmother told you as a child now has a palace, dancers and a white horse. It is far more beautiful than hers.
Ask where the poet learned all these details
The poet smiles. “Poets don’t lie. They make the truth easier to remember.”
Supper is hot rice, a stew of pulses, boiled greens and a drop of ghee. On a good day there is curd with cane sugar too.

Rice, pulses, ghee and curd were the staples of the Ganges valley. Alexander’s admiral Nearchus marvelled at “reeds that make honey without bees”: sugar cane. The Sanskrit word sharkara travelled all the way to become English “sugar”.
Every evening Mother spins cotton into thread. Every piece of clothing in the house is made from cotton you grow.
India was among the first lands to grow cotton for cloth. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that India had trees bearing wool finer and better than a sheep’s; Greeks had never seen cotton.
The monsoon arrives. The sky stays dark all day, the frogs sing all night, and everyone hurries to plant rice while the water lasts.
The Rigveda has a hymn to the frogs, croaking at the first rains like pupils repeating their teacher. Life in the Ganges valley hung on the monsoon; a late or weak monsoon meant a hungry year.
Mosquitoes swarm over the standing water. The neighbour’s child has a fever with fits of shivering every third day.
A fever that returns in cycles like this was probably malaria; ancient Indian medical texts describe such recurring fevers. In this age malaria was one of the great killers of the lowland plains.
Tonight a tiger takes a cow from the pen at the end of the village. The men follow its tracks with torches to the edge of the forest, and stop.

The forests of the Ganges valley were still vast. Tigers, wild elephants and Indian rhinos lived close to villages. One of Ashoka’s edicts forbids killing many kinds of animals, and another addresses the forest peoples within his realm.
On the uposatha day many villagers do no heavy work, go to hear the teaching, and keep the precepts, eating only once.

Moon-day observances were a custom of many ascetic schools before Buddhism. The Vinaya says King Bimbisara asked the Buddha to have monks meet on these days as other schools did. The Thai wan phra holy days descend from this custom.
In the morning people bathe in the Ganges. Not far off, smoke from funeral pyres drifts up from the bank.

Cremation by the river and bathing in a sacred river are ancient customs. Work at the cremation grounds usually fell to candala groups, shunned for that very work, though everyone depended on them at the end of life.
There is a festival in the town square: wrestling, dancers, cockfights and liquor. The old folk grumble that young people today have too much fun.

Festivals like this were called samaja. Ashoka’s first rock edict says he disapproved of them, though some kinds he thought good. Rulers frowning on ordinary people’s fun go back more than two thousand years.
A snake man opens his basket in the village square. The cobra rears and spreads its hood; the children shriek, but none of them leave.
Snakebite has been a major killer in rural India throughout history; even today India loses tens of thousands of people a year to it. No wonder nagas were both worshipped and feared.
The head of the carpenters’ guild calls a meeting in the village. Every guild member must chip in for the family of a carpenter who fell from a scaffold and died.

Jatakas and inscriptions of this age mention guilds of many crafts, with heads and rules of their own; some even took deposits and lent money. Some later inscriptions record money deposited with guilds so that the interest would feed monks.
Your knees ache when the rains come. You sit on the veranda telling the young ones that the forest used to come right up behind the village.
You are starting to forget people’s names, but the verses you learned as a child you still know word for word.
Memories drilled by repetition in childhood often last into old age. That is one reason a culture of recitation could hand on teachings for centuries without writing.
The frogs sing all night after the rain.
A peacock calls from the mango tree.
Ascetics walk past the house in silence on their alms round.
Buffaloes lie wallowing in the mud pool.
The smell of ghee drifts from the kitchen.
Cart bells jingle on the road.
The women sing as they plant the rice.
A monkey steals bananas from the veranda.
Smoke from the Brahmin’s fire rite rises at dawn.
Children play with nut dice under the banyan.
a cobra bite
trampled by a war elephant
a recurring fever
The monsoon comes late and weak. The paddies dry up, the price of rice soars, and the poor gather grass and roots to eat.
The Ganges bursts its banks, flooding fields and villages. Your family flees to higher ground.
An earthquake cracks the mud walls, and thatched roofs come down.
A storm off the sea carries away several fishing boats.
tree spirits, yakkhas, nagas and mother goddesses

No temples or scriptures of its own, yet it never vanished: every faith took it in. Yakkhas became gate guardians of Buddhist, Jain and Hindu temples; in Thailand, the giants at temple gates and Thao Wessuwan. Nagas became temple stair-rails.
the Brahmins’ fire rites

Animal sacrifice slowly faded, but the Vedas were still recited mouth to mouth for over three thousand years, and Brahmin belief merged with devotion to Vishnu, Shiva and local gods into the Hinduism of over a billion people. The court Brahmins of Thailand descend from this line.
the Sangha of the Buddha

Almost vanished from India after the 13th century, when Nalanda was destroyed, but survived in Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet and East Asia. In 2020 there were about 324 million Buddhists. In India, Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of followers turned to Buddhism in 1956.
the Niganthas of Mahavira
Never left India, and never vanished. There are about four and a half million Jains today, and the Jain principle of non-harm influenced Mahatma Gandhi.
the Ajivikas of Makkhali Gosala

Faded from the north after the Mauryas; the last traces are in South India around the 14th century. None of their own scriptures survive; we know them only through rivals, and through the still-gleaming Barabar caves.
the materialists, who taught there is no next life
Almost none of their texts survive; they are known mostly through those who wrote against them. Yet their question, how can we know?, has been asked in every age of philosophy since.
the devotees of Vasudeva
Grew into the worship of Krishna and Vishnu, one of the largest strands of Hinduism; the Bhagavad Gita became one of the most read scriptures in the world.

After you, Magadha will swallow its neighbours one by one, Pataliputra will become the capital of the largest empire India has yet known, and the teachers you heard of will be remembered by disciples who will argue for centuries over what they really said.
After you, Chandragupta’s grandson will conquer Kalinga, regret it, and spend his reign carving his thoughts on rocks across the land.
After you, the Maurya empire will fall apart within fifty years, its last emperor killed in front of his own army. But the monks of Ashoka’s time will carry the teachings across the sea.

After you, the Kushans will rule from Central Asia to the Ganges, images of the Buddha will travel the Silk Road to China, and in Lanka Buddhaghosa will render the commentaries into Pali in the 5th century, the version Thai temples still study.

In your age the Buddha’s Sangha was one school among many, alongside the Niganthas, the Ajivikas, the materialists, the Brahmins, and the spirits every village fed. Historians point to several reasons Buddhism lasted: a community of monks and nuns with rules for living together that outlived its founder; teachings memorised in groups and then written down; kings who gave support (though Ashoka also gave caves to the Ajivikas, who still vanished); monks travelling with merchants by land and sea; and a readiness to welcome villagers’ nagas and yakkhas instead of driving them out. Yet even Buddhism nearly vanished from the land of its birth. It survived because it had already taken root elsewhere, including the land that would become Thailand.

Traces of this age are all around Thailand today: the Buddhist Era counted from the Buddha’s passing, a Thai alphabet descended from Brahmi, chanting in Pali, Khao Phansa, the wan phra holy days, naga stair-rails, giants guarding temple gates, and the hare in the moon.
You told the Buddha’s story just as you heard it, adding nothing, cutting nothing.
You added wonders to the Buddha’s story for the young, like countless tellers before and after you. Stories told with love tend to grow this way.
You told the teaching instead of the life, which is what the early discourses themselves cared most about.
, and almost none of them knew you were there.
m
You knew enough of the teachings by heart to pass them on.
Your name was carved on a stupa railing, where, in this game, it may still be.
You survived the day your homeland fell.

Most people of the Ganges valley were cremated by the river, their bones and ashes given to the water. Revered monks might get a small stupa for their relics. Small children were usually buried instead of burned, and the cremation-ground work fell to candala groups.
Invite ascetics to chant
The chanting rises over the crackle of the fire, and everyone falls quiet.
Give the ashes to the Ganges
The river carries the ashes east, as it has carried everyone.
Give to the poor in the name of the dead
Many of the poor eat their fill that day.
Monks and villagers cremate you and keep your relics in a little stupa beside the monastery, where someone leaves flowers every holy day.
Your disciples cremate you simply, without a grand rite, as you taught them.
Your son lights the pyre with fire from the household altar, and Brahmins chant the Vedas throughout.
Your master pays for a cremation at the burning ground outside town. Only a few people come.
Your family carries you to the riverbank, burns you on a pyre and gives your bones to the water.
In the Buddha’s time ordinary people listened to many teachers and fed ascetics of every school. Do you listen to ideas different from your own?
The Buddha’s story grew each time it was retold. What stories in your own life have grown in the retelling?
Your name at the foot of a stupa railing post, in Brahmi letters.
A stupa of your age.
The faiths you gave to, and what became of them after you
Milk for the naga
Grandmother takes you to the anthill behind the village, sets a cup of milk by the hole, and whispers that a naga lives below. Treat it well, and it will bring the rains on time.

Nagas were sacred serpents who ruled water and rain. Villagers worshipped them before Buddhism or Jainism, and both took nagas into their own stories: in the discourses the naga king Mucalinda spreads his hood to shelter the Buddha from the rain. The naga stair-rails of Thai temples descend from this belief.
Leave a flower too
By morning the cup is empty. You don’t know whether it was the naga or the cat.
Hide and wait to see the naga
You see a cobra, and run home faster than you have ever run.
The yakkha under the banyan

Under the great banyan in the village is a stone platform the villagers smear with red and heap with rice. The grown-ups say the yakkha in the tree protects the village; anger it, and someone will fall sick.

Yakkhas in ancient India were not always demons; many were gods of trees, towns and treasure, and great stone yakkha statues from this age survive. Buddhism took them in as guardians. Thao Wessuwan, whom many Thais worship, is the king of the yakkhas, and the giants guarding Thai temple gates descend from this belief.
Bow to the yakkha every time you pass
You believe it helped you through a fever once. Who knows?
Climb the banyan
Nothing happens except a scolding from Mother, which is scarier than any yakkha.
A strange coin
Father shows you a small bent piece of silver punched with a sun, an elephant and signs you don’t know. He says it will buy a basket of rice.

India’s punch-marked coins began around the 6th–5th century BCE, not long after the world’s first coins in Lydia, and around the time China began using coins. Money helped trade and towns grow, and left merchants with wealth to support ascetics; many historians see this as one reason wandering schools flourished in this age.
You count it every night. It is still only one coin.
Ask why a bit of silver is worth anything
Father thinks a long time and says, “Because everyone believes it is.” The answer is still true 2,500 years later.
Ascetics who stop walking in the rains

When the first rains come, the ascetics who passed through every day stop travelling and stay in one place for the whole wet season. The grown-ups say it is because villagers once complained that they trampled the seedlings and the little creatures.

The Vinaya says lay people complained that monks trampled young grass and small creatures in the rains while ascetics of other schools stayed put, so the Buddha told monks to keep the rains retreat. It is the origin of Khao Phansa, still kept in Thailand every year.
Help build a hut for the ascetics
All through the rains you hear chanting from the hut you helped to thatch.
Take care not to tread on the worms
You walk so slowly that Mother asks if you are ill.
The hare in the moon

Grandmother tells how, long ago, a hare had nothing to give a hungry Brahmin, so it leapt into the fire to offer its own flesh. The Brahmin was a god in disguise, who drew the hare on the moon for everyone to see.

This is the Sasa Jataka, a tale of one of the Buddha’s past lives ✦. Many Jatakas were folk tales already being told, retold as stories of the Bodhisatta. Thais still see “the hare in the moon” from this tale.
Look for the hare on the moon
You see two long ears, and you will see them for the rest of your life.
Ask whether the hare was hurt
Grandmother says the fire was not hot at all for one who gave with a true heart. You don’t quite believe it, but you love the story.
One syllable at a time

Your teacher sits facing you and chants the Vedic hymns two words at a time. You must repeat them with every rise and fall of pitch, and once you know them, chant them again in several patterns of shuffled words, until not one syllable can go wrong.

Brahmins chanted the Vedas in elaborate patterns: word by word, in pairs forwards and backwards. This helped the Rigveda pass by mouth with astonishing accuracy for more than three thousand years, and UNESCO honours Vedic chanting as intangible heritage. Such methods may have set the example for Buddhist monks who kept their teachings without writing.
Recite until your voice is hoarse
That night you recite in your dreams too, without a single mistake.
Ask what the words mean
The teacher says meaning matters, but sound matters more: a wrong sound spoils the rite.
Your family arranges your marriage to a man of your own birth group. An astrologer picks the day; you and the groom take seven steps around the fire, and you move to his family’s house.
Your family and another of your birth group agree on a marriage. An astrologer picks the day, and the bride will come to live in your family’s house.

The seven steps around the sacred fire are a Vedic wedding rite still used in India today. Families usually chose partners from the same birth group. Several Buddhist discourses tell of married couples who were devoted lay followers together, and teach the duties of husband to wife and wife to husband.
Drums and flutes play all night, and the new house smells of the ritual fire for days.
Your family is displeased but agrees to wait. The village aunts talk about it for a long time.
The hall of curiosity

At the hall on the edge of town, ascetics of many schools stay and debate every evening. One, wrapped in a blanket woven of human hair, says death is the end: there is no next life. Another, naked, says all is fixed by fate. A third teaches harming nothing at all. A fourth speaks of a middle way.

The Pali texts call such places kutuhalasala, “halls of curiosity”. The Samaññaphala Sutta names six rival teachers of the Buddha’s time, including Ajita of the hair blanket, who taught there is no next life, Makkhali Gosala, and the Nigantha Nataputta, Mahavira. Ordinary people listened to many schools and fed ascetics of all of them; they did not pick one religion as people often do today.
Believe the hair-blanket man: death is the end
You decide to enjoy your dinner today, since tomorrow may not come.
Believe the naked one: fate decides all
You stop worrying about your lessons, since the outcome is fixed. Which is why it turns out badly.
Listen to the teacher of harmlessness
You start straining your water before you drink, in case tiny creatures are inside.
Listen to the middle way
Not too far either way. It sounds easy; you find it is the hardest of all.
Who comes begging at the door
The third is a devotee of Vasudeva, singing hymns.
The third is naked and carries a staff.

Lay people of this age commonly fed ascetics of many schools. Buddhist monks took food in a bowl; some Jain ascetics received it in their palms and ate standing; Ajivikas carried a bamboo staff. Ashoka’s edicts urge giving to both ascetics and Brahmins, not to one school alone.
Put rice in the bowl
The monk accepts and walks on without thanking you. Later you learn that the giving was your merit.
Put rice in the open palms
The ascetic eats then and there, carefully, not dropping a single grain.
Give to the devotee of Vasudeva
Give to the naked ascetic with the staff
He blesses you with words you have never heard, but they feel warm.
A goat for the rite
The village Brahmin says a goat must be sacrificed this year so the rains come and the fields bear. But a passing ascetic says killing brings no one merit: offer rice and milk instead.

In the Kutadanta Sutta the Buddha tells of a great sacrifice of the past in which no animal was killed, only ghee, oil, milk and honey offered ✦. Jain ascetics opposed killing even more strictly. Over centuries animal sacrifice slowly declined in India and vegetarianism spread, which historians credit to many schools together.
Give the goat for the rite
The rite is splendid and the rains come on time that year. Everyone credits the goat.
Offer rice and milk instead
The Brahmin is displeased. The rains come on time anyway. You say nothing, but your goat is still alive.
May we eat together?
A friend you have known since childhood comes from a family that clears refuse. The grown-ups say you should not eat with him. Today he offers to share his sweets with you in front of everyone.

The Vasala Sutta teaches that “one is not an outcaste by birth, nor a Brahmin by birth, but by deeds”. The Sangha accepted people of every varna; the Theragatha has verses by a monk named Sunita who had swept up withered flowers for a living. Even so, division by birth persisted and grew stricter over the following centuries.
Sit and eat with him
The sweets are sweeter than you expected. The neighbour aunt doesn’t speak to you for a month.
Politely refuse
He smiles as if he is used to it. You think about that smile for a long time.
Going forth

You have seen the old die and children fall sick, and household life feels like nothing but burdens. Many of your age shave their heads, put on dyed cloth and leave home as wandering ascetics. Whom would you follow?

Going forth was a common choice in this age, for men and women alike. Under the Vinaya, slaves, debtors, soldiers in service and those without their parents’ consent could not be ordained, so the Sangha would not become an escape from worldly duties. Jain ascetics were strictest about harming no life; some Ajivikas went naked and practised harsh austerities.
Ask your master to free you first
Your master agrees. You are free, though no longer sure you want to renounce.
Your master refuses. A slave cannot be ordained.
You go back to work, the thought still circling.
Become a nun in the Buddha’s Sangha
Join the Buddha’s Sangha
Your hair falls to the ground, and you feel surprisingly light.
Become a Nigantha ascetic
You are given a little broom to sweep small creatures from your path.
Become an Ajivika ascetic
Your teacher says your path is already fixed; you need only walk it.
Stay and care for your family
Instead you give alms every morning, and find that is a path too.
The reciters
The senior monks divide the community into groups, each responsible for keeping one collection of teachings by heart and handing it on to the next generation. You are invited to join.

The Pali texts and commentaries mention bhanakas, reciters who each kept one collection, such as the Digha-bhanakas who held the long discourses. Many teachings are built of repetitions and numbered lists, the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, which made them easier to memorise. This kept the teachings for centuries before they were written down.
Join the reciters
Became a reciter of the teachings
Every evening you recite with the group until the voices become one. If anyone slips a word, everyone hears at once.
Ask to practise meditation instead
You sit beneath a tree every day until the birds stop being afraid of you.
Your name on the stupa railing
The town’s stupa is being enlarged. Anyone who gives enough for one railing post or crossbar may have their name carved on the stone.

The stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut carry hundreds of donor inscriptions: villagers, merchants, craft guilds, and, surprisingly, many monks and nuns, showing that some renunciants still had money of their own. The stupas belonged to whole communities, not to kings alone.
Give, and have your name carved
Name carved on a stupa railing
The carver cuts your name and your village’s. The letters are tiny, but the stone will outlast you.
Give without a name
No one knows it was yours, and you like it that way.
The new letters
The officer who reads the king’s edicts teaches the letters to anyone who wants to learn. They are simple strokes and circles, written left to right.

The Brahmi letters of Ashoka’s edicts are the earliest securely dated writing in India after the Indus age. From Brahmi came many scripts, including the Pallava script of South India, which led to Old Khmer and at last to Thai. Anyone reading Thai today uses descendants of these letters.
Learn to read
Learned to read Brahmi
Your name takes five letters. You write it in the dust until the wind blows it away.
Listening is enough for you
You remember every word you hear, as people have done for a thousand years.
Pilgrimage to the four places
You have saved enough to travel to the four places: Lumbini where the Buddha was born, Bodh Gaya where he awoke, Sarnath where he first taught, and Kusinara where he passed away.

The Mahaparinibbana Sutta names these four as places the faithful should go to see. Ashoka visited several himself and set up pillars. Today tens of thousands of Thais travel to these sites every year.
Set out
Made the pilgrimage to the four places
You walk for months, wear out two pairs of sandals, and come home with one dry Bodhi leaf.
Keep the money for the family
You tell yourself you will go next year. Next year there is always something else.
Dice of vibhitaka nuts
The village men play dice made of vibhitaka nuts, betting coins. Some have already lost a cow; some say they will win it back tonight.

The Rigveda has the song of a gambler who has lost everything, even his wife, lamenting that the dice draw him like a drug ✦. Vibhitaka nuts were used as dice from Vedic times and are still used in herbal medicine today.
Have one throw
You win two coins and decide to stop while ahead.
You lose two coins and suddenly understand the gambler’s song in the Rigveda.
Walk on by
That night someone else loses a cow. Not you.
The mustard seed

After you lose your child, an old nun tells you of a woman named Kisa Gotami who carried her dead baby through the town begging for medicine. The Buddha told her to bring a mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died. She searched all day, and understood there was no such house.

The story of Kisa Gotami comes from the commentaries ✦; verses attributed to her are in the Therigatha. In this age nearly half of all children did not live to grow up, and almost every family had lost a child. The story is still told in Thai temples to comfort the bereaved.
The grief stays, but you know you are not alone with it.
Go and sit with another mother who has just lost a child
You say nothing, only sit with her, and that is enough.
Yavana neighbours

The Greek family next door call their gods by strange names, yet their son gives alms every morning and their daughter has married your friend. Coins in the market carry two scripts: Greek on one side, Kharosthi on the other.

Greek kings of Gandhara struck bilingual coins; several inscriptions record Greeks giving to Buddhist stupas; and Gandharan craftsmen blended Greek art with Buddhist stories into Gandharan art, which helped shape the earliest images of the Buddha.
Invite them to eat
They bring wine; you bring rice and dal. Everyone eats their fill.
Ask them to teach you Greek letters
Greek runs left to right, like Brahmi, but looks nothing like it.
Telling the young about the Buddha
an ascetic who left home, nearly starved himself to death, found the middle way, awoke under a tree and taught for over forty years.
a story passed down for generations, gaining wonders with every telling.

The early discourses say very little about the Buddha’s childhood and life before he left home. The full continuous story, with its palaces for three seasons, the four sights and many wonders, came together in works written centuries later, such as the Buddhacarita (1st–2nd century CE) and the Nidanakatha (around the 5th century). Stories grow when they are told with love; for Buddhists, the teaching matters more than the details.
Tell it exactly as you heard it
Some of the children doze off, but one asks a question so good you cannot answer it.
Add a wonder or two to liven it up
You tell how lotuses sprang up under each step he took as a newborn. The children’s eyes go wide, and in this game they will pass it on bigger still.
Skip the life; tell the teaching
You teach that everything changes. One child cries, remembering a dog that died. You hold him.
Which order to join
You have chosen the renunciant’s life, but must still choose a teacher. The monks of Gotama, the Nigantha ascetics of Mahavira and the Ajivikas would all welcome you.
In this age all three orders had male and female ascetics and competed for supporters. All three won royal favour at times; only two survive today.
The Buddha’s Sangha
You learn to hold the bowl steady, and to walk slowly.
The Niganthas
Your teacher shows you how to strain water, sweep your path and never eat after sunset.
The Ajivikas
Your teacher says every soul will be freed at its appointed time, not a moment sooner or later.
The alms round
At first light you walk into the village with your bowl, in silence, asking nothing, choosing no house, taking whatever is given. Today a poor woman puts stale rice in your bowl.

Monks of this age begged daily and ate what they received, even meat if it had not been killed for them. Jain ascetics were far stricter, taking only food not prepared specially for them. The morning almsgiving Thais still practise comes straight from this custom.
Eat it gladly
The stale rice is not good, but her intention is.
Pass the rice on to a beggar by the road
The beggar eats it in a blink. You go hungry that day and feel strangely full.
The black polished ware
A master potter teaches you to make ware with a black, mirror-like gloss that rich townsfolk pay dearly for, but keeps back the last secret of how to fire it to that shine.
Northern Black Polished Ware was the fine pottery of the Ganges valley in this age, found in towns from Taxila to Kalinga. Archaeologists still argue over how its gloss was made.
Experiment until you crack it
After thirty spoiled pots, the thirty-first shines so you can see your face in it.
Make plain pots for ordinary people
Your pots don’t shine, but every house in the village owns one.
The forest of yakkhas
Your caravan must cross a great forest. The guide says yakkhas there trick travellers into pouring away their water, then eat the whole caravan. Your people grow afraid.

Many Jatakas tell of caravans of five hundred carts crossing forests and deserts ✦. Merchants were key supporters of Buddhism and Jainism, and ascetics often travelled with caravans, so the faiths spread along the trade routes.
Keep the water, whatever anyone says
Mid-forest, strangers say there is a lake ahead; pour out your water to lighten the carts. You don’t believe them, and everyone survives.
Invite some ascetics to travel with you
The ascetics chant every night, your people lose their fear, and you hear teachings all the way for free.
The priest’s fee
A rich merchant hires you for a great twelve-day fire rite, the fee a hundred cows. But the night before, his son says he has been listening to Buddhist monks and thinks the rite is pointless.

Brahmins were paid a fee called dakshina: cows, gold or land. Buddhist texts criticised lavish sacrifices, yet called a good person “a true Brahmin”, and many Brahmins were among the Buddha’s leading disciples. The relationship was more complicated than simple enmity.
Perform the rite as splendidly as you can
The fires burn beautifully for twelve days. The merchant’s son watches from the back and says nothing more.
Talk with the merchant’s son first
You argue until dawn and agree on one thing: goodness matters more than rites.
Nine thousand elephants
The royal army has more elephants than anyone can count. You are given a young bull that will let no one ride him; it will take months to win each other’s trust.

The Roman writer Pliny the Elder, drawing on Greek reports, recorded that the king of Pataliputra had 9,000 elephants. When Chandragupta made peace with Seleucus, Seleucus received 500 elephants, which later helped him win a great battle in the west.
Sleep beside the elephant every night
Three months later the elephant lifts you onto its back with its own trunk.
Use the hook to make it obey
The elephant flings you off; two ribs crack, and it never trusts you again.
The elephant obeys, but looks at you with eyes that keep you awake at night.
Medicine in every plant
Your patients are merchants, monks and beggars. An older physician says never treat for free, or people won’t trust the medicine. But monks have no money.

The Vinaya has a chapter on medicines, listing what monks might use: ghee, oil, honey, molasses and various roots. Ayurvedic texts such as the Charaka Samhita were compiled later, but drew on centuries of gathered knowledge.
Treat the monks for free
The monks have no money, but they spread the word until every merchant in town comes to you.
Charge everyone the same
You grow richer, and the beggars find another physician.
The yakkhini on the post
You are given a yakkhini to carve, hanging from a branch on a stupa gateway post. The master says she must be lovely enough to stop passers-by, yet look like a guardian, not a dancer.
You carve ivory into combs and boxes for the town’s rich. The master says one day the king will build in stone, and will want carvers with steady hands.

The yakkhinis of the Sanchi gates are fertility goddesses villagers already worshipped. Ivory carvers and woodworkers turned to stone in this age, bringing their techniques with them. Ashoka’s pillars were polished so finely that some people once took them for metal.
Carve with all your care
Two thousand years later, in this game, your work is the most photographed on that gate.
Ask to carve a Jataka scene instead
You carve the monkey king who made himself a bridge for his troop to escape across the river. Everyone who sees it smiles.
The bandit with a garland of fingers

All Savatthi fears a bandit called Angulimala, who kills people and strings their fingers into a garland. One day word comes that he chased an ascetic but, however fast he ran, could not catch him, though the ascetic only walked.

In the Angulimala Sutta the ascetic is the Buddha, who says, “I have stopped; it is you who have not stopped,” and Angulimala throws down his sword and becomes a monk ✦. Thais know the Angulimala paritta, chanted for women in childbirth.
Doubt a bandit can change
Months later you give alms to a thin monk, and someone whispers that it is him. Your hands shake.
Believe anyone can change
You stop talking about the people who once wronged you, and feel lighter.
The naga king and the seven-day storm

People tell that soon after the awakening, a storm raged seven days and nights, and a naga king named Mucalinda came out of a pond, coiled seven times around the Buddha and spread his hood over him against the rain.

This is told in the Udana ✦. The Buddha sheltered by the naga, the image for Thais born on Saturday, comes from this story. Nagas were water gods villagers already worshipped; the story shows Buddhism taking local beliefs in as protectors instead of rejecting them.
Leave milk at the pond
You are not sure whom you are honouring, the naga or the Buddha, or both.
Pass the tale on to the children
In the children’s version the storm lasts ten days and the naga has seven heads.
The yakkhini who ate children

The village mothers tell of Hariti, a yakkhini who stole other people’s children to eat, until the Buddha hid her own youngest child. Then she understood other mothers’ pain and became a protector of children instead.

Hariti’s story is in later Buddhist texts ✦. Statues of Hariti holding children are common in Gandhara, and she became a protector of children as far as China and Japan: another local goddess taken into Buddhism.
Make an offering for Hariti to protect the children
You leave rice at the door. Whoever eats it, your children sleep soundly.
Think of the other mothers
You send food to the house with a newborn.
The prince who gave everything away

A storyteller in the market tells of Prince Vessantara, who gave away the kingdom’s white elephant, his chariot, his children and even his wife. The listeners weep, argue, and come back to hear it again every year.

The Vessantara Jataka tells the last life before the Buddha ✦. It was carved on the Sanchi gates two thousand years ago; Thais hear it at the Thet Mahachat sermon, and people still argue today over whether giving away a wife and children can be good.
Weep when the children are led away
The whole market weeps with you, and the storyteller earns more coins than all year.
Argue that the prince was wrong
An aunt agrees with you, an uncle doesn’t, and they are still arguing after you go home.
Eighty-four thousand stupas

People say Ashoka opened the old stupas, divided the relics into eighty-four thousand portions, and built eighty-four thousand stupas across the land, all finished on a single day, at the moment of an eclipse.

This legend comes from the Ashokavadana, written centuries after Ashoka ✦. Eighty-four thousand is a number meaning “a great many”, found across Buddhist texts, as in the 84,000 teachings. In his real edicts Ashoka mentions enlarging one stupa, of an earlier Buddha.
Believe the legend
You count stupas on every journey, but never reach eighty thousand.
Think the tellers exaggerate
A number that big must mean “an awful lot”. You are right.

Years in this chapter follow many historians’ estimate that the Buddha passed away around 400 BCE. The Thai Buddhist Era counts from 543 BCE, following the Lankan chronicles. Scholars still debate it; proposals run from about 480 to 370 BCE.

You watch ants drag a dead beetle home, every one of them pulling at once.

You wake before everyone else and watch the light come back.
Two neighbours quarrel in the morning and are laughing together by evening.
Your grandmother’s hands, cracked from work, braid your hair.
The first fruit of the season, shared so that everyone gets one bite.
A bad tooth aches for days, until someone pulls it out.
You teach a younger child to tie a knot that will not slip.
An old woman tells how things were when she was young. Nobody knows how much is true.
Suddenly every bird stops singing at once. A moment of silence, then they start again.
You carry an old relative who can no longer walk out to sit in the sun.
A stranger passes through and leaves behind a new word that people here start to use.
A sharp stone cuts your foot. It is weeks before you walk without a limp.
Smoke from the evening fires hangs low over everyone.
Your hands know the work now. You no longer have to think about it.
You sit with someone who is dying and hold their hand until morning.
Children play at being grown-ups, copying every gesture of their parents.
A long dry spell. Everyone keeps looking at the sky.
Only a few people your age are still alive now.
One of the grandchildren walks exactly like you, and everyone laughs.
Frogs call all night from the wet ground.
At noon you wade into the river, and for a moment the heat is gone.
The river is higher than yesterday, brown and fast.
Mosquitoes whine all evening, and everyone sits close to the smoke.
A big wave takes someone’s whole catch. Everyone laughs except them.
You find a shell with a perfect spiral and keep it for years.
The tide goes out further than anyone can remember.
The rain stopped long ago, but water still drips from the leaves.
Something large moves in the trees, and everyone goes silent until it has passed.
Your breath smokes in the morning air. Everyone sleeps pressed together for warmth.
Fresh snow, and the tracks of an animal no one saw.
Dust gets into everything: the food, the water, your eyes.
At midday nothing moves. Even the birds go quiet.
Wind runs across the grass in waves, like water.
Far off, a thin column of smoke: someone else’s fire.
Weeding, weeding and more weeding. Your back aches for days.
Mice get into the stored food. Almost a basket’s worth is lost.
Rain drums on the roof all night, and you sleep better than you have all month.
You help the neighbours bring in their harvest. They will help you with yours.
A roof beam cracks and has to be replaced before the rains.
The noise of the town never quite stops, even at night.
You see someone very rich go by, and think about it for a long while.
A crowd gathers to watch two traders argue in the street.
A rumour runs through the streets in the morning and is forgotten by evening.
The same beggar sits at the same corner every day for years. Then one day they are gone.
Children chase each other through the alleys, shrieking.
The band stops to watch a herd pass far away, counting.
You learn which plants burn your mouth and which are safe.
A night without fire. The wood is all wet, and everyone shivers.
The band argues about which way to walk tomorrow.
Old hands, cracked from work, braid your hair.
Your family buries your small body under a tree behind the house, and leaves rice at the spirit shrine every evening.
One of your children falls ill and dies. The family buries the little body under a tree behind the house and feeds the house spirit to watch over it.

A tiger from the forest

Oc Eo lies in today’s southern Vietnam, about 25 km from the sea, with dug canals running inland to the capital. The French archaeologist Louis Malleret excavated it in the 1940s and found beads, seals, and gold medallions of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius from the mid-2nd century.

Many scholars think the town at Angkor Borei was Funan’s capital for much of its history, linked to Oc Eo by ancient canals. The Chinese called the kingdom Funan; what its own people called it is still uncertain.

U Thong is an ancient moated town whose links with India go back to at least the 4th century. Finds include 3rd-century Roman coins, Dvaravati silver medallions and many clay sealings. Some believe it was the Suvarnabhumi of the texts, but that cannot be proved.

Nakhon Pathom was the great centre of Dvaravati from the 6th to the 10th century; its moat enclosed some 300 hectares, later over 600. The Phra Pathom Chedi seen today was built over an older stupa in the reign of King Mongkut.

Si Thep has an inner town in a round moat and an outer town spreading east, about 4.7 km² in all. Its people worshipped Vishnu, Shiva and the Buddha. It was abandoned around the 13th or 14th century, and UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site on 19 September 2023.

Lavo, today’s Lopburi, was a Dvaravati centre from around the mid-7th century and came under Angkorian authority from about 1005. Chinese records show Lavo still sending its own envoys as late as the end of the 13th century.

Haripunjaya is today’s Lamphun. The chronicles say Queen Camadevi came from Lavo to rule it in the 7th century; archaeologists think the town more probably began around 750. Its people spoke Mon until King Mangrai took it in the late 13th century.
Chaiya sat on the short cut across the peninsula between the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea. Its art was close to that of Srivijaya in Sumatra and Java, and it followed Mahayana Buddhism.
Fa Daet Song Yang in Kalasin was a moated Dvaravati town where many stone boundary markers have been found, some carved with Jataka tales. Markers like these are found most of all in the northeast.
Yasovarman I founded Yasodharapura around 889 to 910 and dug the East Baray, 7.5 km long and 1.8 km wide. The city was Angkor’s capital for centuries; Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom were built here.

Prasat Phimai, one of the largest Khmer sanctuaries in Thailand, was a Mahayana Buddhist shrine built mostly between the late 11th and late 12th centuries. Inscriptions call the town Vimayapura; it stood at the end of the ancient road from Angkor.

Phanom Rung was built on the rim of an extinct volcano in phases from the 10th to the 13th century; nearby is Muang Tam, with its ring of ponds. The “Golden Boy” was found at Lahan Sai, in the same province.

Before it was a Thai capital, Sukhothai was an Angkorian outpost; the Ta Pha Daeng shrine and Wat Si Sawai were built in the Khmer manner. Around 1238 Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao and Pho Khun Pha Mueang took the town and founded the Phra Ruang dynasty.

Most people here grew rice, lived in houses raised on posts above the floods, kept buffaloes, pigs and chickens, fished the ponds and canals, and honoured house and village spirits alongside the gods from India and the Buddha.

Most work ran in families. Khmer inscriptions list many people given to serve sanctuaries: farmers, craftsmen, musicians and dancers. The finest work, bronze images and carved lintels, was made for gods and lords, not for ordinary people.
a family of officials and lords
a merchant family
temple servants, khñuṃ, bound to work for a sanctuary or a master

Khmer inscriptions sort people by rank, family and duty to a sanctuary. A large group were called khñuṃ, bound to work for a temple or a master. Some translate the word as slave, others as servant, since some khñuṃ held land and even servants of their own. Historians still argue over it.

This land spoke many languages: Mon in the Chao Phraya basin and Haripunjaya, Khmer to the east and in the southern northeast, Malay languages in the southern ports. Tai speakers arrived later, and all of them mixed into the people of the region today.
glass beads

fragrant resin and aromatic wood
An army from Angkor reaches Si Thep. The lord of the city must bow to the new king in the east.

An inscription records Rajendravarman II’s victory over the land of Ramanya in 946, and many historians think Si Thep came under Angkor at this time. Afterwards Khmer-style towers were built here for Shiva.
Officials from Angkor take up posts in Lavo. The new inscriptions are in Khmer, not Mon as before.

Lavo came under Angkorian authority from around 1005, in the reign of Suryavarman I, and inscriptions at Lopburi afterwards are in Khmer. Lopburi still has many Khmer-style towers, such as Phra Prang Sam Yot.
A family of strangers from the north settles by the stream. They call rice khao and water nam, and keep the ancestor spirits in the house.

Linguists estimate that south-western Tai speakers moved from the Guangxi region into Southeast Asia between the 8th and 10th centuries. They mixed with Mon, Khmer and other local people rather than “replacing” anyone. Khao, nam and phi are still Thai words today.
A war fleet from South India raids the peninsula ports, plundering goods and carrying people off.

Around 1025 the South Indian king Rajendra Chola sent a fleet against Srivijaya and the peninsula ports. His inscription at Thanjavur names the places attacked, including Madamalingam, thought to be Tambralinga. Srivijaya never fully recovered.
An army from the north that speaks Khmer reaches the capital. Funan’s king flees south; the new lords come from the land the Chinese call Chenla.

The New Book of Tang says Chenla subdued Funan at the start of the Zhenguan era (627–649) and that Funan’s king moved south. Historians today wonder whether Chenla was one kingdom at all, or a loose league of local lords.
Survived the day the Chams took Angkor
A Cham fleet sails up the Mekong, across the Great Lake, and falls on Yasodharapura without warning. The king is killed and the city sacked. Your family flees into the forest.

In June 1177 Jaya Indravarman IV of Champa attacked Angkor by water, killed the king and held the country for about four years, until the prince who became Jayavarman VII drove them out. The naval battle is still carved at the Bayon and Banteay Chmar.
The Tai Yuan army of King Mangrai besieges Haripunjaya. Before long the city falls and its Mon king flees.

King Mangrai took Haripunjaya in the late 13th century, in 1281 or 1292 depending on the source, and made it part of his Lan Na kingdom. Yet Haripunjaya’s temples and stupas were kept up, and the people of Lamphun still honour Queen Camadevi today.
You help load sacks of rice onto a boat and are paid in rice and salt.

Most people here bartered directly. Rice, cloth, salt, gold and silver measured value; Khmer inscriptions price land in cloth, gold, silver and buffaloes. Dvaravati-style silver medallions were few and may have served rites more than trade.
