the monks ordained in the Lankan way
A gold coin from the west

An Indian merchant at the canal market offers a strange gold coin for rice. It shows a bearded man in a crown of leaves. He says he got it from another trader, who got it from another, from a city far to the west.

Excavations at Oc Eo in the 1940s found gold medallions of the Roman emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius from the mid-2nd century. There is no evidence that Romans came here themselves; the coins probably passed through many merchants’ hands by way of India. Players of the Rome chapter will remember Pliny complaining of money draining east.
Trade rice for the coin
You pierce the coin and wear it on a cord, and no one in the village believes where it came from.
Ask how far that city is
He laughs and says it is twice as far as his ship has ever sailed, and twice that again.
The king’s great ships
King Fan Shiman orders dozens of great ships built, and the young men of the village are called up as rowers. People say he means to attack the coastal ports and make them pay tribute.

Chinese histories say Fan Shiman, who ruled Funan in the early 3rd century, built a great fleet and subdued some ten neighbouring states, until Funan controlled the sea trade between India and China. He died on one of his expeditions.
Go as a rower
In a fight at some port a spear grazes your ribs. You come home with a long scar.
You come home with cloth from towns you had never heard of, and stories that never end.
Hide in the forest until the fleet sails
You stay safe, but many in the village won’t speak to you for a long time.
The pale envoys from the north

Two envoys from the great land to the north arrive at court. They write everything down on bamboo strips: the town walls, the houses on stilts, the taxes in gold and pearls, and they raise their eyebrows every time they see a man without a shirt.

Around 245 to 250 the Chinese court of Wu sent Kang Tai and Zhu Ying to Funan. Their own reports are lost, but excerpts survive in later histories: walled towns, stilt houses, rice farming, taxes paid in gold, silver, pearls and perfumes, and books written in a script like India’s. The Chinese histories also say the envoys advised that men should wear a wrap, and the king ordered it. All of this is an outsider’s view.
Show off the household’s silver
One of the envoys writes something and nods. You will never know what he wrote.
Laugh at strangers wearing layers of clothes in the hot season
The envoy is drenched in sweat. You hand him a banana leaf to fan himself.
A king from India
Word comes that a Brahmin has been invited to take the throne. He orders the laws and rites changed to the Indian way, and officials begin to take Sanskrit names.

Chinese histories say that in the early 5th century a Brahmin named Kaundinya was invited to rule Funan and “changed all the laws to conform to the system of India”. Historians today stress that the spread of Indian culture in Southeast Asia was not a conquest: local rulers chose it, because it made them look grand and eased trade.
Learn Sanskrit like everyone else
The long words tie your tongue in knots, but you get a grand new name.
Keep honouring the ancestor spirits as before
The Brahmin rites happen at the palace; the ancestor spirits stay in the house. There is room for both.
The monks who sailed for China
Two monks from your town board a ship for China. People say a Chinese emperor loves the Buddha’s teaching and wants men who know Sanskrit to help translate the sutras.

In the early 6th century the Funan monks Sanghapala and Mandrasena went to the Liang court in China and translated several Mahayana sutras into Chinese. Funan did not only receive religion from India; it passed it on as well.
Give them alms before they sail
Years later a merchant says he saw them translating books in a great temple in China.
Ask to sail with them
You reach a northern port, fall gravely ill on the way, and come home with stories and a fever that keeps returning.
The ship’s master takes no one who cannot pay. You watch the sails vanish over the horizon.
The quiet harbour

Fewer foreign ships come each year. The merchants say the big ships no longer need to stop here; they can sail straight through the straits to the south. Many houses stand empty, and the canals are silting up.

Around the 6th century the sea routes changed: ships sailed straight through the Malacca and Sunda straits without stopping at Funan, while Chenla pressed down from the north. Oc Eo slowly emptied. A city made rich by trade can fade when the routes move.
Move to the inland capital
There people can still farm, even if the ships stop coming.
Stay in the old home
Yours becomes one of the few houses with smoke rising in the evening.
Silver medallions in a clay jar

At a rite at the temple, an official places small silver medallions in a clay jar and buries it under the base of the stupa. One side shows a water pot; the other has a line of letters. The monk says they mean “merit of the Lord of Dvaravati”.

Silver medallions inscribed in Sanskrit śrī-dvāravatī-īśvara-puṇya have been found at Nakhon Pathom, U Thong and elsewhere; they are key evidence for the very name “Dvaravati”. Many scholars see them as ritual deposits for merit rather than money for trade. In 1997 archaeologists dug some up inside a jar at Khok Chang Din.
Add your own silver ring to the jar
The monk smiles at you. You feel light, as if the ring carried your merit into the earth.
Memorise the shape of the letters
You draw the letters in the dirt for days, until the monk says they look right.
Envoys to China
The king sends envoys by ship to the Chinese court with gifts of ivory, fragrant wood and parrots. In town people say that this time the king has asked for something odd in return: fine horses.

Chinese records say Dvaravati sent several missions to the Tang court between 638 and 649; in 649 the ruler asked for fine horses, which some scholars find unusual for a southern sea state. The pilgrim Xuanzang heard of “Duoluobodi” on his travels in India, though he never came here himself.
Volunteer to sail with the embassy
You see a city so big that a whole day’s walk cannot cross it, and come home with a horse that was seasick the whole way.
Help catch parrots for the gifts
One parrot can say a rude word you taught it. You hope the Chinese emperor doesn’t understand Mon.
Vishnu in a tall mitre

At Si Thep the carvers are shaping sandstone into a standing Vishnu with a swaying hip and a tall, eight-sided mitre. The master says the whole figure must stand free, not just raised from a slab, and the stone arms must not snap when it is lifted upright.

Si Thep is famous for its mitred Vishnus and its Krishnas, among the earliest free-standing sculptures in Southeast Asia; scholars date two Krishna images to the late 6th and late 7th centuries. Several are in the Bangkok National Museum, and Si Thep became a World Heritage Site in 2023.
Ask to help polish the stone smooth
Your hands are raw from the sand, but the Vishnu is so smooth that the sunlight flows down its cheeks.
Ask who Vishnu is
The master tells how Vishnu came down as a fish, a boar, Rama and Krishna to save the world. You ask whether he ever came as a buffalo.
Stucco dwarfs on the stupa base

At the sanctuary in the centre of town, plasterers are modelling a row of pot-bellied dwarfs with their arms raised, holding up the base. Some have the heads of lions, elephants or monkeys, and no two make the same face.

Khao Khlang Nai is a Dvaravati Buddhist sanctuary at Si Thep dated to about the 6th–7th century. Its base is decorated with stucco dwarfs and animals, some still in place, and it is one of the monuments that made Si Thep a World Heritage Site.
Model one dwarf pulling a cheeky face
The master frowns, then laughs, and lets it stay.
Help mix the plaster
The plaster stays under your nails for days, but you can point to the part of the base that is yours.
The cowherd who lifted a mountain

A carver is shaping a youth with one arm raised above his head. The master says this is Krishna as a young cowherd, who lifted Mount Govardhana like an umbrella to shield people and cattle from a seven-day storm.

Two images of Krishna Govardhanadhara from Si Thep, dated to about the late 6th and late 7th centuries, are evidence of early Vishnu worship here. The Krishna story is a legend of the Hindu scriptures ✦.
Raise your arm like Krishna
Every child in the yard raises an arm too, and the carvers shoo you all away.
Ask whether rain like that could come here
The carver looks at the sky and says that if it did, we would have no Krishna, only palm-leaf roofs.
Letters like conch shells
At Si Thep stands a stone pillar carved with rows of curling marks like conch shells. Everyone says they are letters, but no one in town can read them, not even the monks or the Brahmins.
In 1998 a pillar inscribed in śaṅkhalipi, “shell script”, was found at Si Thep. Shell script is found mostly in India and very rarely outside it, and to this day no one has deciphered it.
Decide it must be a sacred spell
You touch the pillar every time you pass, just in case the unreadable words bring merit.
Copy the marks onto a palm leaf
You try to find which marks repeat, and the longer you look the more lost you get, like the scholars a thousand years later.
The Chinese monk’s clay seals

A Chinese monk is staying at Si Thep. He presses a stamp into little lumps of clay, a Buddha with Chinese characters, and gives them to those who come to make merit. No one in town can read the characters, but everyone wants one.

Clay sealings bearing the name of a Chinese monk, Wenxiang, dated to around the 8th century, have been found at Si Thep. Even this inland town had direct contact with China, not only the coastal ports.
Ask for a sealing to keep
You keep it in a wooden box beside your pillow until the day you die.
Ask the way to China
He points north-east and says that a year’s walk would still not get you there.
The wheel on the pillar
The carvers raise a great stone wheel onto a pillar before the stupa, with two deer resting beneath it. The monk explains that the wheel is the Buddha’s first teaching, at the deer park in India.

Stone wheels of the law with resting deer are a hallmark of Dvaravati, dating to around the 7th–8th centuries. They are found in unusual numbers in central Thailand. Players of the Ganges chapter will remember the first teaching at the deer park. Many of these wheels are in the museums at Phra Pathom Chedi and Bangkok.
Haul on the ropes to lift the wheel
The wheel settles upright. Everyone cheers, then sits down to get their breath back.
Ask why the deer are lying down
The monk says the deer were listening too. You try lying down to listen like a deer, and fall asleep.
The Vessantara boundary stone

A carver is cutting a great stone boundary marker to stand around the place where the monks hold their rites. It shows a prince handing his two children to an old Brahmin, and the villagers who gather to watch weep.

Many stone boundary markers in the northeast date from the Dvaravati period, roughly the 6th to 9th centuries, and some are carved with Jatakas such as the Vessantara. Old Mon inscriptions of this age are mostly short notes of donors and merit; one is dated 771. Players of the Ganges chapter will remember the Vessantara carved on the Sanchi gate.
Feed the carver until the work is done
The carver cuts your name small at the edge of the stone, in Mon.
Argue the prince should never have given his children
The monk smiles and says people have asked that since before the first stupa was built.
The Chinese monk learning Sanskrit

You sail as a deckhand to deliver goods at the Srivijaya capital on the island to the south. It is full of monasteries. A Chinese monk sits all day reciting Sanskrit words; he says he will study here first, then go on to India.

The Chinese monk Yijing set out in 671 and spent six months in Srivijaya learning Sanskrit before going on to India. He wrote that there were over a thousand monks there and advised Chinese monks to study in Srivijaya first. The name Srivijaya first appears in an inscription at Kedukan Bukit, dated 682.
Ask him to teach you one Sanskrit word
He teaches you karuṇā: compassion that wants to help. You take it home and use it.
Ask what is good about China
He thinks for a long time and says the tea at home. You have no idea what tea is.
The bodhisattva who looks down
The casters of Chaiya pour bronze into a bodhisattva’s torso, slim-waisted, leaning slightly, eyes cast down. The monk says he is Avalokiteshvara, who hears the cries of everyone who suffers.

The Avalokiteshvara of Chaiya, 63 cm tall and dating to about the 7th–8th century, is one of the finest works of Srivijaya art. It was found at Chaiya in 1905 and is now in the Bangkok National Museum.
Work the bellows until the bronze melts
Half your eyelashes are singed, but the bronze runs into the mould without a catch.
Tell the bodhisattva your troubles
He does not answer, but you go home and sleep soundly for the first time in months.
The Srivijaya king’s stone

Officials from a great city to the south raise an inscribed stone in a coastal town, praising the king of Srivijaya who built sanctuaries for the Buddha and the bodhisattvas. A man reads it aloud in Sanskrit.

The Wat Sema Mueang inscription at Nakhon Si Thammarat, one face dated 775, speaks of the king of Srivijaya and of the Shailendra dynasty of Java. Scholars still argue whether Srivijaya’s centre was at Palembang in Sumatra or, at times, at Chaiya.
Listen to the end, though you understand not a word
The Sanskrit sounds like a song, and you can hum along without knowing what it means.
Ask who gains from this stone
The official looks at you a little too long. You hurry home.
The rite on the mountain
Villagers are called to carry offerings up the mountain north of the Great Lake. A Brahmin performs a rite making a prince a “universal monarch”, no longer subject to Java.

The Sdok Kak Thom inscription from Sa Kaeo, written in 1052, says that in 802 Jayavarman II held a rite on Mount Mahendraparvata, Phnom Kulen, declaring himself free of “Java”. Historians take this year as the start of the Angkorian kingdom, though the record was written some 250 years after the event.
Carry the offerings all the way to the top
Your legs shake for three days, but you saw the Brahmin pour the sacred water on the king’s head.
Sneak a bite of the offering rice on the way
No one sees, but you fear the mountain spirits all year.
A sea dug by hand
The king orders a reservoir dug so large you cannot see the far bank. Every village must send people to dig and pile the dyke basket by basket. You dig all through the dry season.

Yasovarman I (r. 889–910) founded Yasodharapura and dug the East Baray, 7.5 km long and 1.8 km wide. Scholars still argue whether the barays watered rice fields or stood mainly for a sacred ocean. Today the East Baray is dry.
Dig until your village’s share is done
Your hands grow as hard as bark, and you know which heap of earth is your village’s.
Slip home at night
The overseer catches you, and you must dig twice as long.
No one comes after you, and the village pretends not to notice.
Three armies for Lavo
An army from Haripunjaya in the north marches on Lavo; Lavo’s king marches north to meet it, and then comes news that an army from Tambralinga in the south has seized Lavo while it was empty.

Chronicles say that between 925 and 927 Lavo and Haripunjaya fought, and King Sujita of Tambralinga seized Lavo, while Lavo’s king took Haripunjaya instead. This comes from chronicles written much later, so the details are uncertain ✦.
Hide the rice in the forest
Whoever wins, your family has rice until harvest.
Welcome the new lord
The new lord remembers your face, and remembers who didn’t come.
The oath at the royal palace

Officials from across the land are summoned to the royal palace. Each holds a flame and swears loyalty to the new king: whoever breaks the oath, may they fall to hell for as long as the sun and moon endure.

Suryavarman I took the throne after a war of succession and summoned some four thousand officials to swear loyalty at the palace. The oath and their names are carved on a palace gateway at Angkor Thom, dated 1011.
Swear in the loudest voice
Your name is written down. You are not sure that is a good thing.
Swear softly, so no one quite hears
The flame in your hand goes out before you finish. You hope the gods weren’t watching.
The sanctuary among the ponds

At the new sanctuary near Phanom Rung, workers dig four L-shaped ponds around the shrine, their rails ending in five-headed nagas rearing up. The Brahmin says this is the ocean that surrounds Mount Meru.

Prasat Muang Tam in Buriram was built around the late 10th to early 11th century for Shiva. It has ponds between its inner and outer walls, unusual among Khmer sanctuaries. Five-headed naga rails like these are ancestors of the naga stair-rails of Thai temples today.
Model a clay naga head to show the carvers
The carvers laugh that your naga looks like the neighbour’s dog, but they copy its fangs.
Help dig the ponds
A year later the ponds are full of lotus, and you are proud every time you pass.
The gilded bronze

The lord orders his foundry to cast a standing bronze almost as tall as a man: a god, or some say a king who will become a god when he dies. When it is done, the whole figure is gilded, and in the morning sun the foundry yard glows gold.

This is the figure Thais call the “Golden Boy”: gilded bronze about 129 cm tall, Khmer art of the 11th century. Villagers dug it up around 1974–75 while digging for wild yams near Prasat Ban Yang in Lahan Sai, Buriram; it was sold and smuggled abroad. The Metropolitan Museum in New York acquired it in 1988 and returned it to Thailand; it landed at Suvarnabhumi Airport on 20 May 2024. Scholars still debate whether it is Shiva or a king, perhaps Jayavarman VI.
Help pour the bronze into the mould
The bronze is so hot the air shimmers. When the mould is broken open, the whole figure is perfect, without a single flaw.
Follow the procession to the sanctuary
The whole town bows as the golden figure passes. You steal a glance up at its eyes.
The brick tower in the Khmer style
A lord who answers to Angkor orders a new tower in the old city for Shiva. Builders from the east bring the plans: tall, like an ear of corn. The old people grumble that the city is no longer itself.

Prang Si Thep and Prang Song Phi Nong were built in the 11th–12th centuries, when Si Thep came under Angkor’s influence and turned to the worship of Shiva. The same city holds Dvaravati and Khmer work, layered over centuries.
Help lay the bricks
One brick carries your fingerprint. No one knows but you.
Go and pray at the old stupa instead
The old stupa is quiet, with only old people and pigeons.
The sanctuary that faces Angkor
At Phimai the carvers are cutting a lintel of the Buddha meditating on the coils of a naga. The sanctuary faces south, straight down the road that runs all the way to Angkor.

Prasat Phimai, one of the largest Khmer sanctuaries in Thailand, was built for Mahayana Buddhism between the late 11th and 12th centuries. Unlike most Khmer sanctuaries, which face east, it faces south toward the road from Angkor. Inscriptions call the town Vimayapura, which became the name Phimai.
Bring rice to the carvers every day
The carvers repay you by teaching you to carve one lotus petal.
Walk the road to see where it ends
You walk for days, past rest houses along the way, and turn back before Angkor because your sandals give out.
Vishnu asleep above the door

The carvers lift a sandstone lintel above the east door of the hilltop sanctuary: Vishnu reclining on a serpent in the ocean, a lotus rising from his navel, and on it Brahma, who will create the world anew.

Phanom Rung’s reclining Vishnu lintel was stolen in the 1960s and displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago from 1967. After a long campaign it came back to Thailand on 10 November 1988 and was set back in place on 7 December. A few days each year the sun shines straight through all fifteen of the sanctuary’s doors.
Haul on the ropes to lift the lintel
The lintel drops neatly into place, and the master slaps your back so hard you cough.
Sit and watch the sunrise through the doors
The first light runs through every door to the inner chamber. The person beside you holds their breath.
Vishnu’s mountain of stone

Every dry season bamboo rafts float sandstone down from the mountains in the north. Thousands of carvers fill the long galleries with the king’s army on parade. One troop looks different, long-haired and in patterned skirts; the carvers label it “Syam Kuk”.

Angkor Wat was built in the reign of Suryavarman II (1113–c. 1150) for Vishnu, facing west. Its outer wall measures 1,024 by 802 metres, and most of its sandstone came from Phnom Kulen, about 40 km away. In the procession relief one troop is labelled “Syam Kuk”, which many read as Siamese, though scholars still debate exactly who they were. Today Angkor Wat stands on the flag of Cambodia.
Work the stone rafts
One raft overturns and its stone sinks. You swim ashore, and see the overseer note one stone lost, not one person.
Watch the carvers at work on the Syam Kuk troop
A carver says they come from the west and speak a language no one understands, and goes on carving.
The king’s house of healing

A new laterite building stands near the village, with a pond and a shrine to Bhaisajyaguru, the healing Buddha. Healers and servants live there and give medicine to everyone who is sick, whatever their station.

The Ta Prohm inscription of 1186 records that Jayavarman VII built 102 hospitals, and the Preah Khan inscription of 1191 lists 121 rest houses spaced about 15 km apart along the roads. The hospital inscriptions carry his vow that the people’s suffering was the king’s own suffering. Hospital ruins survive in Thailand, such as Prang Ku in Chaiyaphum. All of it also took the labour of huge numbers of people.
Take the sick from your village there
The healers give oil and a decoction. The neighbour’s child recovers, and his mother brings you a chicken.
Volunteer to help there
You learn to brew medicines and bind wounds, and hear the names of herbs you never knew.
The temple for the king’s mother
The king dedicates a new temple to his mother. An inscription lists thousands of villages that must send rice, honey, cloth and people to work, and yours is among them.

Ta Prohm was dedicated in 1186. Its inscription says some 80,000 people supplied and served it, among them 18 high priests and 615 dancers. Today great trees grow over its walls, familiar to visitors from the films.
Go to serve at the temple
You sweep the stone courts every morning and eat every day, but you don’t see home until harvest.
Send honey instead of labour
The bees sting you six times while you gather the combs, but you stay home with your family.
The Buddha the king sent

A procession from Angkor brings a new Buddha image to be installed in the town. People say the king has sent the same image to some twenty towns, so every one of them knows whose protection it is under.

The Preah Khan inscription of 1191 says Jayavarman VII sent Jayabuddhamahanatha images to 23 towns, among them Lavo, Ratchaburi, Kanchanaburi and Phetchaburi. It was an act of merit and a statement of power at the same time.
Bow to the new image
The face smiles faintly, as if it knows something you don’t.
Ask what happened to the old image
No one answers, but the old image moves to a small temple at the edge of town, and the old folk still go there to pray.
Faces on the towers

In the middle of the new walled city stands a great temple with dozens of towers, each carved with huge, gently smiling faces turned to the four directions. Wherever you stand, one of them is looking at you.

The Bayon was Jayavarman VII’s state temple at the heart of Angkor Thom. Scholars have read its giant faces as the bodhisattva Lokeshvara, the king himself, or both. Its outer walls show everyday life, markets, cockfights, and the naval battle against the Chams.
Look for yourself on the carvings
You find a woman selling fish who looks just like your aunt, and laugh until you cry.
Avoid the gaze of the faces
You can’t. One of them is always watching. Perhaps that is the point.
Two chiefs take the city
Two Tai chiefs, Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao and Pho Khun Pha Mueang, take Sukhothai from the governor Angkor sent. Pha Mueang hands the city to Bang Klang Hao, who takes the new name Si Inthrathit.

Sukhothai Inscription No. 2 tells of the city taken from a governor subject to Angkor; the usual date is around 1238. The name Si Inthrathit is Sanskrit, showing that the first Thai court took up Khmer customs even as it declared itself free.
Join the chiefs’ army
An arrow strikes your arm as you storm the gate, but you still see the new banner raised.
You are rewarded with a rice field.
Wait to see who wins
The new taxes are not so different from the old, but the language of the court has changed.
Monks from Lanka

A group of monks returns from being re-ordained in Lanka. They wear their robes a new way, chant Pali in a different accent, and say the Lankan ordination is purer. Some of the older monks are not pleased.

In the 12th and 13th centuries Theravada Buddhism of the Lankan lineage spread through Burma, Thailand and Cambodia until it became the faith of most people in the region. A Sukhothai inscription mentions a patriarch who came from Nakhon Si Thammarat. The Buddhism of Thai temples today descends from this line. Players of the Ganges chapter will remember the canon written down at Aluvihare in Lanka.
Go and hear the new monks chant
The accent is strange but beautiful. You bring your mother to listen on the next holy day.
Keep giving to the old monks
The old monks thank you, and say the Buddha never cared how a robe was worn.
The Buddhas chiselled away
The new king’s men climb scaffolds in the temple and chisel the Buddha images off the walls. Some are recut into hermits or Shiva lingas. The monks watch in silence.

After Jayavarman VII, Jayavarman VIII, a devotee of Shiva, had many Buddhist works at Angkor destroyed or altered; the chisel marks can still be seen at several temples. The court’s religion changed with the king, yet most ordinary people were turning to Theravada Buddhism all the same.
Hide a broken piece of a Buddha’s face
You bury it under the bodhi tree behind the house and never tell a soul.
Keep your head down and work
Kings change and gods change, but the rice field still needs ploughing.
The four-sided stone at Sukhothai

In the palm grove stands a new four-sided stone, written in a new kind of letters. Someone who can read it reads aloud: “in the water there are fish, in the fields there is rice”, and anyone with a grievance may ring the bell at the palace gate.

Sukhothai Inscription No. 1, dated 1292, speaks of King Ram Khamhaeng and says he devised the Thai script in 1283. Prince Mongkut found it in 1833. In 1987 a scholar suggested it might be a later fabrication, and a great debate followed; later tests led most scholars to accept it as at least partly genuine. UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World register in 2003. The Thai script grew out of Old Khmer letters.
Ask to be taught the new letters
The new letters set the vowels on the same line as the consonants. It is easier than you expected.
Go and try the bell at the palace gate
The guard looks at you wearily, but writes down your complaint about the neighbour moving your field boundary.
The Chinese man who wrote everything down
A Chinese man with an embassy stays nearly a year near the north gate of the city. He walks the market where women sell their goods on mats, asks the price of everything, and writes it down.

Zhou Daguan reached Angkor in August 1296 and stayed until July 1297. His Customs of Cambodia says trade was women’s work, that markets had no buildings, the sellers sat on mats and paid officials for their spot, that people had no tables or chairs, cooked rice in clay pots, and bathed in the river several times a day. It is the most detailed account of everyday life at Angkor to survive.
Sell him something at a higher price than usual
He pays, then writes something in his book. You wonder whether it’s about you.
Invite him to bathe in the river
He is mortified, but in the end he wades in, and says no one at home bathes three times a day.
Supper is rice with grilled fish, greens from the edge of the pond and a salty fish dip. Afterwards the grown-ups chew betel until their mouths are red.

Rice and fish have been the staples of this region for thousands of years, and betel-stained teeth turn up in prehistoric skeletons at several Southeast Asian sites. There were no chillies yet: they came from the Americas, and reached this region only after 1500.
Your house stands on tall posts. Underneath, the buffalo is tied, the pigs are kept and the tools are stored. When the floods come, the water runs under the house and leaves the sleepers above dry.

Chinese envoys of the 3rd century recorded that the people of Funan lived in raised houses, and the reliefs of the Bayon show them too. Houses on stilts are still the traditional rural home in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and many other countries.
The first rain of the year falls. The whole village goes out to plough with the buffaloes, then plants the seedlings clump by clump in the water held by the dykes.

Rice grown in bunded rain-fed fields underpinned the towns of this region: the surplus let lords collect dues, feed craftsmen and build sanctuaries. Many Khmer inscriptions are lists of rice fields given to temples.
The bead makers blow on the fire until the glass melts, draw it into long tubes, then cut it into tiny beads, red, yellow, blue and green. The children pocket the ones that fall on the floor.
Archaeologists call small drawn glass beads like these “Indo-Pacific” beads. They were made in quantity at sites such as Khlong Thom in Krabi and at Oc Eo, and traded as far as Africa and Korea.
In the dry season the grown-ups scrape up the earth crusted with white salt, wash it, and boil the brine in clay pots until only salt is left. One basket of salt buys several baskets of rice.
Beneath the Khorat plateau lie beds of rock salt. Salt making from salty earth in the Khorat basin goes back to prehistoric times and still goes on in places, such as Bo Phan Khan in Roi Et.
Someone in the house is sick. Grandmother boils turmeric and plai ginger, then ties white thread around the wrist, calling the wandering khwan back into the body.

Belief in the khwan, a life-soul that can wander off in fright or sickness, is found across many Southeast Asian cultures. The wrist-tying baci and su khwan ceremonies are still held in Thailand and Laos.
The villagers set rice, chicken and liquor at the little shrine under the big tree, feeding the spirit that guards the village before the planting.

Belief in local and household spirits here is older than Buddhism or Hinduism. When the Indian religions came, people did not give up their spirits; they kept both. The spirit houses in front of Thai homes today come from this blending.
Your turn to work for the sanctuary
It is your village’s turn to send workers to the sanctuary. You cut laterite into blocks while it is still soft, and leave them in the sun until they set hard as stone.

Laterite is iron-rich earth, easy to cut when damp and hard once dry. Khmer builders used it for foundations and walls, saving fine sandstone for the parts that mattered most. Inscriptions record villages owing labour and rice to the temples.
Work until your turn is done
You come home with aching shoulders, but no one will come asking until next year.
Send rice instead of labour
The granary is lighter, but you are home to help your children with the planting.
On the feast day at the sanctuary dozens of dancers perform for the god in the inner hall. Gongs and harps can be heard down in the village.
Khmer inscriptions record large numbers of dancers and musicians serving temples, and apsaras are carved all over Angkor Wat. The later court dances of Cambodia and Thailand drew on this tradition.
A big ship from India puts in to wait for the monsoon wind to turn. The sailors speak a tongue no one understands, but everyone understands the hand signs for haggling.

Ships crossing the Bay of Bengal had to wait on the monsoon: the south-west wind carried them east and the north-east wind carried them home. Merchants spent months in port, and ideas, religions and scripts travelled with the cargo.
Forest hunters come down to trade ivory, rhinoceros horn, blue kingfisher feathers and beeswax for rice and cloth. The merchants say people in China pay most of all for those feathers.

Zhou Daguan listed kingfisher feathers, ivory, rhinoceros horn and beeswax among the forest goods sent to China; the feathers were used in Chinese jewellery. Hunting for trade like this drove many of the region’s animals into steep decline.
There is a cockfight at the market. The men crowd around shouting, betting rice and cloth.
The Bayon’s wall reliefs include a cockfight with people betting, along with market scenes and cooking: rare evidence of everyday life.
So many fish come up the flooded fields that you can catch them by hand. The whole village salts and ferments them in jars to last the year.

Fish from the floods were a key source of protein, and Cambodia’s Great Lake is still among the richest freshwater fisheries in the world. Fermenting fish to keep it has a long history in this region.
In the morning the monks pass the house on their alms round. Mother has you put a little ball of rice in each bowl.

Both Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism came to this land. Wheels of the law, Buddha images and Pali inscriptions of the Dvaravati period show the Mon of the Chao Phraya basin were Buddhist from around the 6th–7th centuries.
The village Brahmin says never to touch anyone’s head and never to point your feet at a god. You forget so often you get your knuckles rapped.
Head high, feet low: these old manners are still strictly kept in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia today.
Wild elephants in the rice
A herd of wild elephants comes down at night to eat the rice. The whole village beats wooden clappers and lights fires to drive them off until dawn.

Elephants were both a farmer’s enemy and a king’s weapon; the reliefs of Angkor Wat and the Bayon show armies on elephant-back. Capturing and training wild elephants remained important work in this region into the 20th century.
Drum them away
The elephants go, but half the field is flattened.
Let them eat and stay up in the house
You hear chewing all night. In the morning no one is hurt.
At the temple fair someone plays a harp, someone the drums and someone a reed mouth-organ, and men and women sing back and forth late into the night.

Reliefs at Borobudur in Java and at Khmer sanctuaries show many instruments, harps and gongs among them. The khaen, a mouth-organ of bamboo pipes with metal reeds, is an old instrument of this region and still the heart of Isan and Lao music.
People are starting to use some of the newcomers’ Tai words, khao for rice, nam for water. At the market people mix three languages in one sentence.
Modern Thai holds a great many loanwords from Khmer, Mon, Pali and Sanskrit, especially in royal and religious language, while most everyday basic words are Tai.
A gong announces the lord’s order: one more share of rice for the new sanctuary. In the market people grumble under their breath.

The great sanctuaries and temples of this region took rice, labour and materials from many villages. Some historians think such burdens helped weaken Angkor in its later centuries, though this is still debated.
Your neighbours have a land dispute with another family. The official sends both men to sit in little towers in front of the palace, one in each. Whoever falls ill first is in the wrong.

Zhou Daguan recorded twelve small towers in front of the palace at Angkor: two litigants sat in them for several days, and the one who broke out in sores, coughs or fever was judged in the wrong. He also described trial by plunging a hand into hot oil.
Every morning the sugar palm behind the house fills its bamboo tube with sweet sap. You boil it down into brown cakes of sugar; some people ferment it into liquor.

The sugar palm gives sugar, timber and leaves; it is still common in Phetchaburi and Cambodia, and is Cambodia’s national tree. Most palm-leaf manuscripts, though, are written on the leaves of the talipot, another palm.
Your knees ache every time you climb the house ladder, so your children make you a new one with lower steps.
You sit under the house weaving baskets, telling the grandchildren that when you were small the forest came right up behind the fields.
The buffaloes lie wallowing in the mud.
A junglefowl crows at the forest edge before dawn.
The cicadas whine until your ears ring in the afternoon.
The smell of new rice drifts up from under the house.
Children jump into the canal from an old stump.
The sound of a gong comes from a distant sanctuary.
A macaque steals bananas from the veranda.
Mosquitoes whine round the net.
Egrets fly home over the paddies at dusk.
Grandmother lights incense at the spirit shrine.
dragged into the water by a crocodile
trampled by an elephant
a forest fever
shipwreck at sea
The rains come late and thin. The seedlings yellow and die, and people dig in the forest for wild yams and taro.
The flood rises higher than any year, up to the floorboards. Your family drives the buffaloes to a mound and lives up in the house for weeks.
A storm from the sea tears off roofs and sinks several boats in the harbour.
The ground shudders; the house posts sway, and pots fall and break.
the Roman coins of Oc Eo
The finds of Oc Eo are in museums in Vietnam, evidence that this land was tied into trade that reached as far as Rome.
the Funan monks in China
Some of their translations are still in the Chinese Buddhist canon.
the Dvaravati silver medallions
They are in several museums, such as the U Thong National Museum, and are the evidence for the very name “Dvaravati”.
the Vishnu of Si Thep
Several of Si Thep’s Vishnus and Krishnas are in the Bangkok National Museum.
Khao Khlang Nai
It stands in the Si Thep Historical Park, part of a World Heritage Site since 2023; some of the stucco dwarfs still hold up the base.
the shell-script pillar
No one has deciphered it yet.
Wenxiang’s clay sealings
They are evidence that Si Thep had direct contact with China.
the wheel of the law
Many such wheels are in the Phra Pathom Chedi and Bangkok National Museums.
the boundary stones
Many still stand at temples in the northeast; some are in museums.
It is in the Bangkok National Museum.
the East Baray
It has dried up, but its dykes still show in satellite images.
It has been restored, and lotus still grows in its ponds each year.
Dug up, sold and smuggled abroad in the 1970s, it spent over thirty years in a New York museum and came home in May 2024. It is now shown at the Bangkok National Museum.
It still stands in the Si Thep Historical Park.
It is the Phimai Historical Park, and a model for the prang towers of later Thai temples.
Stolen, it spent over twenty years in Chicago and was put back in place in 1988.
Angkor Wat
It was never wholly abandoned; monks still live there, and it is on the flag of Cambodia.
the hospitals
Ruins of several survive in the northeast, such as Prang Ku in Chaiyaphum.
Inscription No. 1
It is in the Bangkok National Museum and on UNESCO’s Memory of the World register; scholars still debate parts of it.
After you, the sea routes will shift, Funan will fade and be absorbed by Chenla, and to this day no one knows for certain what its people called it.
After you, the Mon will raise stupas and boundary stones across the Chao Phraya basin and the plateau, until Angkor’s power reaches west and Khmer towers rise beside the Mon stupas.
After you, the Chams will sack Angkor, and a new king will build hospitals and towers with smiling faces, while the burden passed on to the villages grows ever heavier.

After you, Sukhothai, Lan Na and Ayutthaya will rise. Ayutthaya will take Angkor in the 15th century and carry off Brahmins, craftsmen and Khmer court customs, and the people of this land will slowly come to call themselves Thai.

Before there was any “Thai”, this land had been home for a thousand years to people speaking Mon, Khmer, Malay and many other languages. The religions and scripts of India did not come with armies: local rulers chose them, blended them with the spirits already here, and made them their own. The Tai who came later did not replace anyone; they married, traded and learned from those already living here, so Thais today inherit the blood and culture of all of them. The relics of this age also raise the question of who owns the past: the Golden Boy and the Phanom Rung lintel were both stolen abroad, and came home because people demanded them back.

Traces of this age are all around Thailand today: a Thai script descended from Old Khmer, itself from the Pallava script of South India; royal vocabulary drawn from Khmer, Pali and Sanskrit; the prang of Wat Arun, descended from the Khmer sanctuary tower; Brahmin court rites such as the Royal Ploughing Ceremony; naga stair-rails; spirit houses; and town names ending in -buri and beginning with Nakhon, like Ayutthaya, named after Rama’s city of Ayodhya.
The golden bronze you saw that day will lie under the earth for nine hundred years, be dug up by people looking for wild yams, be sold to the far side of the world, and come home in 2024.
You lived as a monk.
You survived the day your homeland was taken or sacked.
Chinese histories record four ways the people of Funan dealt with their dead: giving them to the river, burning, burying, or leaving them for the birds. Relatives shaved their heads in mourning.

Zhou Daguan recorded that at Angkor the dead were usually wrapped in a mat and laid outside the city for vultures and dogs, though cremation was growing more common, especially in families of Chinese descent.

In this age the dead were usually cremated, following customs that came with the religions of India; in places bones and ashes were kept in clay jars and buried, while the older practice of burial with grave goods slowly faded.
Invite monks to chant
The Pali chanting drowns out the weeping, and everyone falls quiet.
Feed the ancestor spirits so they welcome the soul
Grandmother sets rice, chicken and liquor at the shrine and calls the dead one’s name three times.
Give to the temple in the name of the dead
The dead one’s name is spoken at the next holy day.
Monks and villagers cremate you and keep your relics in a little stupa beside the temple.
Your child lights the pyre while Brahmins chant in Sanskrit.
Your family shave their heads in mourning, then take your body by boat and give it to the river.
Your family wrap you in a mat and lay you outside the town, as Zhou Daguan saw it done.
The sanctuary you served sends some rice for your funeral. Only a few people come.
Your family cremate you at the burning ground outside the village and bury your bones in a clay jar beneath the bodhi tree.
People of Suvarnabhumi honoured house spirits, the Buddha and the Hindu gods all at once without feeling torn. What beliefs sit side by side like that in your own life?
Many relics of this age were stolen abroad, and some came home. Who do you think the past belongs to?
An imitation of the land in your age, not a real image.
Things you saw with your own eyes, and what became of them
The house-spirit shrine

Grandmother takes you to the little wooden shrine in front of the house and sets out a rice ball, bananas and flowers. The house spirit protects everyone under this roof, she says, as long as you don’t forget to feed it.
Belief in ancestor spirits and spirits of place came before the religions of India and never went away. Many Thai homes and buildings still have a spirit house today.
Bow to it every morning
You never forget, and always feel someone is watching over you.
Sneak a banana from the shrine
That night you have a bad dream, and never dare do it again.
The naga in the pond
The grown-ups forbid children to swim in the big pond behind the village: a naga lives below, and when angry it drags people down for good.

Nagas were sacred serpents ruling the waters. People here believed in them before the Indian religions came, and blended them with Buddhist and Hindu nagas; a Funan legend says the royal line descended from a naga princess ✦. Naga stair-rails are found at temples all over Thailand and Laos.
Do as the grown-ups say
You swim in the canal instead, and no one is dragged down.
Dive in to see for yourself
Weeds wrap around your leg and you nearly drown. You make it out, and believe in the naga for the rest of your life.
Down there is only mud and snakehead fish. You tell no one.
The family buffalo
Father puts you in charge of a buffalo: take it to graze, let it wallow, and have it home before dark. It is ten times your size but follows you like a dog.
Water buffaloes have been kept in Asia for thousands of years and were the main power for ploughing. Children herding buffaloes was a picture of rural life here until only a few decades ago.
Give it a name
You call its name across the field, and it turns every time.
Ride it all over the fields
You fall into the mud twice, and laugh both times.
The topknot cutting
You have worn a topknot since you were small. Today a Brahmin and monks come to cut it off, relatives tie threads round your wrists, and they say you are no longer a little child.

The Thai topknot-cutting rite has roots in Brahmin ritual: children kept a topknot until adolescence, and its cutting marked growing up. It was still performed at court and in some families into the 20th century.
Sit perfectly still through the rite
The aunts say you truly are grown up. You are proud all day.
Cry for your lost hair
Grandmother strokes your bare head and says the hair will grow back, but childhood won’t.
Letters from a monk
At the temple a monk teaches the children to write letters in a tray of sand, one by one, and to recite Pali verses no one understands but everyone can remember.
Temples were where boys in this region learned to read for centuries, until modern schools in the 19th century. The scripts of this age came from the Pallava script of South India.
Study hard
By the end of the year you can write your name and read two words on a boundary stone.
Slip away to catch fish
Many fish, few letters.
The groom moves to the bride’s house
The elders of both houses have agreed. After the wedding, the groom will move in with the bride’s parents and work their fields for some years before the couple builds a house of their own.

In many Southeast Asian societies newly-weds lived with the wife’s family, and women had a large role in trade and property; Zhou Daguan noticed that at Angkor it was women who traded. The custom of the groom living with the bride’s family still survives in rural Thailand and Laos.
Marry
Married, settling with the bride’s family
The whole village feasts for three days and ties so many threads on your wrists your arms turn white.
Ask to wait another year
The elders sigh, but agree.
Taking the robe
A monk at the temple asks whether you want to be ordained. If you do, you will shave your head, wear the robe, go for alms each morning, and keep away from women and wealth.

Monks lived in this land from the Dvaravati age or earlier. Evidence of Buddhist nuns in this region is very thin; women who wanted a religious life usually kept the precepts while living near a temple.
Be ordained
Ordained as a monk
You learn to walk slowly, hold the bowl steady, and chant until your legs go numb.
The monk smiles and says the temple will still be here.
A field for the sanctuary
You have enough to give a field to the sanctuary. The priest says your name will be carved in stone and the merit will follow you into your next life.

Many Khmer and Mon inscriptions record gifts of fields, gardens, cattle and people to sanctuaries, with the donors’ names and curses on anyone who would take the gift back. They are a main source on life in this age.
Give it
The carver cuts your name on a stone beside the door, followed by a long curse on anyone who takes the field back.
Keep the field for your children
Your children will have rice for years to come.
A debt you can’t pay

The harvest failed this year and you borrowed rice from a rich man in town to feed your family. Now he has come to collect, and says that if you can’t pay, you must serve him as his khñuṃ until the debt is cleared.

Bondage for debt had a long history here. Khmer inscriptions record khñuṃ being sold and donated, and the later laws of Ayutthaya dealt with debt slaves who could redeem themselves, until King Chulalongkorn abolished slavery in 1905.
Go into his service
Bound into service for debt
You work his fields instead of your own, and count the years left in your head.
Sell the buffalo to pay
The space under the house is empty. Next year you will dig your field by hand.
Sailing with a trading ship
A ship’s master needs more hands for a voyage to the southern ports, back when the wind turns. The pay is good, but the sea spares no one.

Sea trade linked the ports of this region with India, China and the islands. Several ships wrecked in this age have been found by underwater archaeologists, such as the Phanom Surin ship in Samut Sakhon, found in 2013 and dated to around the 8th century.
Sail
A storm at sea overturns the ship.
You come home with spices, beads, and tales of islands with fire-mountains.
You watch the sails vanish over the horizon.
A new colour of glass
A merchant from India sells orange-red beads that no one in town can make. The master wants to know what goes into them.

Bead makers here both borrowed techniques from India and developed their own. Indian carnelian and agate beads appear at Thai sites from before the Common Era, such as Ban Don Ta Phet and Khao Sam Kaeo.
Experiment until you get it
Three crucibles crack. The fourth gives a colour close enough. The master says nothing, but smiles.
Buy them and resell
A small profit, and no burnt fingers.
The wax model

For the first time the master lets you model a god in wax, then coat it with clay. When it is fired, the wax will melt away and bronze will be poured in its place. One mistake anywhere, and you start again.
The lost-wax method was used for this region’s bronze sculpture, including large works like the Golden Boy and the reclining Vishnu from the West Mebon at Angkor.
Model every detail slowly
It takes two months, but the figure comes out flawless.
Rush it for the feast day
The bronze doesn’t fill the mould and one arm is missing.
Just in time, and no one notices the flaw in the toe.
Your first lintel
The master lets you carve the lintel over the small north door, any story from the Ramayana or the Mahabharata, so long as the priest approves.

The lintels and pediments of Khmer sanctuaries carry stories from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the myths of Vishnu and Shiva. The Thai Ramayana, the Ramakien, is still a great classic and the story of the khon masked dance.
Carve Hanuman
The children point at your monkey every time they pass.
Carve the Churning of the Ocean
Gods and demons haul the naga from either end, and you give each one a different face.
An elephant panics in battle
In battle your elephant takes a spear in the leg. It screams and turns, charging back through your own troops.
War elephants were fearsome but hard to control. The reliefs of Angkor Wat and the Bayon show commanders on elephant-back, and elephant duels are still told of in later Thai chronicles.
Calm it with your voice
It doesn’t hear you.
It stops, ears trembling, and lets you lead it from the field.
Jump down
You break your leg but live. The elephant vanishes into the forest.
Dancing at the great feast
The dance teacher picks you to lead on the great feast day before the lord. You practise every hand gesture until your fingers bend backwards.

Backward-bent fingers and bent-knee stances appear both on carved apsaras and in the dance of Thailand and Cambodia today. The Royal Ballet of Cambodia is on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Dance exactly as taught
The teacher nods once, which from her is high praise.
Add a movement of your own
The teacher doesn’t speak to you for three days.
The lord laughs with delight, and next year everyone dances it.
The fever from the forest
The woodcutters come home with a shaking fever, chills and heat every few days. You have many herbs, but none that truly cures it.

Forest fever, malaria, was always a scourge of this region’s forests. Remedies that truly worked, quinine from the bark of the South American cinchona tree and artemisinin, which Chinese scientists extracted from sweet wormwood in the 1970s, came centuries later.
Nurse them through it
Two live, one does not. You remember every face.
Blow spells and tie the wrists
The fever breaks no sooner, but the sick are less afraid.
The Brahmin and the naga princess

The old people tell how long ago a Brahmin from a distant land sailed here. The queen of this land led her people out to fight him; his arrow pierced her boat, so she agreed to marry him, and the royal line of this land began with the two of them.

Chinese histories tell of Queen Liu Ye, “Willow Leaf”, marrying Hun Tian, a man from abroad; a 7th-century inscription tells a similar tale of the Brahmin Kaundinya marrying the naga princess Soma ✦. In Khmer tradition the story of Preah Thong and Neang Neak lives on in the wedding rite, where the groom holds the bride’s sash and follows her.
Believe the kings descend from a naga
You bow to the king in awe of both man and serpent.
Notice that in the story the queen was here first
The teller smiles and says a good story lets both sides own it.
Two monks from India

The monks tell that centuries ago King Ashoka sent two elders, Sona and Uttara, to Suvarnabhumi. A sea ogress was devouring every child born in the palace; the elders drove her away, and tens of thousands were ordained.

This story is in the Lankan chronicles, the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa ✦. No edict of Ashoka mentions Suvarnabhumi, and scholars do not know where it was: Thais place it at Nakhon Pathom or U Thong, Burmese at Thaton. Players of the Ganges chapter may have seen the two elders set out.
Believe it happened here
You are proud that your home was the first to hear the teaching.
Ask how anyone knows it was here
The monk is silent a long while, then says some stories mean something even without a place.
Phraya Kong and Phraya Phan

The tale goes that a soothsayer foretold Phraya Kong’s son would kill his father, so the baby was abandoned and raised by an old woman. Grown, he fought Phraya Kong without knowing who he was and killed him. When he learned the truth he built a great stupa to atone.

The tale of Phraya Kong and Phraya Phan is tied to Phra Pathom Chedi ✦. It is a folk tale written down much later, not history. Stories of a son fated to kill his father exist in many cultures, such as the Greek tale of Oedipus.
Pity Phraya Phan
You think he never chose his wrong, yet had to live with it all his life.
Wonder whether the soothsayer caused it all
Without the prophecy, the child would never have been abandoned. The listeners fall silent a moment.
Queen Camadevi

They say a princess of Lavo sailed up the Ping river for months, bringing monks, craftsmen and physicians, to rule a new city in the north that a hermit had built for her in the shape of a conch shell.

The Camadevivamsa and Jinakalamali, written in the 15th–16th centuries, say she came to rule Haripunjaya in the 7th century ✦; archaeologists think the city more likely began around 750. Whatever the truth, the people of Lamphun still honour her today.
Pay respect to her image
You ask that your daughter grow up as capable as she was.
Ask what a conch-shaped city looks like
An old man draws it in the dirt. It looks more like an egg than a shell.
The Leper King
The villagers whisper that a king of old had leprosy. Some say it was for his sins; others that a serpent spat venom on him in a fight.

At Angkor Thom stands a statue called the “Leper King”, because lichen and stains mottle its stone ✦. The legend is folklore; many scholars think the statue more likely shows Yama, god of death, than any king.
Pity the king
You think that even a king can fall ill like anyone else.
Doubt the rumour
Rumours about kings usually say more about the tellers than the king.
The naga spirit in the tower

People in town say that in the palace tower lives a nine-headed naga spirit in a woman’s form. The king must go up to her every night: if he misses one night, he will die; if she fails to come, disaster will fall on the land.

Zhou Daguan recorded this tale at the end of the 13th century as something local people told him about the Phimeanakas tower ✦. It shows once again how closely the naga was tied to royal power in this land.
Fear her
You never look at the tower after sunset again.
Think it is a tale to make the king seem sacred
You don’t say it aloud; people who say such things tend to find trouble.
Phra Ruang of the sacred word

People tell of Phra Ruang, a young man whose every word came true. An earth-diving Khmer came to seize him; when the Khmer surfaced from the ground, Phra Ruang told him to stay right there, and he turned to stone.

The Phra Ruang legend is folklore ✦, tied to Sukhothai breaking free of Angkor. Historians note that tales like this are told from the winners’ side; in fact the early Tai took script, religion and art from the Khmer.
Cheer for Phra Ruang
The children play Phra Ruang and the earth-diver, all wanting to be Phra Ruang.
Think of your Khmer neighbours
Your neighbours speak Khmer and have never once dived through the earth.
Lady Noppamas and the floating lantern

On the full moon of the twelfth month people set lights afloat on the water. Later, people will say that a royal consort named Noppamas was the first to make a lotus-shaped float for the king in this city.

The tale of Noppamas comes from a book most scholars date to the early Bangkok period ✦, not to Sukhothai. Floating lights has roots in many beliefs, and linking Loy Krathong to Sukhothai grew popular in the 20th century.
Float a light to ask the river’s pardon
The little light drifts downstream until you can see it no more.
Wish for love
Your light bumps into someone else’s from the other bank, and you both laugh.

The land in your age
The granary is lighter, but you are home in time for the planting.
Your knees ache every time you climb the house ladder, so the neighbours help make you a new one with lower steps.
You sit under the house weaving baskets, telling the village children that when you were small the forest came right up behind the fields.
Your kin light the pyre while Brahmins chant in Sanskrit.
Keep the field for the family
Your family will have rice for years to come.
You ask that the girls of your house grow up as capable as she was.

On the ninth morning you see smoke rising from the shore. People have lived on these islands for tens of thousands of years. They speak a language you do not know, but they trade taro for your pottery.

Fully Denisovan. Today your kind’s DNA survives at about 3–5% in Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, and Tibetans carry a gene from you that helps at high altitude.
About 100% sapiens, though some researchers see traces that ancestors inside Africa also mixed with an archaic human no one has found a fossil of yet (debated).

Almost 100% sapiens. Some sapiens have already left Africa and may meet Neanderthals now and then, but the big mixing that still survives in people today comes later, about 50,000–44,000 years ago.

Sapiens leaving Africa are meeting and having children with Neanderthals now; the main mixing happened about 50,000–44,000 years ago. People of your time may carry more Neanderthal DNA than people today.

Counting about 28 years per generation. When sapiens left Africa is debated; most estimates say about 50,000–70,000 years ago.

You are among the earliest sapiens outside Africa, like the people of Skhul and Qafzeh caves, Israel, about 120,000–90,000 years ago. Early groups like this may have left few descendants among people today.

A friend’s wedding
The friend you grew up with is getting married and asks you to help prepare, though your own work is piling up this year.
Help with everything
You barely sleep for three days, but your friend holds you tight on the day.
Help as much as you can
The wedding goes well and so does your own work.
Parents growing old
One of your parents walks more slowly each year, forgets the neighbours’ names, and wakes at night calling for people long dead.
Take them in and care for them
The house feels smaller, but the children hear stories no one else tells any more.
Let a sibling care for them
You visit every month and feel guilty every time you leave.
Someone better than you
Someone your age does the same work you do, and everyone talks only about them. Tonight someone dares you to compete in front of everyone.
Accept the challenge
You win by a hair, and they are the first to shake your hand.
You lose, but learn more than in a year of practice.
Ask to learn from them
They are surprised, then teach you without holding back.
Something lost
The one thing you have from your mother is lost on the way home. Rain is coming.
Go back and search
You find it in the mud by the path, just before the rain.
You search until dark and soaked, and never find it.
You tell yourself that what she really gave you was never in the thing.
A stranger at dusk
A tired stranger asks for a place to sleep for one night. He speaks with an odd accent and will not say where he is from.
Give him a bed and food
In the morning he is gone, with the household’s spare food.
He tells of faraway lands late into the night, and leaves a small gift when he goes.
Turn him away
It rains hard that night. You sleep badly.
A child’s fever
Your youngest has burned with fever for three days and will eat nothing. You have to decide what to do.
Sit up with them all night
The fever breaks at dawn and the child sleeps in your arms.
Fetch a healer
The healer gives a bitter drink and says to give plenty of water. Two days later the child is running about.
Your children quarrel
Two of your children quarrel bitterly over something you never thought mattered. Both come to you to decide.
Side with the one who is right
One smiles. The other does not speak to you for months.
Make them settle it themselves
Both are cross with you, but they make peace in the end.
A youngster who wants to learn
A child from nearby has watched you work every day. Today they finally come and ask if they can learn.
Teach them
Ten years later the child is better than you, and tells everyone who taught them.
Tell them to wait until they are older
The child never comes back. You see them learning from someone else.
The night of the quarrel
You and your partner quarrel bitterly about the old thing that never ends. Tonight one of you has to speak first.
Apologise first
Your partner is quiet a long time, then takes your hand.
Wait for them to speak
The whole house is silent for three days.
A friend asks to borrow
A neighbour who once helped you asks to borrow your spare food until the harvest. But no one has much this year.
Lend it
After the harvest, they return more than they borrowed.
They cannot pay it back, but in your own bad year they are the first to help.
Refuse politely

The Crocodile (the Big Dipper)

Thais call this the Crocodile, Europeans the Big Dipper or Plough, the Chinese the Northern Ladle. Its last two stars point toward the north celestial pole, though which star sits near the pole changes over the ages, because Earth’s axis wobbles once every 26,000 years.
Orion (the Thai Plough)

The three stars in a row across Orion, with the line hanging below them, are what Thais call the Plough, for their shape. The red star at the shoulder is Betelgeuse, a red supergiant that will one day explode as a supernova.
The Pleiades (Matariki)
Nearly every culture has a name for the Pleiades. Māori call it Matariki, and its pre-dawn rising marks the new year. Thais tell of a mother hen and her chicks who leapt into the fire after her ✦
Scorpius (Maui’s fishhook)

Hawaiians saw this as the fishhook of the demigod Maui, who used it to haul islands from the sea. Polynesian navigators memorised where hundreds of stars rise and set on the horizon and used them as a compass ✦
The Southern Cross

The Southern Cross is best seen from the southern hemisphere, though from Thailand it can be seen low in the south. Its long arm points toward the south celestial pole. Many Aboriginal peoples see an Emu in the Sky traced by dark lanes in the Milky Way; its head is the dark patch beside the Cross.
